SeaDream docks in Old San Juan, the oldest part of the city. Parts of this historic port city are still surrounded by stone walls dating back to the 1500’s. Narrow cobblestone streets, small shops, and points of interest like Cathedral of San Juan Bautista make this charming city a great place to stroll. An 11-square-mile island off the northeast coast of Puerto Rico, Culebra is also home to the small adjacent uninhabited islands of Culebrita and Cayo Norte to the east and Luis Peña to the west. Culebra’s breathtaking beautiful Flamenco Beach regularly appears on lists of the “World’s Best Beaches.” Following your day exploring Culebra, that evening we invite you to Vieques Island, where you can kayak in bioluminescent waters filled with glittering sea organisms.

Esperanza is a charming “barrio” located on the south side of the island-municipality of Vieques, Puerto Rico. It is known for El Malecon, which means “The Strip,” the fishing tradition, the fight against the US Navy, and Esperanza Beach, one of the only locations in Isla de Vieques with restaurants and restrooms close by. Children enjoy jumping off the pier at the beach, and for those who enjoy good food and local entertainment without the hustle and bustle of a busy nightlife, El Malecon in Esperanza is the place to be. The island’s name, Vieques, is said to mean “small island” in Taino, and its nickname is Isla Nena, meaning “Little Girl Island”. Puerto Rico’s little sister island - Vieques measures 55 square feet with under 10,000 inhabitants. Along with Culebra and other various small islands, the archipelago makes up the Spanish Virgin Islands, or “Passage Islands.” Vieques was also referred to as “Crab Island” by the British. English and Spanish are both recognized as official languages of the area. As with the other Puerto Rican islands, pre-Columbian history is limited in clarity. Archaeologists believe Vieques was home to Native Americans who migrated from the American continent between 3000 and 2000 BCE. A fragmented human skeleton named “El Hombre de Puerto Ferro” was discovered northwest of the popular Bioluminescent Bay, estimated to be from 1900 BCE. Best known as the people in later centuries of Puerto Rico, the Taino culture was comprised of groups from Venezuela, Cuba, and Hispaniola, who migrated in waves up to 1000 AD. The Taino flourished until Europeans discovered Vieques in the 15th century - often credited to Christopher Columbus. Vieques became the center of the Taino rebellion against Spain, which ultimately ended in the Taino downfall. Despite this, Spain did not colonize for many centuries and Vieques, along with Culebra, became a sanctuary for pirates and outlaws. The French, Danish, Scottish, and English all attempted to secure Vieques but failed - Spain permanently settled by 1811. When the Spanish-American War concluded in 1898, Spain turned the Puerto Rican islands over to the United States, which by the 1940’s (post-WWII) served as a firing range for the Navy. Up until 2003, a multitude of protests continued for decades, pressuring the United Stated Navy enough to withdraw from the islands. Vieques is now a National Wildlife Refuge and growing tourist destination. Because of the lack of human interference, most of the areas previously closed off to civilians by the Navy feature over 40 gorgeous beaches, and many natural ecotourism locations for exploration. Blue Beach features an excellent place for snorkeling, Bioluminescent Bay has quickly become a popular spot for its notorious glowing dinoflagellates, and the island is also known for free-roaming 'feral paso fino 'horses.

Two-thirds of St. John Island has been dedicated as a national park and is the most virgin of the U.S. Virgin Islands. It is blessed with many beautiful beaches and bays, fine anchorages and verdant hills. Enjoy the day with snorkeling trip to Trunk Bay with its underwater guided trail, or join our kayaking land adventure. Ask your Club Director for a guided hike to Caneel Bay stopping at beautiful Honeymoon Beach for a quiet swim. Rental Cars are available should you want to explore on your own or you could borrow a SeaDream Mountain Bike for independent exploration. From Cruz Bay, we offer several Yachting Land Adventures specially created for SeaDream guests, including an exclusive experience at the Lovango Resort & Beach Club, tucked away on a private island just off St. John.

Marigot is the main town and capital on the French side of Saint Martin. The city of Marigot is perhaps the most French in spirit of all the cities in the Caribbean. Colonial houses stand beside cafés and bistros, pastry shops and luxury boutiques, and in many ways, it looks just like any of the French market towns you might expect to find in Europe. At the southern end of town by the harbor is Marina Port la Royale. This area includes elegant stores with the latest in European designer fashion and fine jewelry, all duty and tax-free. The entire city is only four streets wide, so it is very easy to get around. Marigot was named the capital during the reign of King Louis XVI, who built Fort St. Louis on a hill near Marigot Bay. Today, that building is the most important in the city. SeaDream anchors off Marigot and offers several yachting land adventures as well as the possibility to play with the toys at the marina.

Taino Beach on Grand Bahama provides a final anchorage before the yacht returns to Palm Beach, where this deep exploration of the Bahamas comes full circle.

Just off the shores of Andros, this reef teems with exotic fish species. Home to five national parks, more than 180 blue holes, biodiverse ecosystems, and a network of trails that cross the Central Andros National Park, Andros Island is perfect for nature lovers and hikers alike.

Great Exuma Island is known for its brilliant, sparkling waters—waters so clear and aquamarine-blue they are visible from space. voyages.title: Best of the Leeward Islands
voyages.overview: Overview Ports Staterooms Land Adventures Testimonials A rare extended stay in St. Barths and sun-drenched shores across Anguilla, the British Virgin Islands, and Jost van Dyke shape this roundtrip journey from San Juan. Sandy Ground introduces Anguilla at its most relaxed, where calm turquoise water and an unhurried shoreline invite time to settle in before the voyage continues to St. Barths for a rare two-night stay in Gustavia, where two full days allow the island's refined character to reveal itself fully, from boutique-lined streets by day to softly lit terraces long after the harbor has quieted. North Sound follows with Virgin Gorda's expansive natural harbor, where calm protected waters and striking surroundings provide a peaceful contrast before the voyage continues. White Bay in Jost van Dyke provides a sun-drenched finale, where our Champagne & Caviar Splash® sees chilled Champagne and caviar served on the sand, followed by a leisurely beachside barbecue and long, unhurried hours in the water before returning to San Juan.

voyages.title: Bountiful Bahamas
voyages.overview: Overview Ports Staterooms Land Adventures Testimonials From cave systems to swimming pigs, this roundtrip journey from Palm Beach uncovers a side of the Bahamas that goes well beyond its postcard reputation. Andros sets the tone early as the Bahamas' largest and least explored island, its vast cave systems, expansive barrier reef, and dense pine forest interior creating a landscape of quiet drama unlike the rest of the archipelago. The sheltered harbor of Emerald Bay on Great Exuma offers a gentler introduction to the out islands before Gordon's Beach, a secluded stretch of shore where the silence of the surrounding sea feels complete. San Salvador carries a quiet historical weight as the first landfall of Columbus in the New World, its modest size and unspoiled coastline understating its significance. The voyage returns to the Exumas at Staniel Cay, where swimming pigs, crystalline tidal pools, and a colorful waterfront yacht club have made it one of the region's most celebrated stops, before Taino Beach on Grand Bahama provides one final anchorage ahead of the return to Palm Beach.

days.note: The combination of urban centers and cultural treasures make Palm Beach the perfect getaway. Enter the heart of Africa by visiting the Panther Ridge Conservation Center or get up close and personal with manatees at the Manatee Lagoon. If you’re more into urban sightseeing, visit CityPlace for the top-rated dining, entertainment, and shopping experiences.

The untouched island of Andros is nestled in the Bahamas, defined by its archipelago of tiny cays and inlets connected by mangrove estuaries and underwater caves, making it accessible only to boats and small sailing vessels. A favorite of scuba divers and snorkelers, Barrier Reef and Tongue of the Sea is the third largest barrier reef in the world, stretching more than 140 miles long. Just off the shores of Andros, this reef teems with exotic fish species. Home to five national parks, more than 180 blue holes, biodiverse ecosystems, and a network of trails that cross the Central Andros National Park, Andros Island is perfect for nature lovers and hikers alike.

Great Exuma Island is known for its brilliant, sparkling waters—waters so clear and aquamarine-blue they are visible from space. The island is home to powdery white-sand beaches, deserted cays, luxury villas, and exclusive resorts. Paddleboard, snorkel, or swim, and see more of the island from the sandy shores of Emerald Bay.

Colorful coral reefs and serene beaches make Long Island a haven for snorkeling, diving, and bone fishing. Relax under the shade of pine trees at Gordon’s Beach, the southernmost white-sand beach on the island. Explore Long Island from the perspective two of its most impressive natural wonders, the Hamilton Caves, dripping with stalactites, and Dean’s Blue Hole, the world’s second-deepest saltwater blue hole, surrounded by limestone bluffs. The island is also home to St. Mary the Virgin Anglican Church, a now-abandoned stone church constructed by the Spanish in the 1600s and reputed to be the oldest in the Bahamas.

One of the smallest inhabited islands in the Bahamas, San Salvador boasts sparkling inland lakes, reef-filled sea waters, miles of secluded white-sand beaches, and dive sites teeming with sea life. A stone cross on the shores of Long Bay mark Columbus’s landfall on the island; offshore, an underwater monument designates where La Pinta dropped anchor. Pace yourself to the rhythm of the island with a leisurely swim or bike ride around the bay.

As part of the Exuma Cays, Staniel Cay is a magical corner of the Bahamas. Located south of Nassau, this island is an unsung paradise. Visit the infamous swimming pigs at Pig Beach, where numerous pigs race over to get your attention right above crystal-clear waters. Dive or snorkel in the sun-kissed beaches of Exumas and enjoy local dining options for an exclusive look at the Bahamas’ culture and cuisine.

voyages.title: Spanish Caribbean & the Leewards
voyages.overview: Overview Ports Staterooms Land Adventures Testimonials The islands between San Juan and the British Virgin Islands reveal themselves one by one on this roundtrip journey, each anchorage adding something distinct to the voyage. Cruz Bay opens with the protected forests and reef-lined shores of St. John, where the national park's trails wind down to some of the most unspoiled beaches in the Virgin Islands. Philipsburg follows with the lively energy of St. Maarten's Dutch waterfront before continuing to St. Barths for an overnight stay in Gustavia, where boutique-lined streets and softly lit terraces settle into a more intimate rhythm once the harbor quiets for the evening. Charlestown reveals Nevis at its most unhurried, where Georgian architecture, a black-sand shoreline, and a lush volcanic interior reward those who venture beyond the pier. Two days in Virgin Gorda follow, from Spanish Town to North Sound, where the island's sheltered bays and striking natural harbor invite time to linger at a slower pace. Our signature Champagne & Caviar Splash® brings the voyage to a memorable close on the soft sands of White Bay in Jost van Dyke, where chilled champagne and caviar give way to an elegant beachside barbecue and long, unhurried hours in the water before returning to San Juan.

Two-thirds of St. John Island has been dedicated as a national park and is the most virgin of the U.S. Virgin Islands. It is blessed with many beautiful beaches and bays, fine anchorages and verdant hills. Enjoy the day with snorkeling trip to Trunk Bay with its underwater guided trail, or join our kayaking land adventure. Ask your Club Director for a guided hike to Caneel Bay stopping at beautiful Honeymoon Beach for a quiet swim. Rental Cars are available should you want to explore on your own or you could borrow a SeaDream Mountain Bike for independent exploration. From Cruz Bay, we offer several Yachting Land Adventures specially created for SeaDream guests, including an exclusive experience at the Lovango Resort & Beach Club, tucked away on a private island just off St. John.

Philipsburg is the main town on the Dutch side of St. Maarten. The town is situated on a narrow stretch of land between Great Bay and the Great Salt Pond. Philipsburg was founded in 1763 by John Philips, a Scottish captain in the Dutch navy. The settlement soon became a center for international trade. The main shopping district is located on Front Street and is in the heart of the city. Many consider Philipsburg to be the best shopping opportunity in the Caribbean. Depending on the traffic, SeaDream has the option to anchor or dock alongside. One of the highlight activities may be to participate in the America’s Cup 12 Metre Regatta.

Nevis is one of our favorite islands, and we encourage you to explore Nevis beyond the small town to make the most of your visit! We offer several excellent and varied options for you to do so and still leave you with plenty of time on your own for the beach. Less commercial and laidback than its large neighbor St. Kitts, Nevis, at first glimpse, offers a stunning approach with dramatic views of the potentially active volcanic Nevis Peak (3,232 feet/985 meters). Your SeaDream tender will bring you within a few steps of the small town center. Charlestown does not offer too many sightseeing or shopping opportunities though the house where American statesman Alexander Hamilton was born is only a short walk away along the waterfront (now the Museum of Nevis History). To enjoy Nevis to its full potential, we recommend that you divide your day into Morning, Lunch/Afternoon and Evening activities. Morning - Start your day by exploring the island, above or under water, on one of our fun optional Land Adventures. They are all enjoyable & exciting, and you will also support the local community. The Four Seasons Resort still offers incredible golf options as well as beautiful beach and dining facilities. Another option for lunch is the L'Escale French Caribbean-style bistro, just down the road near the Oualie Pier. Evening - For a romantic sunset with cocktails and a snack or dinner, we like to take the short drive to see Gillian, the owner of the charming Bananas Restaurant, which offers lovely views surrounded by lush tropical gardens. Of course, there is also Sunshine's Beach Bar & Grill, home of the famous "Killer Bee" Caribbean rum drink. We hope that the above recommendations allow you to plan your special day on Nevis. Now, all you have to do is to decide which of the optional morning activities to join.

voyages.title: Transatlantic Spring Voyage I
voyages.overview: Overview Ports Staterooms Land Adventures Testimonials Palm Beach gives way to open ocean on this eastward crossing, where days at sea set the pace for a voyage defined by stillness, indulgence, and the particular freedom that only deep-water travel affords. Unhurried days invite time to stargaze beneath endless horizons, rediscover favorite pastimes, and indulge in world-class cuisine crafted by SeaDream's chefs. Soothe body and mind at the only Thai-certified spa at sea, then embrace the spirit of leisure with yoga and Tai Chi sessions held beneath wide open skies. Throughout the crossing, an engaging enrichment program led by distinguished guests and experts offers insights, stories, and inspiration from around the world. As the voyage nears its end, Funchal appears on the horizon, a lush Portuguese island where terraced vineyards, mountain vistas, and a charming harbor welcome the yacht to land. The crossing concludes in Lisbon, one of Europe's most captivating capitals, where pastel-colored facades, ancient hilltop viewpoints, and a vibrant waterfront provide a fitting arrival after days spent at sea.

days.note: The combination of urban centers and cultural treasures make Palm Beach the perfect getaway. Enter the heart of Africa by visiting the Panther Ridge Conservation Center or get up close and personal with manatees at the Manatee Lagoon. If you’re more into urban sightseeing, visit CityPlace for the top-rated dining, entertainment, and shopping experiences.

Funchal is considered the sixth largest city in Portugal, and for five centuries, it has also been the capital of Portugal’s Autonomous Region of Madeira. Funchal has a rich history, which quickly became a populated settlement due to its productive soils, and its surrounding valley having a natural amphitheater shape that provided shelter for early settlers. SeaDream guests may visit top tourist locations such as Blandy's Wine Lodge, the open Worker's Market and the Sacred Art Museum. You will find a passenger gondola lift (Funchal Passenger Ropeway), that transports people from the lower section of the city to the suburb of Monte. Aside from the city of Funchal, there are more tourist destinations such as Santana, beaches of Porto Santo Island, Porto Moniz, Ribiera Brava, Curral das Freiras, and the UNESCO Natural site, the Laurisilva forest.

Portugal's bustling capital showcases a rich contrast of the historical and modern. Situated near the Tagus River and endlessly sunny, Lisbon embodies a unique beauty and an internationally acclaimed architectural singularity. Its charming hilly neighborhoods boast winding, cobblestone streets and pastel-painted homes and cafés, which happily serve up the city’s signature cuisine, including pastel de nata and custard tarts. From imposing Sao Jorge Castle, the view encompasses the city’s Old Town, Tagus Estuary, and suspension bridge; the National Azulejo Museum displays 5 centuries of decorative ceramic tiles.

voyages.title: Best of the Virgin Isles & St. Barths
voyages.overview: Overview Ports Staterooms Land Adventures Testimonials A journey of volcanic peaks, hidden anchorages, and sun-filled days unfolds from San Juan, where each stop reveals a more unexpected side of the Caribbean. Cruz Bay offers a first glimpse of St. John's protected national park lands, where forested trails wind down to pristine reef-lined shores, before arriving in Jost van Dyke for our signature Champagne & Caviar Splash®, where chilled champagne is served alongside caviar on the soft sands of White Bay. Continue to Virgin Gorda for two days from Spanish Town to North Sound, where the island's sheltered natural harbor and striking landscapes reward those who linger. In Saba, lush hills rise steeply from the sea, its near-carless roads and untouched interior offering one of the Caribbean's most singular island experiences. Continue to St. Barths for a rare two-night stay in Gustavia, where boutique-lined streets and softly lit terraces invite unhurried exploration long after the day boats have gone, with an additional day to discover the island's most secluded shores and waterfront cafés at a leisurely pace before returning to San Juan.

Narrow cobblestone streets, small shops, and points of interest like Cathedral of San Juan Bautista make this charming city a great place to stroll. Guests sailing into or departing from San Juan will enjoy views of Castillo de San Felipe del Morro, a mid- 1700’s Spanish fortress. San Juan Luiz Munoz Marin Airport is approximately a 30-minute drive to the port in Old San Juan. Currency in Puerto Rico is USD.

Two-thirds of St. John Island has been dedicated as a national park and is the most virgin of the U.S. Virgin Islands. It is blessed with many beautiful beaches and bays, fine anchorages and verdant hills. Enjoy the day with snorkeling trip to Trunk Bay with its underwater guided trail, or join our kayaking land adventure. Ask your Club Director for a guided hike to Caneel Bay stopping at beautiful Honeymoon Beach for a quiet swim. Rental Cars are available should you want to explore on your own or you could borrow a SeaDream Mountain Bike for independent exploration. From Cruz Bay, we offer several Yachting Land Adventures specially created for SeaDream guests, including an exclusive experience at the Lovango Resort & Beach Club, tucked away on a private island just off St. John.

The BVI’s barefoot island and home of the "Painkiller" drink. Population depends on the month – typically 250-300. This is another SeaDream destination where you may be served Champagne & Caviar Splash® followed by a beach barbecue lunch. A hike is always offered to guests to visit the famous Foxy’s Bar at Great Harbour (hopefully, the boutique is open) or you can stroll a few meters down the beach to the Soggy Dollar Bar. Snorkeling equipment is provided as well as some of our water toys!

Nearly every publication written about Virgin Gorda will emphasize the need to visit “The Baths” – don’t miss it! SeaDream generally arrives early and anchors off Spanish Town to give guests an early start to view The Baths before all of the tourists arrive from the neighboring Islands. You may also consider excellent scuba diving options or an opportunity to swim with the dolphins. SeaDream navigates scenically up the coast and arrives in North Sound to anchor just off the Bitter End Yacht Club. Here we offer watersports, land adventures, hiking options with the crew and tenders to the Bitter End! Depending on the voyage, you may also visit Prickly Pear Island for another signature Champagne & Caviar Splash® option with an incredible setting.

This Caribbean paradise is a special municipality of the Netherlands. Due to this fact, Saba is actually the location of the tallest, or highest point/elevation of the Netherlands, even though it is a few thousand miles away from its European homeland. With an estimated local population of just over 2,000 people, Saba is now primarily supported by tourism, and is known for a concentration on “eco-tourism”. This includes diving, hiking, and climbing its mountainous terrain. The island is so small that there is only 1 main road, and its airport is well-known for having one of the shortest commercial runways in the world. The island’s intimate size, picturesque Red rooftops and lush vegetation make it a perfect port to call on during your special Caribbean yachting vacation.

Perhaps our most treasured destination in the Caribbean! This small island belonging to the French West Indies has so much to offer our SeaDream guests. Incredible shopping only steps away from the pier. Incredible beaches, resorts, restaurants and activities both day and night. SeaDream has created various land adventures for you to discover the island from sea or land. Ask one of the officers to take you on a hike or bike ride around the island. Another great activity here is to simply relax and watch all of the incredible yachts arriving and departing just off your SeaDream yacht.

voyages.title: Yachting the Leeward Islands
voyages.overview: Overview Ports Staterooms Land Adventures Testimonials A roundtrip journey from San Juan that moves through sun-drenched shores and refined island stops, where each port reveals a different expression of the northeastern Caribbean. In St. John, Cruz Bay offers access to pristine beaches and protected national park lands before continuing to Philipsburg, where St. Maarten's colorful Dutch waterfront and lively harbor provide a vibrant contrast. Continue to St. Barths for an overnight stay in Gustavia, where boutique-lined streets and softly lit terraces take on a more intimate character once the harbor settles into evening. Spend two days in Virgin Gorda, from Spanish Town to North Sound, where the island's sheltered bays and expansive natural harbor reward those who linger. Your journey concludes in Jost van Dyke, where the signature Champagne & Caviar Splash® unfolds on the soft sands of White Bay, with chilled champagne and caviar served at the water's edge, followed by an elegant beachside barbecue and long, unhurried hours in the sun before returning to San Juan.

Philipsburg is the main town on the Dutch side of St. Maarten. The town is situated on a narrow stretch of land between Great Bay and the Great Salt Pond. Philipsburg was founded in 1763 by John Philips, a Scottish captain in the Dutch navy. The settlement soon became a center for international trade. The main shopping district is located on Front Street and is in the heart of the city. Many consider Philipsburg to be the best shopping opportunity in the Caribbean. Depending on the traffic, SeaDream has the option to anchor or dock alongside. One of the highlight activities may be to participate in the America’s Cup 12 Metre Regatta.

voyages.title: Transatlantic Spring Voyage II
voyages.overview: Overview Ports Staterooms Land Adventures Testimonials San Juan slips beneath the horizon as this eastward crossing begins, where days at sea set a rhythm of stillness, indulgence, and the particular freedom that only open ocean travel affords. Unhurried days invite time to stargaze beneath endless horizons, rediscover favorite pastimes, and indulge in world-class cuisine crafted by SeaDream's chefs. Soothe body and mind at the only Thai-certified spa at sea, then embrace the spirit of leisure with yoga and Tai Chi sessions held beneath wide open skies. Throughout the crossing, an engaging enrichment program led by distinguished guests and experts offers insights, stories, and inspiration from around the world. As the voyage nears its end, Funchal appears on the horizon, a lush Portuguese island where terraced vineyards, mountain vistas, and a charming harbor welcome the yacht to land after days spent at sea. The crossing concludes in Malaga, where sun-drenched plazas, Moorish architecture, and a vibrant waterfront provide a fitting arrival on the southern coast of Spain.

Funchal is considered the sixth largest city in Portugal, and for five centuries, it has also been the capital of Portugal’s Autonomous Region of Madeira. Funchal has a rich history, which quickly became a populated settlement due to its productive soils, and its surrounding valley having a natural amphitheater shape that provided shelter for early settlers. SeaDream guests may visit top tourist locations such as Blandy's Wine Lodge, the open Worker's Market and the Sacred Art Museum. You will find a passenger gondola lift (Funchal Passenger Ropeway), that transports people from the lower section of the city to the suburb of Monte. Aside from the city of Funchal, there are more tourist destinations such as Santana, beaches of Porto Santo Island, Porto Moniz, Ribiera Brava, Curral das Freiras, and the UNESCO Natural site, the Laurisilva forest.

Malaga, together with adjacent towns and municipalities such as Rincon de la Victoria, Torremolinos, Benalmadena, Fuengirola, Alhaurin de la Torre, Mijas, and Marbella, forms the Malaga Metropolitan area. The important cultural infrastructure and the rich artistic heritage have culminated in the nomination of Malaga as a candidate for the 2016 European Capital of Culture. The internationally acclaimed painter and sculptor Pablo Picasso and actor Antonio Banderas were both born in Malaga. SeaDream calls to Malaga both as an embarkation point as well as a typical port of call. Kindly check on the land adventures tab to see all of the activities and options. Should you need embarkation information, it’s also available there.

voyages.title: The Inaugural Journey: Japan, the Ryukyus & Korea
voyages.overview: Overview Ports Suites Land Adventures Testimonials Twenty-seven nights. Two nations. One maiden voyage. SeaDream III sails for the first time through Japan on this inaugural voyage from Hong Kong to Tokyo, anchored by a three-night Christening and Showcase, the ship's official naming ceremony and a rare occasion to be aboard for it. Along the way, an overnight at Ishigaki reveals water so clear it seems lit from below, with Kabira Bay's coral and manta rays just offshore. Yakushima's overnight call opens a UNESCO-listed forest of thousand-year cedars wrapped in moss and cloud, and Amami Oshima, also UNESCO listed, invites a kayak through mangrove tunnels in search of the island's rare black rabbit. The Christening itself takes center stage in Tokyo, three full nights of celebration marking SeaDream III's arrival in Japan. The journey turns toward Korea next, an overnight in Busan bringing Gamcheon's painted hillside and the stalls of Jagalchi fish market. After twenty-seven nights, the voyage concludes in Japan with SeaDream III back in Tokyo, a fitting close to this historic first sailing.

days.note: Glide into Victoria Harbour as the skyline ignites, SeaDream III overnights here, so the Symphony of Lights becomes your private nightcap from the deck. Ride the century-old Star Ferry at dusk, hunt Michelin-starred dim sum in Central, then take the funicular up Victoria Peak for the whole city laid out at your feet. A dawn sampan through Aberdeen's floating village and a fitting with a bespoke tailor round out a port that rewards those who stay long past sundown.

Manta rays glide through cleaning stations off this Yaeyama Islands hub in numbers rare anywhere else in Japan, drawing serious divers from around the world for a close encounter most only see on film. Kabira Bay's black-pearl farms and impossibly clear, multi-hued water are protected from swimming to preserve the ecozystem, best seen instead from a glass-bottom boat. Egrets and herons crowd the island's mangrove river mouths, while a beach-forward, laid-back pace sets the whole island apart from mainland Japan. Japan's tropics, genuinely.

Shuri Castle, seat of the independent Ryukyu Kingdom for four centuries before Japan absorbed it, reflects a distinct culture, cuisine and even language found nowhere else in the country. Okinawa's population includes some of the highest concentrations of centenarians on earth, a longevity researchers have studied for decades and one that shows up in the local diet of bitter melon, purple sweet potato and slow-cooked pork. Coral reefs ring the main island for some of Japan's best snorkeling, while herons and egrets work the coastal wetlands. Japan, but genuinely, distinctly its own place.

A UNESCO World Heritage subtropical rainforest covers much of this Ryukyu island, home to the Amami rabbit, a primitive, dark-furred species found nowhere else on earth and often called a living fossil. Traditional Oshima tsumugi silk, dyed in mud using a centuries-old technique, is still handwoven here and prized as one of Japan's finest textiles. Mangrove kayaking and some of the clearest coral reef in the Ryukyus round out an island that feels closer to Okinawa's wild heart than to mainland Japan.

Ancient cedar trees, some more than a thousand years old and one estimated at over seven thousand, stand deep in this UNESCO World Heritage rainforest, the same moss-draped landscape that inspired Hayao Miyazaki's Princess Mononoke. Waterfalls tumble through forest so wet it rains, locals joke, thirty-five days a month, while onsen dot the coastline for a soak after the hike. One of the most primeval landscapes anywhere in Japan.

This small fishing port turned its most famous native son into a genuine tourist industry, a mile-long shopping street lined with more than a hundred bronze statues of yokai spirits from manga artist Shigeru Mizuki's work, best known abroad as GeGeGe no Kitaro. The port itself lands some of the best crab and seafood on the Sea of Japan coast, sold fresh at the harbor market each morning. A quirky, characterful stop unlike anywhere else in Japan.

South Korea's second city wraps around Haeundae Beach's high-rise skyline on one side and the pastel, cliffside houses of Gamcheon Culture Village on the other, a former slum reinvented as an open-air art installation. Jagalchi Fish Market, the country's largest, sells the day's catch straight off the boats each morning, while a serious spa and jjimjilbang bathhouse culture offers a properly restorative afternoon between meals. A round of golf and some of Korea's best beaches round out a genuinely dynamic port city.

Fukuoka's old merchant quarter still runs on the yatai food stalls that line its rivers each evening, plastic-sheet tents serving the tonkotsu pork-bone ramen this city is credited with inventing. Canal City's shopping and entertainment complex shows the region's more modern face, while Dazaifu's shrine and gardens, a short train ride out, offer a quieter, more contemplative counterpoint. A strong onsen and wellness culture in the surrounding hills, and clean beaches along Hakata Bay, round out one of Kyushu's most food-obsessed cities.

The Peace Memorial Park and its skeletal Atomic Bomb Dome confront the city's 1945 history directly and without flinching, one of the most moving sites in Japan and a genuine pilgrimage regardless of nationality. A short ferry ride away, Miyajima's floating torii gate at Itsukushima Shrine appears to hover on the tide, one of Japan's most photographed views, while the city's own okonomiyaki, layered rather than mixed, has passionate defenders against Osaka's version. A dining scene, a wellness culture and a genuinely uplifting sense of renewal round out a city defined by resilience.

Japan's most celebrated beef takes its name from this handsome port city, and a proper teppanyaki dinner here remains one of the country's great culinary rites of passage. Arima Onsen, one of Japan's oldest hot spring resorts, lies a short cable-car ride up Mount Rokko, while a small but historic winery tradition, among Japan's earliest, still operates in the surrounding hills. A round of golf, a walk through the Nunobiki herb gardens, and beaches along the bay round out one of Japan's most cosmopolitan port cities.

Kokichi Mikimoto perfected the cultured pearl on the small island in this bay that now bears his name, and Mikimoto Pearl Island still stages daily demonstrations by the ama, traditional female free-divers who have harvested these waters for centuries. Ise Grand Shrine, the most sacred site in Shinto and rebuilt in an identical form every twenty years for over a millennium, lies a short drive away. A properly restorative onsen soak and fresh Ise-ebi lobster round out one of Japan's most historically resonant coastal regions.

The view of Mount Fuji from this small port made Hokusai's woodblock prints famous well beyond Japan, and it remains one of the classic vantage points on the mountain today, framed by the same pine-lined shore. Tagonoura shirasu, tiny whitebait landed fresh each morning, is the local delicacy worth seeking out. A round of golf, an onsen soak and Fuji looming over every one of them round out a small port built entirely around one extraordinary view.

Few cities anywhere absorb this much contrast this comfortably, centuries-old shrines sit blocks from neon-lit crossings, and a Michelin-starred meal is as easy to find as a standing-room ramen counter. Meiji Shrine's forested grounds, planted from donated trees a century ago, shelter a genuine variety of birdlife within sight of Shibuya's skyscrapers, while Tsukiji Outer Market still trades on the same seafood obsession that built the city's reputation. A round of golf at a classic Kanto course and an evening in Ginza or Shinjuku round out a capital that never quite runs out of new things to show you.

voyages.title: The Southern Islands & the Silk Road to Hong Kong
voyages.overview: Overview Ports Suites Land Adventures Testimonials The journey begins the moment you embark in Tokyo, its restless energy still with you as the yacht eases out toward open water. Shimizu offers an early view of Fuji-san rising above the bay before an overnight stay in Osaka, time enough for Dotonbori's neon food stalls, the golden turrets of Osaka Castle, and a private day reaching Kyoto's temples and Nara's bowing deer. Takamatsu's Ritsurin Garden, three centuries in the shaping, gives way to a ferry crossing for Naoshima's buried art galleries, while Shimonoseki sits on the hard-running Kanmon Strait, known for its Karato market fugu and the Meiji cannon batteries still facing the water. Jeju, a volcanic island unlike the Korean mainland, holds Hallasan's cloud-wrapped slopes and the haenyeo, free-diving grandmothers who still work these waters. Nagasaki opens two centuries of sealed history through Dejima and Glover Garden, with the ghost city of Gunkanjima reachable offshore, and Fukue's Goto Islands hide UNESCO-listed churches built in secret above turquoise bays. The final stretch threads Yakushima's ancient cedar forest, Amami Oshima's mangrove wilderness, the Ryukyu Kingdom's Shuri Castle in Naha, and Ishigaki's coral shallows, before a day at sea brings the voyage to a close in Hong Kong, its skyline rising to greet you. This voyage offers guests the exclusive opportunity to extend their stay for SeaDream III's Hong Kong Showcase on October 2, 2029, a rare chance to conclude with a celebration of the yacht in her first year of sailing.

Few views of Mount Fuji rival the one from Miho no Matsubara, a UNESCO-listed pine grove sweeping along the shore here that has been painted and photographed for centuries as the classic frame for the mountain beyond. Shimizu's port lands more tuna than almost anywhere else in Japan, and a proper sushi lunch here is close to essential. A round of golf with Fuji on the horizon and a soak in one of the region's onsen round out one of Japan's most scenically blessed ports.

Dotonbori's canal-side neon and giant mechanical crab signs set the tone for a city that treats eating out as a genuine pastime, kuidaore, or eating until you drop, is practically the local motto. Osaka Castle's gleaming keep anchors a park thick with cherry trees each spring, while a nascent wine scene has emerged in the surrounding Kansai hills. Herons and cormorants work the Yodo River's banks, and a nightlife scene as loud and warm as the food rounds out Japan's unofficial culinary capital.

Ritsurin Garden, laid out over more than a century for the local feudal lords, is widely considered one of Japan's finest, its ponds and pine-covered hills designed to reveal a new view at every turn. Takamatsu claims the title of Japan's udon capital, and a proper sanuki udon lunch, chewy noodles in a simple, clear broth, is close to compulsory. Naoshima, the contemporary art island a short ferry ride away, has turned an old industrial backwater into one of the art world's more unlikely pilgrimage sites. A quietly excellent gateway to Shikoku.

Fugu, the potentially lethal pufferfish prepared only by licensed chefs, is close to a civic obsession in this strait-side city, credited with popularizing the delicacy across Japan. The Kanmon Straits just offshore were the site of the decisive 1185 naval battle that ended the Genpei War, a history still commemorated in local festivals. A relaxed onsen culture and a strong seafood dining scene round out a city defined by the narrow, fast-moving water at its front door.

A volcanic island UNESCO has recognized three times over, for its lava tubes, its crater cone and its overall natural heritage, Jeju rises to Hallasan, South Korea's tallest peak, at its center. The haenyeo, free-diving women who have harvested the seafloor here by breath alone for centuries, are themselves recognized by UNESCO as a living cultural tradition. Championship golf courses take advantage of the island's volcanic terrain and mild climate, while black-sand beaches and citrus groves round out Korea's most popular island escape.

One of the only Japanese ports open to the outside world during the country's two centuries of self-imposed isolation, Nagasaki absorbed Dutch, Portuguese and Chinese influence long before the rest of Japan did, still visible in Glover Garden's colonial mansions and the historic Chinatown quarter. The Peace Park tells the city's 1945 history with the same unflinching honesty as Hiroshima's, a profoundly important stop regardless of nationality. Champon noodles, a genuine fusion dish born of that same cosmopolitan history, and a strong onsen tradition round out one of Japan's most historically layered cities.

The largest of the Goto Islands hides one of Japan's most poignant hidden histories, Christian communities driven underground by centuries of persecution built secret churches and shrines across these islands, several now recognized by UNESCO. Fukue Castle's moat once opened directly onto the sea, an unusual design for a Japanese fortress. Quiet, uncrowded beaches and clear water round out an island still well-off Japan's main tourist circuit.

Ancient cedar trees, some more than a thousand years old and one estimated at over seven thousand, stand deep in this UNESCO World Heritage rainforest, the same moss-draped landscape that inspired Hayao Miyazaki's Princess Mononoke. Waterfalls tumble through forest so wet it rains, locals joke, thirty-five days a month, while onsen dot the coastline for a soak after the hike. One of the most primeval landscapes anywhere in Japan.

A UNESCO World Heritage subtropical rainforest covers much of this Ryukyu island, home to the Amami rabbit, a primitive, dark-furred species found nowhere else on earth and often called a living fossil. Traditional Oshima tsumugi silk, dyed in mud using a centuries-old technique, is still handwoven here and prized as one of Japan's finest textiles. Mangrove kayaking and some of the clearest coral reef in the Ryukyus round out an island that feels closer to Okinawa's wild heart than to mainland Japan.

Shuri Castle, seat of the independent Ryukyu Kingdom for four centuries before Japan absorbed it, reflects a distinct culture, cuisine and even language found nowhere else in the country. Okinawa's population includes some of the highest concentrations of centenarians on earth, a longevity researchers have studied for decades and one that shows up in the local diet of bitter melon, purple sweet potato and slow-cooked pork. Coral reefs ring the main island for some of Japan's best snorkeling, while herons and egrets work the coastal wetlands. Japan, but genuinely, distinctly its own place.

Manta rays glide through cleaning stations off this Yaeyama Islands hub in numbers rare anywhere else in Japan, drawing serious divers from around the world for a close encounter most only see on film. Kabira Bay's black-pearl farms and impossibly clear, multi-hued water are protected from swimming to preserve the ecozystem, best seen instead from a glass-bottom boat. Egrets and herons crowd the island's mangrove river mouths, while a beach-forward, laid-back pace sets the whole island apart from mainland Japan. Japan's tropics, genuinely.

Glide into Victoria Harbour as the skyline ignites, SeaDream III overnights here, so the Symphony of Lights becomes your private nightcap from the deck. Ride the century-old Star Ferry at dusk, hunt Michelin-starred dim sum in Central, then take the funicular up Victoria Peak for the whole city laid out at your feet. A dawn sampan through Aberdeen's floating village and a fitting with a bespoke tailor round out a port that rewards those who stay long past sundown.

voyages.title: Grand Indochina
voyages.overview: Overview Ports Suites Land Adventures Testimonials Depart Hong Kong, its skyline still aglow from an overnight alongside for the Symphony of Lights and dim sum in Central, for Vietnam's Ha Long Bay, anchored among thousands of UNESCO-listed limestone karsts in a stillness few large ships find, kayaking into hidden grottoes as mist curls off the water. Da Nang opens onto Hoi An's UNESCO-listed old town, its lantern-lit lanes and silk tailors able to finish a suit within the day, then Nha Trang, where the swim platform drops into warm reefs beside amber-lit, centuries-old Cham towers. Con Dao, a marine park almost no other ship calls at, offers nesting turtles and colonial history, before Ho Chi Minh City's Cu Chi tunnels and a Mekong Delta sampan, and Phu Quoc, where snorkelling the An Thoi islets pairs with fish sauce aged a year in oak. Cambodia's Sihanoukville and Thailand's Ko Kut, its waterfall and tender-only coves unspoiled, lead to an overnight in Bangkok for the Grand Palace, Wat Pho, and a long-tail boat through the khlongs, with Ko Samui's Big Buddha and Bophut's teak shophouses along the way. In Malaysia, the Perhentian Islands, shallow bays alive with turtles and reef sharks and too fine for any large ship, and jungled, reef-fringed Tioman precede a final call at Singapore, where SeaDream ties up on Marina Bay for chilli crab beneath the glittering Supertrees. This voyage offers guests the exclusive opportunity to begin with SeaDream III's Hong Kong Showcase on October 2, 2029 or conclude with the Singapore Showcase on October 24, 2029, a rare chance to mark either end of the journey with a celebration of the yacht in her first year of sailing.

Few ships can linger where SeaDream III can, anchored among Ha Long Bay's thousands of emerald limestone pinnacles, far from the day-tripper flotillas. Kayak into hidden grottoes and floating fishing hamlets, then watch mist curl around the karsts at first light with a coffee in hand. Overnight at anchor and this UNESCO seascape belongs, for a few golden hours, almost entirely to you.

Come ashore at Da Nang for two of Vietnam's great treasures. By day, explore the cave-temples of the Marble Mountains and the jungle-clad Cham ruins of My Son; by dusk, wander Hoi An's lantern-lit lanes, where silk tailors stitch to measure and street kitchens perfume the day air. Order a bespoke suit at breakfast and collect it before you sail. China Beach's golden sands await in between.

Vietnam's premier beach resort city pairs a long, café-lined seafront with Cham Ponagar, a cluster of red-brick towers built by the Champa civilization over a thousand years ago and still an active place of worship. Mud baths and mineral hot springs at nearby Thap Ba have turned the city into a genuine wellness destination in its own right, while a round of golf takes advantage of the coast's reliable sunshine. A polished, well-organized introduction to Vietnam's central coast.

Once one of Southeast Asia's most notorious prison colonies, the French and later South Vietnamese governments held political prisoners here in conditions the preserved cells and infamous tiger cages still convey with real weight. That grim history sits in stark contrast to the archipelago's present, some of Vietnam's cleanest water and best-protected reef, and beaches where hawksbill and green turtles still nest undisturbed. Seabird colonies crowd the outer islands. A profound history alongside a genuine natural sanctuary.

Saigon assaults the senses in the best possible way, a million motorbikes, French-colonial grandeur and rooftop bars above the fray. Trace the country's history at the Cu Chi tunnels and the War Remnants Museum, then barter through Ben Thanh Market for silk and spice. Cross into the Mekong Delta by sampan for floating markets and fruit orchards. Return to SeaDream's calm at day, the day's intensity happily left ashore.

Vietnam's largest island has grown quickly into a genuine beach destination, its long white-sand coastline and clear water a world away from the country's bustling mainland cities. Phu Quoc's fish sauce, fermented in wooden barrels using methods unchanged for generations, is considered the finest in Vietnam and makes for a genuinely interesting distillery-style visit. Night markets sell the day's seafood catch grilled to order along the harbor front. Vietnam's tropical island escape, still finding its final shape.

Thailand's fourth-largest island has stayed deliberately undeveloped, no high-rise resorts, no real nightlife, just clear water, powder sand and a rainforest interior threaded with waterfalls. Fishing villages built on stilts over the water at Bang Bao give a sense of a slower, more traditional Gulf of Thailand life. About as close to an untouched Thai island as still exists within reach of the mainland.

From the port, plunge into the glorious chaos of the City of Angels. Watch dawn gild the spires of the Grand Palace and the reclining Buddha at Wat Pho, then trade tuk-tuks for a long-tail boat threading the khlongs to the flower and fruit markets. As day falls, a rooftop bar and a private table of som tam, massaman and mango sticky rice await. With overnights aboard, you savor Bangkok's cool evenings without ever repacking a bag.

Samui greets you with swaying coconut palms and the serene golden gaze of the Big Buddha above the bay. Laze on Chaweng's fine sand, browse Fisherman's Village at Bophut where old teak shophouses become a Friday walking street, or retreat to a hilltop spa for a traditional Thai massage. Chase jungle waterfalls inland, then let SeaDream's marina turn the warm Gulf into your private playground.

A quiet Malaysian state capital on the South China Sea coast, known well beyond its size for a genuinely excellent Malay dining scene, keropok lekor fish crackers and nasi dagang among the local specialties worth seeking out at the waterfront night market. Traditional boat-building and songket weaving, a hand-loomed brocade once reserved for royalty, are still practiced in workshops around town. A relaxed, unhurried introduction to Malaysia's less-visited east coast.

Trade the tide for the tropics of the Malaysian capital. Ride to the summit of the Petronas Twin Towers, climb the rainbow steps into the Hindu shrines of Batu Caves, and lose an afternoon among the spice-scented lanes and street food of Chinatown and Little India. Docking at Port Klang puts this glittering metropolis within easy reach, while SeaDream's intimacy means no queues, no coach convoys, just you and a curated run at Malaysia's greatest hits.

The Perhentians are the stuff of desert-island dreams, turquoise water so clear the coral reads like a map, and no room for large ships in their shallow bays. SeaDream III anchors offshore, and the marina delivers you straight to reefs alive with green turtles, blacktip reef sharks and clouds of parrotfish. Laze on flour-soft sand between swims. This is barefoot Malaysia at its most pristine and private.

Legend says a dragon settled here and became an island, and Tioman's jungled twin peaks and cascading waterfalls do feel mythic. Once a film-set stand- in for Bali Hai, it remains gloriously undeveloped: anchor offshore, snorkel coral gardens from the swim platform, trek the rainforest to hidden falls, or spot monitor lizards and hornbills ashore. Duty-free and delightfully remote, it is best reached exactly as you do, by yacht. Swimming and non-motorised craft only here; motorised watersports need the local authority's permission.

Begin where garden-city futurism meets old Asia. Marvel at the Supertrees and misty Cloud Forest of Gardens by the Bay, raise a Singapore Sling at Raffles' Long Bar, then graze Maxwell hawker center for chili crab and Hainanese chicken rice. Being small, SeaDream berths right on Marina Bay, a front-row seat the mega-ships can't claim, and an overnight lets you watch the light show glitter long after the crowds have thinned.

voyages.title: Volcanoes, Temples & Secret Isles
voyages.overview: Overview Ports Suites Land Adventures Testimonials Depart Singapore, docked right on Marina Bay itself for chilli crab at Maxwell and the glow of the Supertrees, then set out for the scattered, barely charted Anambas Islands, electric-blue lagoons few large ships reach. Bangka's rose-gold granite boulders and Belitung's UNESCO-recognized seascape of giant granite formations and a historic lighthouse follow, before the smoking cone of Anak Krakatau, still warm underfoot within its 1883 caldera. Ujung Kulon's UNESCO wilderness, the last refuge of the Javan rhino, gives way to the Thousand Islands, a scatter of coral cays off Jakarta reached by almost no cruise ship, where hatchling turtles are released near a 17th-century Dutch fort on Onrust. Jakarta's Dutch-colonial old town and a bowl of soto Betawi precede a long, rewarding inland day from Semarang to Borobudur, the world's largest Buddhist monument, its five hundred Buddhas emerging from drifting mist. Karimunjawa's shark-patrolled reefs, remote Bawean's endemic deer and tide-vanishing sandbar, and Surabaya's old Arab and Chinese quarters and its rawon lead to Probolinggo, for a climb into Mount Bromo's smoking Tengger caldera and crater stairs. Bali's quiet northern coast at Celukan Bawang, with its lakeside temple and rice-terrace monastery, brings the voyage to Benoa, where the Island of the Gods, its cliffside Kecak dancers and incense-scented temple gates, awaits your arrival. This voyage offers guests the exclusive opportunity to arrive early for SeaDream III's Singapore Showcase on October 24, 2029, a rare chance to open the journey with a celebration of the yacht in her first year of sailing.

Almost no cruise ship reaches the Anambas, a scattering of jewel-like islands adrift in the South China Sea, routinely ranked among Asia's most beautiful and least visited. In the stilted fishing town of Tarempa, life unfolds at its own gentle pace over plates of fresh-grilled seafood. Anchor to snorkel untouched reefs, kayak to the seven-tier Temburun waterfall, and savour the rare thrill of a place the world hasn't found. SeaDream III makes the impossible itinerary possible.

Granite boulders, the same striking formations that made neighboring Belitung famous, line this quieter beach on Bangka Island, long overshadowed by its more photogenic neighbor. Bangka's centuries-old tin-mining wealth built a genuinely distinct Chinese-Indonesian Peranakan food culture, still on full display in the island's markets and kitchens. A handful of beachfront spas take advantage of the island's calm, clear water. Belitung's scenery, without Belitung's crowds.

Granite boulders the size of houses tumble straight into turquoise water along Belitung's coastline, a landscape made famous well beyond Indonesia by the bestselling novel and film Laskar Pelangi, both set on this small tin-mining island. A relaxed, unhurried dining scene built around fresh seafood and Chinese-Indonesian influences reflects the island's long tin-trading history. Some of the clearest, calmest snorkeling in western Indonesia lies a short boat ride from any of its beaches. An island still, remarkably, ahead of the crowds.

Few places on earth carry a name as loaded with history, the 1883 eruption here was heard nearly three thousand miles away and killed tens of thousands in the tsunamis it triggered, one of the deadliest natural disasters ever recorded. Anak Krakatau, the child of Krakatoa, has risen from the same caldera since the 1920s and remains active today, a genuinely rare chance to sail past a volcano still actively rebuilding itself. Approach depends entirely on current activity and official clearance. A sobering, spectacular piece of geological history.

A UNESCO World Heritage rainforest at the far southwestern tip of Java, and the last refuge on earth of the critically endangered Javan rhinoceros, fewer than a hundred survive, all within this one park. Peucang Island's white-sand beaches and turquoise shallows sit within full view of Anak Krakatau's smoking cone across the strait, while the surrounding forest holds gibbons, leopards and a genuinely rich variety of birdlife. About as close as most travelers will ever get to one of the rarest large mammals on the planet.

Just off frenetic Jakarta lies its antidote: the Thousand Islands, a scatter of palm-topped coral cays within a national marine park. Anchor over clear shallows to snorkel bright reef gardens and visit the turtle hatchery on Pramuka, or step ashore at Onrust to explore the ruins of a 17th-century Dutch East India fortress. Drop the marina for a lazy afternoon of paddleboards and swimming in bathwater-warm seas. A castaway idyll a world away from the megacity's roar.

Indonesia's electric capital rewards the intrepid. Stroll Kota Tua's Dutch-colonial squares and the treasure-filled National Museum, browse the antique stalls of Jalan Surabaya, then dive into a bowl of soto Betawi rich with coconut and lime. As the largest city in South-East Asia hums around you, retreat each evening to the calm of your suite. Being small means we tuck close to the old harbour, delivering you straight into the heart of the action.

Semarang is your gateway to Borobudur, the largest Buddhist monument on Earth: a mountain of grey volcanic stone crowned with bell-shaped stupas, best met at sunrise as mist lifts off the Kedu plain and 500 serene Buddhas emerge from the haze. Pair it with the soaring Hindu spires of Prambanan, then stroll Semarang's Dutch colonial Old Town and its candy-pink Blenduk church. It's a long, rewarding day inland, and you return to your own suite rather than a hotel.

A cluster of twenty-seven small islands scattered across the Java Sea, protected as a national marine park and rewarding anyone who makes the crossing with some of the clearest water and healthiest coral in the region. Frigatebirds and terns wheel over largely uninhabited islets, while mangrove channels on the main island shelter smaller reef fish nurseries. Deliberately low-key and difficult to reach, which is precisely why the reef here has stayed so intact.

A small volcanic island adrift in the Java Sea, home to the critically endangered Bawean deer, found nowhere else on the planet and rarely seen even here. Two crater lakes fill the island's interior, ringed by forest thick with hornbills and other endemic birdlife, while a fringing reef offshore remains largely untouched by the dive tourism that has reshaped so much of Indonesia's coastline. A genuine hidden corner of Java's own backyard.

Indonesia's second city wears its role in the independence struggle openly, the Heroes Monument commemorates the fierce 1945 battle that gave the country's National Heroes Day its name. The House of Sampoerna, a beautifully preserved colonial-era cigarette factory turned museum, still shows the hand-rolling process that built one of Java's great commercial fortunes. A round of golf and a genuinely serious East Javanese dining scene, heavier and spicier than Bali's, round out Indonesia's often-overlooked second city.

The gateway to one of Indonesia's most photographed landscapes, Mount Bromo's smoking crater rises from a sea of volcanic sand inside the vast Tengger Caldera, best seen at dawn from the Penanjakan viewpoint as the sun clears the surrounding peaks. The Tenggerese people who farm this harsh volcanic soil still hold an annual offering ceremony, Yadnya Kasada, throwing produce into the crater itself. A four-wheel-drive sunrise excursion here is one of the most dramatic short trips in all of Indonesia.

The quieter gateway to North Bali, well removed from the crowds of Kuta and Seminyak, Celukan Bawang opens onto the Buleleng coast's black-sand beaches, waterfalls at Gitgit and Sekumpul, and dolphin pods that surface reliably off Lovina each morning. Bali's small but increasingly serious wine country has taken root in these volcanic soils, alongside a wellness tradition of natural hot springs at Banjar. Rice terraces and temple villages fill the hills behind the coast. Bali as it was before the south became famous.

Benoa opens the whole of Bali to you. Watch the sun drop behind the sea-cliff temple of Uluwatu as barefoot dancers stamp out the hypnotic Kecak fire ritual, or rise early for the mirror-calm Tegallalang rice terraces above Ubud. Wander incense-scented temple gates, browse the silver workshops of Celuk, and feast on crackling babi guling. Back aboard by evening, you sidestep the resort crowds who never see Bali empty. The Island of the Gods, on your schedule.

voyages.title: Dragons & the Forgotten East
voyages.overview: Overview Ports Suites Land Adventures Testimonials Depart Benoa, Bali, where the Kecak fire ritual burns beneath Uluwatu's clifftop temple, for Lombok's turtle-filled Gili shallows, volcano-grown coffee, and a Sasak weaving village. Satonda's uninhabited crater lake gives way to Komodo, its UNESCO-listed dragons tracked across Rinca's tawny hills, Padar's three scalloped bays climbed for their view, and Pink Beach's crushed coral glowing underfoot, before Larantuka, a devoutly Catholic town of candlelit Portuguese chapels beneath Ile Mandiri's volcano. Kupang's Dutch-colonial waterfront gives way to Dili, its Cristo Rei statue watching over a hard-won capital, before the record-breaking, biodiverse reefs of Atauro Island. Darwin's barramundi-laden frontier markets open the way into Australia's true wilderness: Seven Spirit Bay, an Arnhem Land refuge almost nobody else reaches, where crocodiles bask and dugongs graze; the Wessel Islands, threading the tidal Hole in the Wall few ships ever attempt; and Yirrkala, where a rare, permitted audience with Yolngu artists and their bark paintings reveals the world's oldest continuous culture. Thursday Island's old pearling-lugger port and Green Hill Fort precede the powder beaches of Lizard Island, its Cod Hole and giant clams off the platform, leading at last to Cairns, gateway to the Great Barrier Reef, where your voyage comes ashore at the threshold of Australia's underwater wonder.

Bali's quieter neighbor rises to the volcanic cone of Mount Rinjani, Indonesia's second-highest peak, its crater lake a multi-day trek for the properly fit. Gili Trawangan's car-free beaches and reef lie a short boat ride offshore, while Sasak villages in the island's interior keep traditional weaving and thatched longhouse architecture very much alive. A wellness and spa culture has grown up quickly around the island's south coast resorts. Bali's calmer, less developed alternative.

A tiny, uninhabited island off the north coast of Sumbawa hides a genuine geological oddity at its center, a saltwater crater lake, connected to the sea by seepage rather than any visible channel, ringed by fossilized coral microbialites found in only a handful of places worldwide. The surrounding reef, largely untouched, shelters turtles and reef sharks in clear, current-free water. One of the strangest and least-visited natural formations anywhere on this itinerary.

A small Catholic town on Flores's eastern tip that holds one of Asia's most extraordinary religious traditions, a centuries-old Holy Week procession, rooted in 16th-century Portuguese missionary heritage, that still draws pilgrims from across the region each Easter. Outside of that week, quiet beaches and a slower pace define a town most visitors pass en route to Komodo further west. A genuinely singular pocket of Portuguese-Catholic culture, marooned in the middle of Muslim-majority Indonesia.

West Timor's capital looks and feels different from the rest of Indonesia, a largely Christian city on the edge of a Muslim-majority nation, its markets built around lontar palm sugar and handwoven ikat rather than batik. Sandalwood once made this coast one of the most fought-over in the archipelago, a history still visible in the old Dutch fort. Frigatebirds and terns work the harbor, and a seafood-heavy dining scene reflects the strong Timorese and Rotinese influence on the local kitchen. A genuinely distinct corner of eastern Indonesia.

Dili wears its history openly: Portuguese pastel facades, the soaring Cristo Rei statue watching over the bay, and museums that tell Timor-Leste's hard- won independence. But the real prize lies offshore at Atauro Island, whose reefs were crowned the most biodiverse waters on Earth, richer in reef-fish species than anywhere yet surveyed. Drop the marina and snorkel walls ablaze with color, then sip single-origin Timorese coffee ashore. A frontier nation, met on its own terms.

A short but rough crossing from Dili delivers some of the most biodiverse reef in the world, surveys here have recorded more fish species per site than almost anywhere else on the planet. The island's isolation has kept both its coral and its traditional way of life largely intact, small fishing villages, a handful of guesthouses and very little else. Frigatebirds and other seabirds nest along the cliffs above beaches that see barely any visitors at all. One of Southeast Asia's last genuinely undiscovered dive destinations.

Australia's tropical northern capital carries its Second World War history openly, this was the only Australian city bombed by Japan, in a 1942 raid larger than Pearl Harbor, told in full at the wartime tunnels beneath town. The Mindil Beach sunset markets pair a fire-orange Top End sky with satay and laksa stalls, while jumping-crocodile cruises on the Adelaide River nearby put saltwater crocodiles almost close enough to touch. A golf round in the tropical heat and some of the country's richest birdlife in the surrounding wetlands round out a genuinely frontier city.

A genuinely wild stretch of the Cobourg Peninsula in western Arnhem Land, reachable only by boat or light aircraft and home to one of Australia's original ecotourism retreats. Saltwater crocodiles patrol the mangroves, while the surrounding monsoon forest and wetlands hold some of the Top End's richest birdlife, jabirus, brolgas and sea eagles among them. Traditional Aboriginal owners still manage much of the land. About as remote and untouched as Northern Territory wilderness gets.

A remote, largely uninhabited chain off the tip of Arnhem Land that carries evidence of Australia's first real contact with the outside world, Macassan fishermen from what is now Indonesia sailed here to harvest sea cucumber centuries before European settlement, leaving tamarind trees and pottery shards still being found today. Pristine reef and empty white beaches ring islands that see barely any visitors of any kind. One of the least-known corners of the entire Australian coast.

This small Arnhem Land community changed Australian law from its own church hall, the 1963 bark petitions presented here, painted testimony backed by written text, were the first Indigenous documents recognized by the Australian Parliament and remain a founding document of the land rights movement. The Buku-Larrnggay Mulka art center still represents the Yolngu artists who continue that tradition today, their bark paintings and prints held in major collections worldwide. Sea eagles and other coastal birdlife are abundant along the surrounding shoreline. A community where art and political history are inseparable.

Where the Coral Sea meets the Arafura, tiny TI is the beating heart of the Torres Strait. Climb to Green Hill Fort for its old guns and a 360-degree island panorama, trace the boom-and-bust saga of the pearling luggers, and feel the distinct Melanesian pulse of Islander song and dance. A crossroads of empires and oceans that only a nimble, shallow-draught small ship can comfortably reach and truly savor.

Lizard Island is the Reef's most exclusive outpost, twenty-four powder-white beaches ringing a granite isle few vessels can reach. Dive the legendary Cod Hole to meet potato cod the size of a Labrador, or snorkel the giant clams at Watsons Bay straight from the swim platform. Hike to Cook's Look for the panorama that showed Captain Cook his escape through the reef. With just 230 aboard, the anchorage feels like your own private atoll. Swimming and non-motorized craft only here; motorized watersports need the local authority's permission.

Cairns is your threshold to the Great Barrier Reef, a short run out to the outer-reef pontoons and the best snorkeling in Australia. Snorkel the coral gardens of the outer Agincourt Ribbons, drift past clownfish and reef sharks, then trade the sea for the world's oldest rainforest at Daintree, where cassowaries stalk the Kuranda canopy. Toast the day with a chilled Margaret River white as the tender returns. Big ships queue at the pier; you simply dive in.

voyages.title: Great Barrier Reef & Legendary Pacific Isles
voyages.overview: Overview Ports Suites Land Adventures Testimonials Depart Cairns for the outer reef pontoons of the Agincourt Ribbons, then trade coral for rainforest in the ancient canopy of Daintree. Continue south to Townsville, where wild koalas doze in the gum trees above Magnetic Island's granite headlands and coral gardens fringe Florence Bay, before threading the Whitsundays: mirror water and Ngaro rock art at Nara Inlet, then Airlie Beach's palm-lined esplanade with a seaplane view over Heart Reef and Whitehaven's silica sands. At remote Middle Percy Island, row ashore to the driftwood-plaqued rafters of the fabled A-frame hut and leave one of your own. Great Keppel's seventeen white beaches and giant clams in Monkey Bay give way to Lady Elliot Island, a coral cay reached by very few ships, where manta rays glide through a lagoon lit from below. After Brisbane's riverside galleries and the sand islands of Moreton Bay, call at Norfolk Island, a landing few vessels attempt, to wander the UNESCO-listed convict ruins of Kingston above a turquoise bay and meet islanders descended from the Bounty mutineers. New Zealand unfolds through the Bay of Islands' Hole in the Rock and its bow-riding dolphins, Great Barrier Island's protected dark sky, and Waiheke's vineyard terraces, before your voyage concludes in Auckland, the City of Sails, where the Sky Tower's panorama crowns a harbour cradled by dormant volcanic cones. This voyage offers guests the exclusive opportunity to extend their stay for SeaDream III's Auckland Showcase on December 14, 2029, a rare chance to conclude with a celebration of the yacht in her first of sailing.

North Queensland's largest city looks out toward Magnetic Island and, further offshore, the Museum of Underwater Art, submerged sculptures designed to grow into a living reef of their own. Castle Hill's granite dome offers a walk-up view over the whole city and the reef beyond, while Reef HQ's aquarium tells the wider Great Barrier Reef story for anyone not yet diving it. A round of golf in the dry tropical heat and beaches busy with birdlife round out a genuinely underrated Queensland city.

One of the Whitsundays' most sheltered anchorages doubles as one of its most significant cultural sites, a cave deep in the inlet holds ochre rock art left by the Ngaro people, sea-going Aboriginal navigators who called these waters home for thousands of years before European contact. Steep, forested hills wrap tightly around the water on every side, keeping the anchorage glass-calm even when the open Coral Sea beyond is not. A quiet, protected corner with a much older story than most itineraries acknowledge.

The gateway to seventy-four islands of the Whitsundays, Airlie Beach trades any real waterfront for a lively strip of restaurants and a purpose-built lagoon pool, then sends everyone straight back out onto the water. Whitehaven Beach, its silica sand so pure it squeaks underfoot, lies a short sail away and regularly tops the world's best-beach lists. A relaxed, sailing-mad town that exists almost entirely as a launchpad for the reef beyond it.

One of the most remote anchorages on the Queensland coast, better known to generations of cruising sailors than to any tour operator. Middle Percy Island's A-Frame shelter, a ramshackle hut built and re-built by decades of passing yachties, is plastered floor to ceiling with the carved names, flags and mementos of everyone who has sheltered there. Turtles and dugongs graze the surrounding reef flats largely undisturbed. About as far off the beaten track as this coast still gets.

Seventeen white-sand beaches ring this Keppel Bay island, most of them empty even on a busy day, backed by coastal woodland thick with birdlife. Snorkel straight off the sand over fringing coral, or simply walk from one perfect cove to the next along tracks that see barely any traffic. A long-derelict resort has slowly given way to a quieter, more unspoiled island than the one package tourists once knew.

The southernmost coral cay of the Great Barrier Reef is also one of its most protected, a green zone where no fishing has been allowed for decades, and the reef has rewarded that restraint. Manta rays gather at a cleaning station just offshore in numbers rare anywhere else on the reef, and green and loggerhead turtles nest on the beach in season. Access is by small plane or boat only, keeping numbers, and impact, low. A working case study in what an undisturbed reef still looks like.

Australia's river city wraps a genuinely subtropical, laid-back energy around a compact, walkable center. Streets Beach at South Bank is the only inner-city artificial beach in the country, a short stroll from the Queensland Art Gallery and a riverside food scene that has boomed in recent years. Rainbow lorikeets and kookaburras crowd the parklands along the Brisbane River, while the Granite Belt's cool-climate vineyards lie a scenic few hours inland. A confident, sunny counterpoint to Sydney and Melbourne.

Descendants of the Bounty mutineers, resettled here from overcrowded Pitcairn in 1856, still make up much of Norfolk's small population and still speak Norf'k, a language found nowhere else on earth. The convict ruins at Kingston, part of the Australian Convict Sites World Heritage listing, sit on a headland as beautiful as it is grim, a past the island does not gloss over. Towering, endemic Norfolk pines line the coast, and a single golf course and quiet beaches round out an island barely touched by modern tourism. A genuinely singular culture, isolated in the middle of the Pacific.

New Zealand's founding document, the Treaty of Waitangi, was signed on the lawn at Waitangi in 1840, and the treaty grounds tell that complex history with real depth. Beyond the history, the bay itself is one of the country's great game-fishing waters, marlin drew Zane Gray here nearly a century ago, and dolphin pods still work the same channels daily. The colonial town of Russell, once a rough-and-ready whaling port, now offers some of Northland's best waterfront dining. History, wildlife and a well-earned reputation for the water in between.

The world's first island granted International Dark Sky Sanctuary status has almost no mains power and barely any light pollution to compete with it, making its night sky one of the clearest anywhere in New Zealand. Kiwi roam the bush here in numbers rare on the mainland, while natural hot springs at Kaitoke reward a short forest walk. Mobile signal drops out almost entirely once you're off the wharf, an increasingly rare kind of genuine escape. Wild, dark and deliberately undeveloped.

A thirty-minute ferry from downtown Auckland delivers an entirely different pace of life, more than thirty boutique wineries share this one small island, many with cellar-door lunches looking straight out over the Hauraki Gulf. Olive groves, art galleries and a genuinely excellent dining scene have grown up alongside the vines over the past few decades, while sheltered beaches ring the coastline for a swim between tastings. Auckland's wine country, without ever leaving the harbor.

New Zealand's largest city rises from no fewer than fifty extinct volcanic cones, several of them, like Mount Eden, an easy climb for a full harbor view. The City of Sails' waterfront has been reinvented around Wynyard Quarter and Britomart's warehouse-turned-restaurant precinct, drawing on some of the country's best produce and wine lists. A short ferry ride puts Waiheke's vineyards within easy reach for anyone who doesn't linger in town. Volcanic, maritime and increasingly serious about its food.

voyages.title: Auckland Ship Showcase
voyages.overview: Overview Ports Suites Land Adventures Testimonials Volcanic cones cradle Waitematā Harbour as the SeaDream III Auckland Showcase marks a bold step into her next chapter. This exclusive event closes SeaDream III's passage through Australia's Queensland coast and New Zealand's North Island and opens her journey south through New Zealand's South Island and Tasmania to Sydney, introducing our newest yacht to the City of Sails. Access to the Auckland Showcase is available only to guests joining the voyage immediately before or after this event. Back-to-back savings are not applicable to Showcase experiences.

voyages.title: Fiords, Fireworks & the Southern Summer
voyages.overview: Overview Ports Suites Land Adventures Testimonials Guests aboard this rare SeaDream voyage will experience both Christmas and New Year's at sea. Auckland's harbour opens the journey toward Napier, rebuilt after the 1931 earthquake into the world's most complete Art Deco town, then Wellington, where the red cable car climbs to hillside gardens above a capital anchored by Te Papa's collections and renowned for its coffee and craft beer. In Picton, wander the drowned-valley maze of the Marlborough Sounds before tasting sauvignon blanc at Cloudy Bay's cellar doors. Cross to Lyttelton for Christchurch's reinvented street art and a drive out to Akaroa, where rare Hector's dolphins play in a sunken volcanic harbour. At remote Stewart Island, listen for kiwi foraging in the undergrowth and watch for the aurora australis rippling green overhead. Sail in silence through Doubtful Sound, engines cut beneath waterfalls and rainforested cliffs, before a hushed Christmas Eve and Christmas Day at sea crossing the Tasman, carols and a festive table marking the holiday aboard, then Boxing Day welcomes you to Hobart's Georgian sandstone and the subterranean provocations of MONA. Wander the UNESCO-listed convict ruins of Port Arthur and cruise past the solemn Isle of the Dead, then ride the chairlift above Launceston's Cataract Gorge, before Eden, where humpbacks and southern rights throng Twofold Bay. Sydney Harbour hosts the celebration's finale, the yacht sailing past the Opera House and beneath the great steel arch of the bridge as New Year's Eve fireworks light the water, one of the most celebrated ways anywhere to welcome the new year. This voyage offers guests the exclusive opportunity to begin with SeaDream III's Auckland Showcase on December 14, 2029 or conclude with the Sydney Showcase on January 2, 2030, a rare chance to mark either end of the journey with a celebration of the yacht in her first year of sailing.

Leveled by a catastrophic 1931 earthquake and rebuilt almost entirely in the fashionable style of the day, Napier is now one of the most complete and best-preserved Art Deco cities on the planet, its pastel facades a genuine architectural pilgrimage. Cape Kidnappers, a short drive along the coast, holds the largest mainland gannet colony in the world, tens of thousands of birds nesting in full view. Hawke's Bay's Gimblett Gravels have become one of New Zealand's most serious wine districts, its Syrah and Bordeaux-style blends now taken seriously well beyond the region. A disaster turned, deliberately, into a design statement.
