New Zealand's compact, hilly capital has built a reputation on precisely the things that fill a short visit well, a world-class national museum in Te Papa, a coffee and craft-beer scene that rivals any city its size, and Zealandia, a fenced urban sanctuary where takahe and kaka have returned to a capital city for the first time in generations. Wind off Cook Strait keeps the city famously bracing, but a cable-car ride up to the botanic gardens rewards it with one of the best harbor views in the country. Weta Workshop's props and creatures, built for Middle-earth, are a short drive from the wharf. Small, sharp and unmistakably creative.

Picton sits at the head of the Marlborough Sounds, a drowned river valley system of forested inlets that the Queen Charlotte Track threads for four days for anyone with the time. It is also the gateway to Marlborough, the wine region that put New Zealand Sauvignon Blanc on the world's tables, its vineyards a short and scenic drive from the wharf. The Sounds shelter the king shag, a rare cormorant found nowhere else on earth, alongside dolphins and fur seals. Greenshell mussels from nearby Havelock round out a region built on both wine and water.

Christchurch has rebuilt itself with real ambition since the 2011 earthquake, a new cathedral square, riverside gardens and an innovative container-mall precinct standing where rubble once did. Its historic port, Lyttelton, tunnels through the hills separately and has its own tight-knit, artsy character worth a wander in its own right. Banks Peninsula, just beyond, shelters Akaroa's French-founded harbor town and some of the only reliable sightings anywhere of Hector's dolphin, the world's smallest and rarest marine dolphin. Canterbury's vineyards and a strong new dining scene round out a region very much back on its feet.

New Zealand's third and least-visited main island offers the best real chance in the country to see a kiwi in the genuine wild, rather than behind glass, its birds are unusually active by day here thanks to an absence of mammalian predators. Barely four hundred people live on Rakiura, as the island is known in Maori, and its International Dark Sky Sanctuary status makes for some of the clearest stargazing in the Southern Hemisphere. Predator-free Ulva Island, just offshore, is a working sanctuary for some of the country's rarest birds. About as far south, and as wild, as New Zealand gets.

Milford Sound's wilder, larger cousin takes three times as long to reach and rewards every extra mile of it, Doubtful Sound sees a fraction of the visitors and correspondingly more silence, the Sound of Silence being its unofficial nickname among those who know it. Rain-fed waterfalls drop hundreds of meters down sheer, forested walls into water so still it mirrors them perfectly on a calm morning. Bottlenose dolphins and fur seals work the fjord's mouth, and Fiordland crested penguins nest along its more sheltered arms. A slow, wordless cruise through some of the most untouched wilderness left in New Zealand.

Australia's southernmost city pairs convict-era sandstone warehouses at Salamanca Place with one of the world's most talked-about museums, David Walsh's subterranean, deliberately provocative MONA, a short ferry ride up the Derwent. Tasmania's cool-climate wine country fans out from the city in every direction, its pinot noir and sparkling wine now taken seriously worldwide, while Bruny Island's oysters are a short drive south. Mount Wellington looms over it all, often snow-capped even in the shoulder seasons. Small, sharp-edged and increasingly essential.

The ruins of Australia's most notorious convict penal colony sit improbably beautifully on the Tasman Peninsula, sandstone shells of a prison, church and asylum now framed by manicured lawns running down to the water. The Isle of the Dead offshore holds the graves of nearly two thousand convicts and settlers, while the wider site's history, both convict-era and more recent, is told with real care rather than spectacle. Coal Valley's vineyards and a strong regional dining scene lie a scenic drive back toward Hobart. A profoundly moving stop, handled with the seriousness it demands.

Tasmania's second city sits where the Tamar meets the dramatic cliffs of Cataract Gorge, a short walk from the city center and improbably wild for something so central. The Tamar Valley's vineyards, some of the coolest-climate wine country in Australia, produce a sparkling wine and pinot noir now sought out well beyond Tasmania, while colonial architecture lines streets barely touched since the 19th century. A compact, characterful base for Tasmania's north.

A deep natural harbor with one of the strangest true stories on the New South Wales coast, for decades, a pod of wild orcas actively helped local whalers hunt baleen whales in Twofold Bay, an extraordinary interspecies partnership documented at the town's Killer Whale Museum, skeleton of the lead orca, Old Tom, included. Ben Boyd National Park's dramatic cliffs and pink pipe-clay headlands ring the bay, and the town's fishing fleet still lands some of the best seafood on this stretch of coast. One of Australia's more improbable, and true, tall tales.

The harbor city needs no introduction, but it rewards a slow look anyway, the Opera House's sail-like shells and the Harbor Bridge's steel arc framing a working harbor still busy with ferries. Bondi's sweep of sand and the coastal walk to Coogee show the city's beach culture at its best, while rainbow lorikeets and sulphur-crested cockatoos crowd the Royal Botanic Garden along the water's edge. A round at one of the city's championship golf courses caps a day in a city that rarely runs out of things to show you.

voyages.title: Sydney Ship Showcase
voyages.overview: Overview Ports Suites Land Adventures Testimonials Beneath the sails of the Opera House, the SeaDream III Sydney Showcase turns a milestone voyage into a landmark occasion. This exclusive event closes SeaDream III's passage through New Zealand's South Island and Tasmania and opens her journey to the Great Barrier Reef, introducing our newest yacht to Sydney Harbour for the new year. Access to the Sydney Showcase is available only to guests joining the voyage immediately before or after this event. Back-to-back savings are not applicable to Showcase experiences.

voyages.title: Silver Sands & the Great Barrier Reef
voyages.overview: Overview Ports Suites Land Adventures Testimonials Depart Sydney for Brisbane, where riverside galleries and laneway restaurants give a last taste of city polish before the wilder north. At K’gari, the UNESCO-listed world's largest sand island, float in the sapphire perfection of Lake McKenzie beneath rainforest grown from pure sand. Lady Musgrave Island's coral cay rings a luminous lagoon, sheltered enough for a full day at anchor among reef sharks and turtles. Wind through the Whitsundays, tendering into Nara Inlet's mirror-still fjord and its Ngaro rock art, then Airlie Beach's palm-lined esplanade for a seaplane view over Whitehaven's silica sands. Off Townsville, wild koalas doze in the gum canopy above secluded coral bays. Dunk Island's jungle trails flicker with Ulysses butterflies before Port Douglas, gateway to both the outer reef and the ancient Daintree rainforest. Your voyage concludes docked alongside Cairns, threshold to the Great Barrier Reef, its coral gardens of the Agincourt Ribbons just a short run offshore. This voyage offers guests the exclusive opportunity to arrive early for SeaDream III's Sydney Showcase on January 2, 2030, a rare chance to open the journey with a celebration of the yacht in her first year of sailing.

Australia's river city wraps a genuinely subtropical, laid-back energy around a compact, walkable center. Streets Beach at South Bank is the only inner-city artificial beach in the country, a short stroll from the Queensland Art Gallery and a riverside food scene that has boomed in recent years. Rainbow lorikeets and kookaburras crowd the parklands along the Brisbane River, while the Granite Belt's cool-climate vineyards lie a scenic few hours inland. A confident, sunny counterpoint to Sydney and Melbourne.

The world's largest sand island, and the only place on earth where rainforest grows on pure sand, K'gari (formerly known as Fraser Island) is a genuine geological anomaly. Lake McKenzie's silica-white shore and impossibly clear, mineral-pure water rank among Australia's most photographed swimming holes, while the island's wild dingo population is among the country's most genetically pure. Traditional owners, the Butchulla people, whose name for the island was restored in 2023, still guide much of what visitors learn here. Rainforest, desert dunes and a perched lake, all on one island.

A true coral cay ringed by one of the reef's largest and calmest lagoons, sheltered enough to snorkel in almost any weather. A dense pisonia forest covers the island's interior, home to one of the largest seabird rookeries on the southern Great Barrier Reef, black noddies and wedge-tailed shearwaters by the tens of thousands in season. Turtles nest on the same narrow beach through the summer months. A small, low-key cay that rewards anyone who makes the effort to reach it.

Seventeen white-sand beaches ring this Keppel Bay island, most of them empty even on a busy day, backed by coastal woodland thick with birdlife. Snorkel straight off the sand over fringing coral, or simply walk from one perfect cove to the next along tracks that see barely any traffic. A long-derelict resort has slowly given way to a quieter, more unspoiled island than the one package tourists once knew.

One of the Whitsundays' most sheltered anchorages doubles as one of its most significant cultural sites, a cave deep in the inlet holds ochre rock art left by the Ngaro people, sea-going Aboriginal navigators who called these waters home for thousands of years before European contact. Steep, forested hills wrap tightly around the water on every side, keeping the anchorage glass-calm even when the open Coral Sea beyond is not. A quiet, protected corner with a much older story than most itineraries acknowledge.

The gateway to seventy-four islands of the Whitsundays, Airlie Beach trades any real waterfront for a lively strip of restaurants and a purpose-built lagoon pool, then sends everyone straight back out onto the water. Whitehaven Beach, its silica sand so pure it squeaks underfoot, lies a short sail away and regularly tops the world's best-beach lists. A relaxed, sailing-mad town that exists almost entirely as a launchpad for the reef beyond it.

North Queensland's largest city looks out toward Magnetic Island and, further offshore, the Museum of Underwater Art, submerged sculptures designed to grow into a living reef of their own. Castle Hill's granite dome offers a walk-up view over the whole city and the reef beyond, while Reef HQ's aquarium tells the wider Great Barrier Reef story for anyone not yet diving it. A round of golf in the dry tropical heat and beaches busy with birdlife round out a genuinely underrated Queensland city.

A rainforest-clad Great Barrier Reef island once made famous by the writer E.J. Banfield, whose Confessions of a Beachcomber turned his hermit's life here into a bestseller. Ulysses butterflies, their wings an improbable electric blue, drift through the island's walking trails in numbers found almost nowhere else. Cyclone Yasi flattened the resort in 2011 and nature has largely reclaimed the island since, leaving a quieter, wilder Dunk than Banfield himself might recognize.

The only place on earth where two UNESCO World Heritage sites meet, the Great Barrier Reef and the ancient Daintree Rainforest both within easy reach of the same small marina town. Four Mile Beach stretches along the front of town for exactly that, framed by rainforest-covered headlands, while Mossman Gorge's crystalline swimming holes lie a short drive inland. A cluster of genuinely excellent day spas, several championship golf courses and some of Queensland's best dining round out a town built entirely around its two great natural neighbors.

Cairns is your threshold to the Great Barrier Reef, a short run out to the outer-reef pontoons and the best snorkeling in Australia. Snorkel the coral gardens of the outer Agincourt Ribbons, drift past clownfish and reef sharks, then trade the sea for the world's oldest rainforest at Daintree, where cassowaries stalk the Kuranda canopy. Toast the day with a chilled Margaret River white as the tender returns. Big ships queue at the pier; you simply dive in.

voyages.title: The Coral Sea & the Dragon Isles
voyages.overview: Overview Ports Suites Land Adventures Testimonials Depart Cairns for Lizard Island, a granite outpost ringed by twenty-four white beaches where potato cod patrol the legendary Cod Hole. Sail into the Northern Territory's far frontier at Yirrkala, a call almost no other ship makes, where Yolngu artists welcome you into the Buku-Larrnggay Mulka centre to see bark paintings and larrakitj poles carrying stories tens of thousands of years old. Glide by tender through the mangrove creeks of Seven Spirit Bay, a Cobourg Peninsula wilderness reached by very few vessels, where saltwater crocodiles bask and dugongs graze the seagrass shallows. Darwin's Mindil Beach markets and WWII tunnels give way to Kupang's Dutch-colonial waterfront on West Timor, then Komodo, a UNESCO World Heritage site, where a ranger leads you across Rinca's tawny hills to meet the world's largest lizard, and Pink Beach blushes with crushed coral at the water's edge. In Lombok, snorkel the Gili Islands' turtle-filled shallows before your voyage concludes at Benoa, gateway to Bali's temple-crowned cliffs and incense-scented courtyards.

Lizard Island is the Reef's most exclusive outpost, twenty-four powder-white beaches ringing a granite isle few vessels can reach. Dive the legendary Cod Hole to meet potato cod the size of a Labrador, or snorkel the giant clams at Watsons Bay straight from the swim platform. Hike to Cook's Look for the panorama that showed Captain Cook his escape through the reef. With just 230 aboard, the anchorage feels like your own private atoll. Swimming and non-motorized craft only here; motorized watersports need the local authority's permission.

This small Arnhem Land community changed Australian law from its own church hall, the 1963 bark petitions presented here, painted testimony backed by written text, were the first Indigenous documents recognized by the Australian Parliament and remain a founding document of the land rights movement. The Buku-Larrnggay Mulka art center still represents the Yolngu artists who continue that tradition today, their bark paintings and prints held in major collections worldwide. Sea eagles and other coastal birdlife are abundant along the surrounding shoreline. A community where art and political history are inseparable.

A genuinely wild stretch of the Cobourg Peninsula in western Arnhem Land, reachable only by boat or light aircraft and home to one of Australia's original ecotourism retreats. Saltwater crocodiles patrol the mangroves, while the surrounding monsoon forest and wetlands hold some of the Top End's richest birdlife, jabirus, brolgas and sea eagles among them. Traditional Aboriginal owners still manage much of the land. About as remote and untouched as Northern Territory wilderness gets.

Australia's tropical northern capital carries its Second World War history openly, this was the only Australian city bombed by Japan, in a 1942 raid larger than Pearl Harbor, told in full at the wartime tunnels beneath town. The Mindil Beach sunset markets pair a fire-orange Top End sky with satay and laksa stalls, while jumping-crocodile cruises on the Adelaide River nearby put saltwater crocodiles almost close enough to touch. A golf round in the tropical heat and some of the country's richest birdlife in the surrounding wetlands round out a genuinely frontier city.

West Timor's capital looks and feels different from the rest of Indonesia, a largely Christian city on the edge of a Muslim-majority nation, its markets built around lontar palm sugar and handwoven ikat rather than batik. Sandalwood once made this coast one of the most fought-over in the archipelago, a history still visible in the old Dutch fort. Frigatebirds and terns work the harbor, and a seafood-heavy dining scene reflects the strong Timorese and Rotinese influence on the local kitchen. A genuinely distinct corner of eastern Indonesia.

Bali's quieter neighbor rises to the volcanic cone of Mount Rinjani, Indonesia's second-highest peak, its crater lake a multi-day trek for the properly fit. Gili Trawangan's car-free beaches and reef lie a short boat ride offshore, while Sasak villages in the island's interior keep traditional weaving and thatched longhouse architecture very much alive. A wellness and spa culture has grown up quickly around the island's south coast resorts. Bali's calmer, less developed alternative.

Benoa opens the whole of Bali to you. Watch the sun drop behind the sea-cliff temple of Uluwatu as barefoot dancers stamp out the hypnotic Kecak fire ritual, or rise early for the mirror-calm Tegallalang rice terraces above Ubud. Wander incense-scented temple gates, browse the silver workshops of Celuk, and feast on crackling babi guling. Back aboard by evening, you sidestep the resort crowds who never see Bali empty. The Island of the Gods, on your schedule.

voyages.title: Volcanoes, Temples & Island Jewels
voyages.overview: Overview Ports Suites Land Adventures Testimonials Depart Benoa for Probolinggo, crossing the whispering Sea of Sand by jeep to watch Mount Bromo exhale smoke over the Tengger caldera's sea of mist, then climbing the crater stairs to peer into its heart. Continue to Semarang, gateway to Borobudur, the world's largest Buddhist monument, its bell-shaped stupas emerging from soft haze on the Kedu plain beneath a horizon of smoking volcanic cones. At Karimunjawa, a 27-island marine park in the Java Sea, wade a floating shark nursery and kayak mangrove boardwalks, before Belitung's UNESCO-listed granite islets rise from impossibly clear seas around the old Dutch lighthouse at Lengkuas. Bangka's Parai Tenggiri offers a sculpture garden of car-sized boulders glowing rose-gold above clear shallows. In Singapore, wander the Supertrees of Gardens by the Bay and sip a Sling at Raffles before island-hopping through the Gulf of Thailand: Ko Samui's Big Buddha, the sheer emerald islands of Ang Thong that inspired The Beach, and Ko Tao's coral gardens. Your voyage concludes in Bangkok, where the gilded spires of the Grand Palace and the reclining Buddha of Wat Pho crown the City of Angels.

The gateway to one of Indonesia's most photographed landscapes, Mount Bromo's smoking crater rises from a sea of volcanic sand inside the vast Tengger Caldera, best seen at dawn from the Penanjakan viewpoint as the sun clears the surrounding peaks. The Tenggerese people who farm this harsh volcanic soil still hold an annual offering ceremony, Yadnya Kasada, throwing produce into the crater itself. A four-wheel-drive sunrise excursion here is one of the most dramatic short trips in all of Indonesia.

Semarang is your gateway to Borobudur, the largest Buddhist monument on Earth: a mountain of grey volcanic stone crowned with bell-shaped stupas, best met at sunrise as mist lifts off the Kedu plain and 500 serene Buddhas emerge from the haze. Pair it with the soaring Hindu spires of Prambanan, then stroll Semarang's Dutch colonial Old Town and its candy-pink Blenduk church. It's a long, rewarding day inland, and you return to your own suite rather than a hotel.

A cluster of twenty-seven small islands scattered across the Java Sea, protected as a national marine park and rewarding anyone who makes the crossing with some of the clearest water and healthiest coral in the region. Frigatebirds and terns wheel over largely uninhabited islets, while mangrove channels on the main island shelter smaller reef fish nurseries. Deliberately low-key and difficult to reach, which is precisely why the reef here has stayed so intact.

Granite boulders the size of houses tumble straight into turquoise water along Belitung's coastline, a landscape made famous well beyond Indonesia by the bestselling novel and film Laskar Pelangi, both set on this small tin-mining island. A relaxed, unhurried dining scene built around fresh seafood and Chinese-Indonesian influences reflects the island's long tin-trading history. Some of the clearest, calmest snorkeling in western Indonesia lies a short boat ride from any of its beaches. An island still, remarkably, ahead of the crowds.

Granite boulders, the same striking formations that made neighboring Belitung famous, line this quieter beach on Bangka Island, long overshadowed by its more photogenic neighbor. Bangka's centuries-old tin-mining wealth built a genuinely distinct Chinese-Indonesian Peranakan food culture, still on full display in the island's markets and kitchens. A handful of beachfront spas take advantage of the island's calm, clear water. Belitung's scenery, without Belitung's crowds.

Begin where garden-city futurism meets old Asia. Marvel at the Supertrees and misty Cloud Forest of Gardens by the Bay, raise a Singapore Sling at Raffles' Long Bar, then graze Maxwell hawker center for chili crab and Hainanese chicken rice. Being small, SeaDream berths right on Marina Bay, a front-row seat the mega-ships can't claim, and an overnight lets you watch the light show glitter long after the crowds have thinned.

Samui greets you with swaying coconut palms and the serene golden gaze of the Big Buddha above the bay. Chase jungle waterfalls inland, then let SeaDream's marina turn the warm Gulf into your private playground.

Forty-two emerald islands rise sheer from the Gulf of Thailand, and there is no pier here, only anchorages that SeaDream III was built for. Kayak from the swim platform to the hidden Emerald Lagoon, climb to the panoramic viewpoint that inspired the novel The Beach, then snorkel turquoise shallows and picnic on a sandbar all your own. A day of raw natural drama, reachable only by those who arrive by sea. Swimming and non-motorized craft only here; motorized watersports need the local authority's permission. Discover with SeaDream.

A tiny island that built its entire reputation on diving, some of the cheapest PADI certification anywhere in the world drew a generation of backpackers here, and the reefs that made it famous are still genuinely excellent. Sail Rock, a submerged pinnacle a short boat ride offshore, remains one of the Gulf of Thailand's best dive sites for spotting whale sharks in season. A laid-back, castaway atmosphere persists even as the island has grown more comfortable. Thailand's diving capital, in miniature.

From the port, plunge into the glorious chaos of the City of Angels. Watch dawn gild the spires of the Grand Palace and the reclining Buddha at Wat Pho, then trade tuk-tuks for a long-tail boat threading the khlongs to the flower and fruit markets. As day falls, a rooftop bar and a private table of som tam, massaman and mango sticky rice await. With overnights aboard, you savor Bangkok's cool evenings without ever repacking a bag.

voyages.title: Royal Thailand & Malaysia’s Emerald Islands
voyages.overview: Overview Ports Suites Land Adventures Testimonials Depart Bangkok for Hua Hin, Thailand's original royal retreat, where a palm-lined beach and old fishing-jetty cafes set an unhurried tone. Continue to Ko Samui, greeting the Gulf with swaying coconut palms and the golden gaze of the Big Buddha above the bay. At Kuala Terengganu, wander Southeast Asia's largest state museum and the boatyards of Pulau Duyong, where craftsmen still build traditional bedar and pinas by eye. The Perhentian Islands, a call few large ships can make, reveal water so clear the coral reads like a map, reefs alive with green turtles and blacktip reef sharks straight off the yacht's own marina. Redang answers with Malaysia's most celebrated crescent of blinding white sand, and Tioman rises next, its jungled twin peaks said to be a dragon turned to stone, laced with waterfalls and hidden coral gardens. Your voyage concludes in Singapore, where the Supertrees of Gardens by the Bay glitter long after the light show has drawn its last crowd.

Thailand's original royal retreat trades big-city buzz for genteel seaside charm. Stroll the palm-lined beach and the atmospheric old fishing-jetty cafes, browse the artful Cicada day market, or tour Monsoon Valley's improbable tropical vineyards with a chilled glass in hand. It is refined, unhurried Thailand, a graceful match for an intimate yacht that favors the roads less travelled. Discover with SeaDream.

A quiet Malaysian state capital on the South China Sea coast, known well beyond its size for a genuinely excellent Malay dining scene, keropok lekor fish crackers and nasi dagang among the local specialties worth seeking out at the waterfront night market. Traditional boat-building and songket weaving, a hand-loomed brocade once reserved for royalty, are still practiced in workshops around town. A relaxed, unhurried introduction to Malaysia's less-visited east coast.

The Perhentians are the stuff of desert-island dreams, turquoise water so clear the coral reads like a map, and no room for large ships in their shallow bays. SeaDream III anchors offshore, and the marina delivers you straight to reefs alive with green turtles, blacktip reef sharks and clouds of parrotfish. Laze on flour-soft sand between swims. This is barefoot Malaysia at its most pristine and private.

Redang wears the crown for Malaysia's most beautiful beaches, a long crescent of blinding white sand fringing water in impossible shades of blue. Protected as a marine park, its reefs teem with life just metres from shore; slip in from SeaDream's marina to drift over giant clams and shoals of reef fish. Few itineraries call here, and fewer still can linger at anchor as evening gilds the bay. Pure, unhurried tropical bliss.

Legend says a dragon settled here and became an island, and Tioman's jungled twin peaks and cascading waterfalls do feel mythic. Once a film-set stand- in for Bali Hai, it remains gloriously undeveloped: anchor offshore, snorkel coral gardens from the swim platform, trek the rainforest to hidden falls, or spot monitor lizards and hornbills ashore. Duty-free and delightfully remote, it is best reached exactly as you do, by yacht. Swimming and non-motorised craft only here; motorised watersports need the local authority's permission.

voyages.title: The Andaman Sea & the Spice Coast
voyages.overview: Overview Ports Suites Land Adventures Testimonials Depart Singapore, where the illuminated Supertrees of Gardens by the Bay give way to hawker-stall aromas of chilli crab, and set a course for Penang, whose UNESCO-listed George Town unfolds in shophouses, clan jetties and incense-laced temples. Phuket follows, its limestone stacks and hidden hongs opening onto the untouched islands of the Andaman Sea, before Port Blair reveals the sober history of the Cellular Jail and reefs among Asia's most pristine. Anchor in Trincomalee's vast natural harbour, ringed by white sand and crowned by clifftop Koneswaram Temple, then feel the pulse of Colombo, where tuk-tuks, frangipani and the Gangaramaya Temple's gilded spires set a joyful Sri Lankan overture. Glide into Cochin, the Queen of the Arabian Sea, where cantilevered Chinese fishing nets dip beneath a coppering sky, spice warehouses recall centuries of trade, and palm-lined backwaters thread inland, then wander Goa's baroque, UNESCO-listed churches and sun-warmed beach shacks. Your voyage concludes in Mumbai, sailing beneath the Gateway of India into a dazzling metropolis of Victorian-Gothic grandeur and ceaseless energy. This voyage offers guests the exclusive opportunity to extend their stay for SeaDream III's Mumbai Showcase on March 3, 2030, a rare chance to conclude with a celebration of the yacht in her first year of sailing.

George Town's UNESCO-listed streets layer Chinese shophouses, Indian temples and colonial British architecture within a few blocks of each other, a genuine reflection of the trading crossroads this island has been for centuries. Its hawker food scene, char kway teow and asam laksa chief among the essentials, is regularly named among the best street food anywhere in Asia. A funicular ride up Penang Hill rewards with sweeping views and noticeably cooler air, while a round of golf and serious birdlife along the coastal wetlands round out one of Malaysia's most rewarding stops.

Thailand's grande dame of the Andaman is best seen from the water. Long-tail past the towering limestone stacks of Phang Nga Bay, kayak into hidden hongs, and dive the coral gardens of the Similans, then dine on fiery tom yum and grilled seafood at a beach shack come dusk. Rather than the crowded main pier, SeaDream anchors off quieter shores and drops the marina so you swim and paddle in bathwater seas before an overnight at anchor.

The Cellular Jail's silent, radiating wings once held India's freedom fighters in solitary confinement, a sobering counterpoint to the turquoise water and coral reef that ring these islands today. Beaches at Corbyn's Cove and Radhanagar, regularly ranked among Asia's best, give way just offshore to some of the richest, least-dived reef in the Bay of Bengal. Indigenous Andamanese and Nicobarese communities, some still living in voluntary isolation, make this archipelago as culturally singular as it is remote. A genuinely off-the-map corner of India.

One of the finest natural deep-water harbors in the world drew colonial navies here for centuries, and the same clear water now shelters some of Sri Lanka's best diving and, from spring through autumn, regular sightings of blue and sperm whales just offshore. Koneswaram Temple perches dramatically on Swami Rock above the bay, one of the island's most sacred Hindu sites. Quiet, uncrowded beaches and a growing wellness retreat scene round out Sri Lanka's least-developed major coastal city.

Sri Lanka's capital layers colonial Dutch and British architecture over a much older trading history, this coast drew Arab, Chinese and European merchants for spices and gems long before any of them built a fort here. Galle Face Green's seafront promenade fills each evening with kite-flyers and street-food carts, while the National Museum holds one of the finest collections of Kandyan royal treasures anywhere. Ayurvedic wellness traditions run deep across the island, and wetland birdlife crowds the lagoons at the city's edge. A layered, unpretentious capital.

Chinese fishing nets, cantilevered and unchanged since traders from the Ming court first strung them here six centuries ago, still dip into the harbor at Fort Kochi each evening. Kathakali dancers, Portuguese churches and a Jewish synagogue dating to the 1500s sit within a few streets of each other, testament to a port that has absorbed traders from every direction for a thousand years. Kerala's ayurvedic tradition runs deep here, genuine multi-day treatments rather than a spa-menu approximation, while backwater cruises reveal kingfishers and darters working the palm-lined canals. India's most layered, and most relaxed, port city.

Sun-drenched, palm-fringed and endlessly seductive, Goa blends Portuguese soul with tropical abandon. Wander the baroque churches of Old Goa, a UNESCO treasure, then lose an afternoon among whitewashed villas and fragrant spice plantations in the hinterland. Feni-fuelled beach shacks, prawn balchao and that famous susegad ease, it is India at its most laid-back and colourful. Palolem and Colva put the Arabian Sea at your feet before you toast the sunset with something cold.

India's dazzling maximum city assaults the senses in the best possible way. Sail in beneath the Gateway of India, tour the grand Victorian-Gothic and Art Deco waterfront, take a launch to the rock-cut Elephanta Caves, then dive into the dabbawalas, bazaars and street food of a metropolis that never pauses. SeaDream berths in the heart of the harbour, and being small means a swift, personal shore experience rather than a coach-bound scrum.

voyages.title: Mumbai Ship Showcase
voyages.overview: Overview Ports Suites Land Adventures Testimonials Marine Drive curves along the bay in a long arc of light as the SeaDream III Mumbai Showcase marks a striking arrival. This exclusive event closes SeaDream III's passage from Singapore through Sri Lanka and India's western coast and opens her journey into the Arabian Gulf, introducing our newest yacht to the Gateway of India. Access to the Mumbai Showcase is available only to guests joining the voyage immediately before or after this event. Back-to-back savings are not applicable to Showcase experiences.

voyages.title: Arabian Kingdoms & the Gulf
voyages.overview: Overview Ports Suites Land Adventures Testimonials Depart Mumbai beneath the Gateway of India for the little-known Portuguese enclave of Diu, its sea-battered fort and whitewashed churches drowsing above calm coves, then pause off Porbandar, birthplace of Mahatma Gandhi. Reach Muscat, where the Sultan Qaboos Grand Mosque glows in marble and chandeliers above the Mutrah Souq's frankincense stalls, before threading the fjord-like inlets of Khasab, nicknamed the Norway of Arabia, aboard a dhow trailing dolphins. Anchor off Sir Bani Yas, a UNESCO-listed island sanctuary where oryx and cheetah roam beside a 1,500-year-old Christian monastery, then stand beneath the eighty-two domes of Abu Dhabi's Sheikh Zayed Grand Mosque and the light-dappled galleries of the Louvre. In Doha, wander the sculptural, UNESCO-listed Museum of Islamic Art and the restored lanes of Souq Waqif before the singing dunes of the inland sea. Your voyage concludes in Dubai, where the Burj Khalifa's glittering height gives way to Bedouin firelight and the hush of the Empty Quarter. This voyage offers guests the exclusive opportunity to arrive early for SeaDream III's Mumbai Showcase on March 3, 2029, a rare chance to open the journey with a celebration of the yacht in her first year of sailing.

A little-known former Portuguese enclave off Gujarat, all whitewashed churches and sea-battered forts. Explore the imposing Diu Fort above the waves, the atmospheric St Paul's Church, and quiet lanes where two cultures have blended for centuries. Sandy coves and calm waters ring the island. This is the sort of overlooked, shallow-water gem big ships bypass entirely, SeaDream anchors close, drops the marina, and turns a forgotten coast into a private discovery.

Oman's handsome capital nestles between stark mountains and the Gulf of Oman. Marvel at the marble and chandeliers of the Sultan Qaboos Grand Mosque, haggle for frankincense and silver in the labyrinthine Mutrah Souq, and admire the fortified harbour where superyachts and wooden dhows share the water. SeaDream berths near the corniche, and an overnight lets you take a desert-edge sundowner or a late dinner in Muttrah before exploring at your own pace.

Nicknamed the Norway of Arabia for its dramatic fjords, this rugged peninsula is made for a small yacht. Cruise the sheer cliffs of Khor Ash Sham by dhow as dolphins ride the bow, snorkel hidden coves, and visit the mountain-top Khasab Fort. Big ships simply can't thread these narrow inlets, SeaDream can, folding out the marina in a sheltered fjord so you kayak and swim beneath towering rock in near-total solitude.

An extraordinary wildlife sanctuary rising from the Arabian Gulf. Once a private nature reserve, the island now shelters free-roaming Arabian oryx, gazelles, giraffes and cheetahs across its Arabian Wildlife Park, alongside a 1,500-year-old Christian monastery. Nature drives, mountain biking and salt- flat trails await ashore. SeaDream anchors off this quiet island retreat and drops the marina, pairing a genuine safari with a swim in warm Gulf waters.

The UAE capital marries staggering ambition with genuine culture. Stand humbled beneath the 82 domes of the Sheikh Zayed Grand Mosque, drift through the light-dappled dome of Louvre Abu Dhabi, then chase falcons or dunes in the Empty Quarter. SeaDream berths close to the action, and its scale means the emirate's icons without the mega-ship masses, an elegant, personal finale to a World Cruise leg through Arabia.

Qatar's futuristic capital gleams where desert meets the Gulf. Lose yourself in the sculptural I.M. Pei-designed Museum of Islamic Art, wander the restored Souq Waqif for oud and grilled meats, then head inland to ride the singing dunes to the inland sea. SeaDream docks close to the corniche, and its intimacy means a tailored, unhurried day in a city that rewards curiosity, followed by a glittering skyline sail-away.

Begin where the desert meets ambition. Ascend the Burj Khalifa at dusk, then trade the skyline for the hush of the Empty Quarter, dinner beneath the stars beside a Bedouin fire and a falcon on the wrist. Back aboard, the yacht lies in the heart of Port Rashid while the big ships queue far offshore. It is the rare luxury of arriving grand and slipping away quietly, the city's glitter dissolving astern as SeaDream III melts into the day.

voyages.title: Pharaohs & Ancient Empires
voyages.overview: Overview Ports Suites Land Adventures Testimonials Depart Dubai, where the Burj Khalifa's glass spire gives way to desert hush, for Sur, where craftsmen still build ocean-going dhows by hand in yards little changed for centuries. Reach Salalah, where the Dhofar hills weep frankincense and the UNESCO ruins of Al Baleed rise beside a lagoon, then call at Jeddah's newly UNESCO-listed Al-Balad, a labyrinth of coral-stone houses and carved roshan balconies barely touched by tourism, with Yanbu's restored Old Town and pristine reefs following soon after. From Safaga, journey inland to Luxor's colossal Karnak columns and the painted tombs of the Valley of the Kings, then from Aqaba climb to Petra, where the Treasury glows rose-pink at the end of a wind-carved canyon, Wadi Rum's sands stretching beyond. Sail on past Sharm el-Sheikh's coral walls before threading the Suez Canal itself, a slow, cinematic passage between two seas with desert running to both horizons. Alexandria opens the road to Giza's pyramids and Tutankhamun's gold, Kuşadası to the marble streets of Ephesus, and Syros to Ermoupoli's neoclassical squares. Your voyage concludes in Piraeus, gateway to Athens, where the Parthenon's honeyed marble crowns the Acropolis above a city that still belongs to its goddess.

Sur still builds ocean-going dhows by hand, their timber hulls rising in yards little changed for centuries. Wander the whitewashed lighthouse village of Ayjah at the harbor mouth, then drive to Ras al-Jinz, where green turtles haul ashore to nest under moonlight. Few large ships can call here; SeaDream III's shallow draught slips into a working Arabian port most cruisers only read about, leaving you among fishermen and frankincense rather than crowds.

In the Dhofar hills, gnarled frankincense trees still weep the resin that once made this coast richer than gold. Walk the UNESCO ruins of Al Baleed beside the lagoon, taste bananas and coconuts straight from roadside farms, then watch the sea explode through the blowholes at Mughsail. Call after the khareef monsoon and the desert turns improbably, emerald green. This is Arabia at its most fragrant and least expected, a harbor the fleets sail past.

Jeddah's Al-Balad quarter is a labyrinth of coral-stone houses and carved wooden roshan balconies, newly UNESCO-listed and barely touched by tourism. Sip cardamom coffee in a merchant's courtyard, haggle in souks thick with oud and spice, then walk the corniche as the Red Sea turns molten at sunset. The historic gateway to Mecca, one of Arabia's most beguiling old cities, has opened to guests only recently and is reached by ship rarer still.

A historic Red Sea trading port that once supplied pilgrims traveling overland to Mecca, Yanbu's old town, Al-Balad, still holds coral-stone merchant houses several centuries old. The reef just offshore, part of the same system that runs the length of the Red Sea, remains far less dived than its Egyptian counterparts, and the beaches here are correspondingly quieter. A genuinely under-the-radar stop on Saudi Arabia's newly opening coast.

Safaga (Luxor) is your desert doorway to Luxor, the greatest open-air museum on earth. Stand small before the colossal columns of Karnak, descend into the jewel-bright painted tombs of the Valley of the Kings, and drift over the Nile's temples in a dawn hot-air balloon. Return to the ship's cool as the day's heat breaks, no sprawling resort, no scramble for the tender. Few voyages deliver ancient Thebes and a thalassotherapy soak in the same afternoon.

From Aqaba's coral-fringed shore, the road climbs to Petra, where the Treasury glows rose-pink at the end of a mile-long canyon slot carved by wind and water. Spend the afternoon among Nabataean tombs, then let Wadi Rum's Martian sands, where Lawrence once rode, take your breath at dusk. Back at the Gulf, the fringing reefs off Aqaba's beach clubs and dive centres are a few minutes from the berth. Three deserts, one warm sea, and never a ship to change.

Sharm is where the Red Sea shows off. Snorkel the coral walls of Ras Mohammed, where the reef drops sheer into cobalt depths teeming with fusiliers and turtles, then take the afternoon at a Naama Bay beach club. Ashore, a moonlit drive into the Sinai reaches St Catherine's Monastery beneath the mountain of Moses. Bright reef by day, ancient desert silence by day, and no crowded resort in sight.

Few days at sea rival this one. Take your coffee to the rail as SeaDream III threads the Suez Canal, a ribbon of water splitting two continents, desert running to both horizons while camel trains and fishing skiffs drift past at eye level. On a small ship you feel the scale intimately, the bridge wing close enough to wave to the pilots. It is a slow, cinematic passage between two seas, one to be savoured rather than merely crossed.

Alexandria wears its layers openly, the modernist Bibliotheca echoing the lost ancient library, the Qaitbay fort standing where the Pharos lighthouse once blazed. Then comes the pilgrimage inland to Giza, where the Pyramids and Sphinx rise from the sand exactly as promised and still astonish, before Tutankhamun's gold in the vast Grand Egyptian Museum. Return to a quiet berth in the evening while the giant ships anchor far offshore.

Kusadasi is a beach resort town on Turkey’s Aegean coast and the center of the seaside district of the same name in Aydin Province. The seaside town is also your gateway to the classical ruins at nearby Ephesus, among the world’s best preserved ancient Greco-Roman remains, including its excavated Terrace Houses and House of the Virgin Mary. Kusadasi’s seafront promenade, marina, and harbor are lined with quaint restaurants. Just offshore on Pigeon Island stands a walled thirteenth-century Byzantine castle that once guarded the town. Meet resident wild boars at nearby Dikek National Park, comprised of four secluded beaches, a spectacular coastline, and incomparable views of the Aegean Sea, just one of Turkey’s many protected conservation areas.

The small island of Syros offers the quintessential Greek island holiday experience without the crowds often found in the more well-known Greek Isles. With pristine blue waters, Syros’ breathtaking beaches are sure to impress. Kini, Vari, Azolimnos and Yalissás Beach are among its most famous options to bask in the sun. Beyond its beautiful beaches, Syros is part of the Cyclades, an island group in the Aegean Sea, and is filled with culture and history. The island is also commonly recognized for its Aegean cuisine which features several local specialties, making Syros a culinary destination.

Piraeus, roughly translating to “the place over the passage”, is an important Greek port located within the Athens agglomeration, in the Attica Basin. It is 12 kilometers from the municipality of Athens, considered the fourth largest and is the third most populous amongst all the municipalities of Greece. Now a peninsula, Piraeus, originally a rocky island, was developed in early 5th Century B.C. when it was initially designated as Athens’ import and transit trade port. It is the largest marine-based shipping center of Greece, one of the largest ports in Europe, and considered the second largest passenger port in the world. Inhabited since the 26th Century, it wasn’t until the 6th Century B.C. that Piraeus began catching attention. The land of Piraeus was essentially impassable, flooded by the sea most of the year until centuries passed and the flooding ceased. By the 5th Century B.C. it became a navy base for the Athenian fleet for the natural harbors and the strategic potential they carried. Athenian general and politician Themistocles fortified Piraeus’ three harbors Kantharos, Zea and Munichia, created ship houses and completed his walls in 471 B.C., which led to the port becoming a great military and commercial harbor. There are many archaeological sites, points of interest and entertainment available in Piraeus. Most famous for its tavernas and cuisine, several popular events take place in Piraeus, such as the Ecocinema International Film Festival, the Maritime Festival, the Piraeus Rock Wave Festival and the Three Kings’ Way Festival. There are also many theaters, including the Municipal Theater, the open air Veakeio Theater, and the Menandreio Theater. Museums in Piraeus include the Archaeological Museum of Piraeus, the Merchant Shipping History Institute Exhibition, the Panos Aravantinos Decor Museum, the Georgios Averof Museum Ship and the Museum of Electric Railways. Be sure to catch the panoramic views available from the hill of Kastella, overlooking Athens and the Saronic Gulf!

voyages.title: The Dalmatian Shore
voyages.overview: Overview Ports Suites Land Adventures Testimonials Embark on a 14-night journey from Piraeus, ancient Athens receding astern, for volcanic Milos, its Sarakiniko moonscape and hidden sea caves reached by a yacht's shallow draught, then Fiskardo, the one Kefalonian harbor spared by earthquake, its Venetian pastel houses leaning over the water, with a call at Paxos' hidden coves along the way. Corfu's UNESCO-listed old town unfolds in Venetian arcades and turquoise coves, before SeaDream sails deep into Europe's southernmost fjord to Kotor, its walled UNESCO old town met by 1,350 ramparts steps and an overnight stay in port, one of the Dalmatian coast's storied walled cities alongside Dubrovnik and Hvar. Walk Dubrovnik's mighty medieval walls above terracotta rooftops and the marble Stradun, then wander lavender-scented, UNESCO-listed Hvar and Zadar, where the sea itself plays music through the stone Sea Organ. Rovinj's ochre houses climb to St Euphemia's belltower, with a stop in storybook Piran along the way. Concluding in Venice, arriving by sea past domes and palazzi into the lagoon's shimmering heart, a spectacle few ships are small enough to enter.

Perhaps providing the most diverse and dramatic coastline of all the Greek islands, sheltered, horseshoe-shaped Milos boasts more than 70 beaches and is heralded as the location where Venus de Milo (the ancient Greek goddess Aphrodite) was discovered. Milos has been named “the island of colors” thanks to its volcanic origin, which offers beaches and waters with a variety of colors and distinct beauty. Due to the volcanic origin of its ground, Milos presents an impressive coastal morphology and diversity. There are white-yellow beaches, bays with pebbles surrounded by stones, and white, red, yellow or black rocks. While discovering your favorite sand upon which to relax, don’t overlook Sarakiniko’s volcanic white cliffs and Papafragas’s emerald-green swimming holes and caves—shaped by the island’s unique minerals, including obsidian, barite, and sulphur, which happily bubble up in abundant hot springs.

Fiskardo is a village located about 54 km north of Argostoli and a district of the city of Erisos.The coast around Fiskardo is mainly rocky with numerous pebble-beached coves. There are numerous viewpoints in the area around the village that offer panoramic views of the Ionian Sea including Daskalio island, Ithaca, northwestern Aetolia-Acarnania and the island of Lefkada.

Gaios is a charming port town and spreads itself along the waterfront. You can enter Gaios town from a northerly or southerly direction passing two small islands, the first at the mouth of Gaios harbor is called Panayia (Virgin Mary) on which there is a beautiful white monastery. Gaios is the main port on Paxoi, the smallest of the seven principal Ionian Islands (the Heptanese), in Greece. Gaios is situated on the east coast of the island. It is named after a homonymous pupil of Paul the Apostle, who brought Christianity to the island. Depending on the local conditions, the yacht can anchor on the north side or south side of the town and offers water sports in some of the clearest waters imaginable.

Corfu’s rich multicultural heritage, historic monuments, and unsurpassed natural landscape make the island notable as one of the most cosmopolitan of all Mediterranean destinations. Corfu is the second largest Greek island in the Ionian Sea, situated so far north that parts of its coastline lie off the Albanian coast of Sarandë. In Greek, the island is named Kerkyra, Homer’s beautiful and rich land described in The Odyssey and Odysseus’s last stop on his ten-year journey home to Ithaca. With vibrant wildflowers and slender cypress trees rising from olive groves, Corfu is considered by many to be the most beautiful—and greenest—of all the Greek Islands. Unlike the rest of Greece, Corfu never fell under the Ottoman oppression. Due to the successive domination of the Venetians, French, and the British over the centuries the island has become part of the Western rather than the Levantine world. Venetian culture wielded strong influence throughout the island, the town of Corfu reminiscent of Venice and Florence, Italy. In the beautifully preserved Old Town, a UNESCO World Heritage site since 2007, Renaissance, Baroque, and Classical influences came to be successfully applied to local artistic traditions. The cobblestone streets and pastel-colored Venetian architecture of the Old Town are a gem for sightseeing, boasting the fifteenth-century Old Fortress of Corfu, constructed on the site of a former Byzantine castle. To the West, the Venetian-constructed New Fortress features a network of underground tunnels and views that overlook the harbor. The Archaeological Museum contains artifacts from the Archaic period, including bronze and marble statues, clay pottery, and parts of ancient temples. Best explored by foot, visitors to Old Town note the charm of Spianada Square and Liston Street, reminiscent of Rue de Rivoli in Paris. Nearby, explore the Achillion Palace, built in 1890 as the summer retreat of Austria’s Empress Elizabeth. Nature lovers will find unmatched scenery at secluded La Grotta Beach, where swimming, snorkeling, and cliff diving opportunities are plentiful, and the Corfu Trail, extending from Asprokavos along the south coast up to Agios Spiridon in the north. This off-the-beaten-path hiking trail passes through rolling olive groves, rugged gorges, traditional Greek villages, and ancient monasteries that line its route.

Kotor is a coastal town in Montenegro. The old Mediterranean port of Kotor is surrounded by an impressive city wall built by the Republic of Venice and the Venetian influence remains dominant among the architectural influences. In 1979 the Bay of Kotor, City of Kotor and the surrounding territory have been listed in the UNESCO Heritage as a Cultural Site. SeaDream usually navigates close by the small islands of St. George and Our Lady of the Reef. The Bay of Kotor stretches 28 km and is one of the most indented parts of the Adriatic Sea. It is sometimes called the southern-most fjord in Europe (though it is actually a submerged river canyon called a ria). SeaDream typically docks steps away from the town. SeaDream has arranged a few different Yachting Land Adventures. One of them is a walking discovery and the other will show you the heritage and countryside of Montenegro. For the active guests, there’s incredible biking along the coast as well as a hike up to the fortress. On occasion, SeaDream may dock in the bay and tender directly to the town. We regret that watersports are not allowed in this protected area.

Jutting into the southern Adriatic Sea coast, Dubrovnik—dubbed the “Pearl of the Adriatic”—is perhaps the most picturesque city on the Dalmatian Coast. A key Mediterranean maritime power from the 13th century, Dubrovnik has preserved its storied mix of Gothic, Renaissance, and Baroque churches, monasteries, palaces, and fountains. Its Old Town is a UNESCO World Heritage site adorned with the ancient city walls and Rector’s Palace. SeaDream anchors off the walled city as a port of call and tenders directly to the town gate.

Korčula may be the actual birthplace of Marco Polo! This is an island in the Adriatic Sea, in Southern Dalmatia and is considered by our guests as one of their favorites. One activity offered sells out every time so book early the Buggy Safari. As SeaDream typically anchors off Korcula expects the water toys to be used from the marina platform. As the island is relatively flat, this is a great biking destination as well.

Hvar is a Croatian island in the Adriatic Sea. The island of Hvar is somewhat unusual as it is blessed with a large fertile coastal plain and fresh water springs. Its hillsides are covered in pine forests, with vineyards, olive groves, fruit orchards and lavender fields in the agricultural areas. The climate is characterized by mild winters and warm summers with many hours of sunshine. Guests have an option to kayak down the coastline on one of our land adventures or take an independent hike up to the fortress to have some incredible views of the picturesque harbor. You also have an option to bike across the island to Starigrad and meet up with the other guests on the land adventure called “The best of Both Worlds".

Welcome to the Dalmatian Coast. Zadar is the oldest inhabited city in Croatia, and dates back to 59 BC when the city was a Roman municipality featuring traditional Roman infrastructure and early urban planning. The city’s modern history includes major transformations during World War II and during the 1990’s during the country’s war of independence. Enjoy the beautiful streets, amazing architecture, and beautiful culture that the city had to offer.

Opatija is a tranquil resort sometimes referred to as “Croatian Monte Carlo” on the sheltered east coast of the Istrian peninsula of Croatia. This village is a complete contrast to the dry Dalmatian coastal towns further south. Green hillsides give way to gardens and parks full of exotic plants down by the ocean. This town was developed in the 1880s specifically as a chic resort. Its mild climate and stunning setting made it a favorite winter destination for the 19th century Austrian and Hungarian aristocracy. Most of the hotels in town were constructed from this period. Opatija's highly jagged and rocky coast is bordered by a shady promenade, the Lungomare, which extends for 12km to the picturesque village of Lovran. Along the way, there are dozens of picturesque secluded coves to stretch out a towel along the rocks and jump into the sea.

Rovinj is a popular tourist resort in Croatia situated on the north Adriatic Sea. It is situated on the western coast of the Istrian peninsula and remains as one of the last true fishing ports. SeaDream has arranged some unique land adventure options including; Porec, a Touch of History, Culture & The Family Tradition of Wine Making, and the very popular Searching For Truffles in the Countryside. SeaDream is scheduled to anchor to offer water sports activities from the marina (Permission and conditions pending).

Piran may be the most beautiful of Slovenia's coastal towns. It is perched on a tiny piece of land jutting into the sea. It has the feeling of being more like an Italian coastal town, without all the tourists. Piran was part of the Venetian empire from the late 13th century to the end of the 18th century and also had some influence from Austria-Hungary Empire.

Venice has been known as the "Queen of the Adriatic", "City of Water", "City of Masks", "City of Bridges", "The Floating City", and "City of Canals". Luigi Barzini, writing in The New York Times, described it as "undoubtedly the most beautiful city built by man". Venice has also been described by the Times Online as being one of Europe's most romantic cities. Founded in the 5th century, the city stretches across 118 small islands in the marshy Venetian Lagoon along the Adriatic. In 1987 Venice and its Lagoon was inscribed as a UNESCO Heritage site. SeaDream typically docks at the San Basilio pier after navigating by the famous St. Mark’s Square down the grand canal. With its yacht stature, SeaDream vessels are amongst the very few commercial vessels that can navigate this famous waterway. SeaDream does offer Land Adventures when overnighting. You can also contact our destination specialists should you need a private arrangement, transfer or hotel recommendation.

voyages.title: The Tyrrhenian & Riviera
voyages.overview: Overview Ports Suites Land Adventures Testimonials Depart Venice, the lagoon's domes fading behind, for Ravenna, where eight UNESCO mosaic monuments blaze in gold and lapis beside Dante's tomb, then Otranto, Italy's easternmost point, its cathedral floor a medieval world map in tesserae. Round Sicily's coast to Taormina, where the ancient Greek theatre frames smouldering Mount Etna, before the pastel villages of the Amalfi Coast cling to cliffs above a jewel-blue sea, limoncello and a striped cathedral awaiting ashore, with Stromboli's volcanic glow visible on the Aeolian horizon beyond. Capri rewards a lingering call, its Blue Grotto glowing sapphire and the Faraglioni sea-stacks rising beyond SeaDream's marina, while Civitavecchia opens the road to Rome's Colosseum, Forum and Sistine ceiling, a UNESCO city of endless layers. Elba's Napoleonic fortifications, Livorno's gateway to Michelangelo's David and Pisa's leaning tower, and the Cinque Terre views from UNESCO-listed Portovenere follow in turn, before Portofino's yacht-filled harbour and Castello Brown crown the Ligurian coast. Your voyage concludes in Nice, where the Promenade des Anglais unfurls beneath a cobalt Riviera sky.

Once the capital of the Western Roman and Byzantine empires, Ravenna guards the finest mosaics outside Istanbul. Stand beneath the gold-ground dome of the Basilica of San Vitale, then the star-strewn ceiling of the Mausoleum of Galla Placidia, sights that stopped even Cole Porter in his tracks. Dante wrote his final lines here and lies in a quiet tomb near San Francesco, while the Po Delta's wetlands just beyond town shelter flamingos and herons among the reeds. Round out the day with a glass of Sangiovese di Romagna and a folded piadina, Ravenna's own street food. History, wine and birdlife in one understated port.

The easternmost town on the Italian mainland, Otranto enchants with its medieval architecture and relaxed beachfront atmosphere. As you approach the modest façade of the town’s 11th-century cathedral, admire the delicately carved rose window, a preview of the wonders found within, which include an extraordinary mosaic floor known as the Tree of Life. The imposing Castello Aragonese invites exploration both along the ramparts and in the dry moat, a perfect vantage point from which to admire the fort’s massive cylindrical towers. Sun-lovers flock to the town’s beaches, which wrap around a protected cove lapped by gentle waves. While roaming the Old Town’s warren of narrow streets and cozy squares, you’ll discover enticing shops and eateries housed in age-old stone buildings. Later in the day, both residents and visitors congregate on the seaside promenade for their passeggiata, a typical Italian stroll that affords marvelous views of the sparkling sea. Stop at one of Otranto’s many excellent restaurants for a taste of orecchiette, which amusingly means small ear in Italian and is a popular regional pasta often served with savory ricotta.

SeaDream yachts anchor in the bay of Giardini Naxos and offer fantastic views of recently awarded UNESCO Natural Site of Mt. Etna (2013) as well as Taormina perched on the cliffside. Shuttle bus service has been arranged to transport guests from Giardini Naxos to the entrance gate of Taormina town up to Castelmola which provides amazing views of the surrounding areas. Perhaps the “must do” adventure here would be to ascend Mt. Etna with your fellow SeaDreamers. Kindly check the Land Adventure tab for the specifics. Other options include an incredible and authentic feast at the Godfather Villa. As we are anchored and if conditions allow, we will offer water sports both in the morning and in the afternoon.

Amalfi is a picturesque town in the province of Salerno, in the Campania region of Italy. With its incredible views, it is the central town that makes up the very famous and UNESCO awarded Amalfi Coast (Costiera Amalfitana). Amalfi sports some impressive medieval architecture including; its cathedral of Sant'Andrea (St. Andrew), the church tower, the convent of the Cappuccini, founded by the Amalfitan Cardinal Pietro Capuano. They richly represent the artistic movement prevailing in Southern Italy. From Amalfi, we have created two exciting land adventures for you. One to Scenic Ravello and the other to Fascinating Pompeii. You may also choose to play from the yacht’s marina (Permission and conditions pending) or go on a very scenic hike with one of the officers.

Sitting pretty in the Gulf of Naples, just off the Sorrentine Peninsula, the island of Capri is well known today for its breathtaking landscapes and upscale beach resorts. The island has two harbors, Marina Piccola and Marina Grande. While human presence on the island can be dated back to the Neolithic and the Bronze Age, it was Emperor Augustus who most famously developed Capri by building villas, temples, and planted gardens. Popular to both visitors and native Italians alike, Capri is known for its boutique hotels, trendy restaurants, and annual international film festival, and is a favorite yachting destination. The island also offers many historic landmarks and highlights, including Grotta Azzurra, Villa Jovis, Giardini di Augusto, Certosa di San Giacomo, Villa San Michele di Axel Munthe, and the uniquely shaped Faraglioni Rocks. Mt. Solero marks the highest point of Capri, at 589 meters (about 1932 ft) at its peak. There is also a statue of Emperor Augustus on the mount, who first landed on Capri, over 900 species of vegetation, and, of course, incredible views. Two different hiking routes lead up the mountain and are worthy of exploration. On many itineraries, SeaDream yachts dock alongside in Capri until midnight, allowing guests to step off the yacht and into Capri with ease, without tendering ashore—a unique experience due to the intimate size of our yachts. For those who may not be familiar with the island, Capri offers a sophisticated charm that comes alive in the evening. A guest favorite includes boarding the funicular that runs between the port in Marina Grande and the Piazzetta in Capri town above, where incredible views, buzzing bistros, and luxe boutiques await.

Civitavecchia is a major port located in Rome, primarily utilized for maritime transportation of goods, as well as a fishing port. The commune’s name means “ancient town” and is one of the “Motorways of the Sea” in the Mediterranean, functioning as one of the main links between the mainland of Italy and Sardinia. The ancient name of the port was “Centumcellae,” first mentioned in a letter written by Pliny the Younger in 107 A.D., although scholars debate on whether the name was about the number of rooms of the Trajan Villa, or the number of natural creeks on the coast. Civitavecchia is a part of the Lazio Territory, an area which was confirmed to have social groups since pre-historic times, and the modern town was built over a pre-existing settlement of the Etruscan people in 107-108 B.C.E. (who debated to have founded Rome). In the beginning of the 2nd century, the harbor and town of Centumcellae were simultaneously developed by Emperor Trajan in the territory of Aquae Tauri. As the town became more popular for ships traveling westbound, the Thermal Baths were constructed on the hill of Ficoncella. Centumcellae flourished in the Imperial Age, and by 538 A.D., it had become a Byzantine stronghold. In 728 A.D., it became a member of the Papal States. The Saracens raided Centumcellae many times in the 9th century, prompting Pope Leo VII to have a newer and more secure settlement built by 854. The town, then known as Civita Vetula, was under the rule of several lords, and the Popes temporarily lost control during the French Rule in 1798-1815. In 1870 it entered the Kingdom of Italy. Civitavecchia was severely damaged during WWII, destroying many of the ancient monuments including Forte Michelangelo, which would be rebuilt in the 1950’s. Popular points of interest include the Forte Michelangelo, Terme Taurine, and Cattedrale di San Francesco. There is a wealth of Roman and Vatican architecture and tourists are encouraged to visit many of the museums and take the cultural tours available in this important sea port.

Porto Ercole meaning “Port Hercules”, is a town located in the municipality of Monte Argentario, in the Province of Grosseto, Tuscany. It is one the two major towns that form the township, along with Porto Santo Stefano located on the opposite side of this unique peninsula. It’s a very picturesque marina with sidewalk boutiques, cafes and restaurants. This is a great start for the Land Adventure traveling to Montalcino for the tasting of fantastic Brunello in one of the most famous Italian wine regions. Other options include hiking to the few castellos (castles) located on top of the three hills surrounding the port. As well as an adventures bike ride to Porto Santo Stefano or for the really energetic to the convent on top of the mountain. There’s also a great golf course and a fantastic boutique hotel called Il Pelicano where guests can enjoy a nice atmosphere and lunch. As we are anchored, guests will also enjoy water sports from the marina platform (Pending local conditions and approvals).

The name Portoferraio, meaning “Iron Port” in Italian, comes from the iron mills that prospered the small town during the 19th century. Due to Napoleon’s exile to Elba in 1814, the entire island enjoyed an age of glory and soon blossomed into a melting pot of different cultures. There are several memories of the past worthy of exploration—from the archaeological findings in Portoferraio’s museums to the impressive fortresses and military constructions such as the Castello del Volterraio and Napoleonic residences. Today Elba’s main attractions include the tranquil beauty of its rugged hills and the crystal-clear blue waters of its bays.

Not only is Livorno a fantastic hub to visit neighboring Pisa, Lucca and Florence. Livorno itself is a great destination. To start with, SeaDream docks in the city center rather than further down in the commercial port that would require shuttle bus service. SeaDreamers can easily walk into town or even to the train station. Some of our officers may offer a bike ride from the port to either Pisa or Lucca – possibly both for the extremely active guest. SeaDream has arranged some expertly guided land adventures to take you to the Unesco Awarded Sites. See the Land Adventures tab for more information.

One word – Incredible! Cinque Terre, Portovenere and the three Island of Palmaria, Tino and Tinetto have been added to the UNESCO World Heritage List in 1997. They have been selected for being distinguished examples of the ways in which man has been able to modify and transform the environment without altering the beauty of the original natural landscape. Most of our valued guests will participate in the ever popular “Cinque Terre: Don’t go Home Without It” Land Adventure. Others may enjoy the guided village walk or go hiking on several trails leading down the coast. Most guests will make a purchase of the amazing local pesto and we are fairly certain our Executive Chef will do the same. Be prepared for an incredible dinner al fresco this evening!

The picturesque fishing village of Portofino can be found along the Italian Riviera, and is one of the most popular resort getaways in all of Italy. Portofino has been a staple of tourism in Italy since the 19th century, officially replacing fishing as its chief industry in 1950. Portofino is twinned with Kinsale, Ireland, and Palma (de Mallorca), Spain. Roman philosopher and military commander Pliny the Elder declared that Portofino was founded by the Romans, and with the high concentration of dolphins found in the Tigullian Gulf, it was named the “Port of the Dolphin” - Portus Delphini. Portofino was primarily a member of the Republic of Genoa in early days, and never provided more than a resting area for the merchant navy due to its naturally cramped harbor. The Republic of Florence purchased Portofino in 1409 from French King Charles VI, yet returned when the Florentines were ousted. Portofino became a part of the Kingdom of Sardinia in 1815, and during Risorgimento, it became a member of the Kingdom of Italy in 1861. Aristocratic visitors from Northern Europe began visiting the town in the 19th century, leading to eventual vacation homes and celebrities appearing in Portofino. Portofino is naturally beautiful port with colorful, iconic architecture that was even replicated as a hotel resort at the Universal Orlando Resort in Orlando. The Tokyo Disney Resort in Japan also created a seaside town based on Portofino. Tourists like to visit the museum Castello Brown, which provides a great view of the town, as well as the churches of St. Martin, Oratorio di Nostra Signora Assunta, and St. George - the latter containing some relics of saints. When visiting Portofino, be sure to take a guided dive to the Portofino Marine Park, as well as take a glimpse at the recently restored famous underwater statue, the Christ of the Abyss.

Nice is the fifth most populous city in France and the second largest on the Mediterranean coast. The city's famous seaside promenade, the Promenade des Anglais ('the Walkway of the English') owes its name to the earliest settlers to this seaside resort. For over a quarter century, the picturesque Nicean surroundings have attracted not only those in search of relaxation but also those seeking inspiration. SeaDream docks in the small port and offers several land adventure options as well as private arrangements and transfers.

voyages.title: Riviera Sun & the Iberian Shore
voyages.overview: Overview Ports Suites Land Adventures Testimonials Journey from Nice to Monte Carlo, superyachts gleaming beneath Monaco's clifftop palace before the harbor's giants stay tethered and SeaDream slips into the old town, then St. Tropez, where a fishing village still hides beneath the glamour of Place des Lices and Pampelonne's golden sand, one of the Riviera's glittering trio alongside Monaco and Portofino. Sanary-sur-Mer's painted fishing boats and Port Vendres' salted-anchovy quays give way to Dali's Costa Brava at Roses and Cadaques, wind-carved cliffs framing a surreal coastline. Barcelona's UNESCO-listed Sagrada Familia pours light through a forest of coloured columns, while Valencia dazzles with Calatrava's futuristic City of Arts and Sciences beside a Gothic old town, a UNESCO treasure of its own. History layers deep in Cartagena's rediscovered Roman theatre, Motril opens the road to Granada's Alhambra, and Puerto Banus berths amid supercars and designer boutiques on the Costa del Sol. The UNESCO-listed Rock of Gibraltar rises improbably, half garrison town, half Mediterranean crag, before Setubal's estuary beaches precede the finale. Disembark in Lisbon, its seven hills glowing gold as fado drifts from candlelit taverns.

The Principality of Monaco is an independent sovereign state composed of four quarters Fontvieille (the newest), Monaco-Ville (the oldest), La Condamine, and Monte Carlo. Monte Carlo is widely known for its casino as well as the Monaco Grand Prix. Monte Carlo is one of Europe's leading tourist destinations as it simply has so much to offer. Some of the sights include the Cathédrale Paroisse, Eglise Sainte Dévôte, Jardin Exotique et Grottes de l'Observatoire, Monaco Top Cars Collection, Musée Océanographique and of course the Palace. SeaDream calls to Monte Carlo for embarkation and on certain voyages as a port of call typically docking along the new pier. There are a few occasions where the yacht may anchor offering tender service to the pier downtown or at Fontvieille. Kindly check the Land Adventures tab to see all of the options including transfers and private arrangements.

St. Tropez located on the French Riviera quite simply may be the most famous resort town in Europe. It is a playground for the fashion models, athletes, movie stars, entertainers and other extremely wealthy summertime guests. There’s much to offer in this resort town, shopping, nightlife (Byblos hotel’s Les Caves du Roy nightclub) exceptional beach clubs such as Le Club 55 and Nikki Beach at Pampelonne. Nearby you can explore some of the hill towns and visit the award winning rose wineries. You can also visit neighboring Grimaud and Port Grimaud or just a little further out golf at a few highly rated courses. SeaDream anchors just off the break wall and tenders directly to the pier downtown.

Sanary-sur-Mer is a Provencal village located in the Var department in the Provences-Alpes-Côtes d'Azur region of France. Most visitors fall in love with the town shortly after they arrive. The harbor has several traditional wooden boats called “pointus” that are used by the fisherman daily. They sell their catch each morning on the harbor front. Market day is always a special treat so plan accordingly. The nearby village of Bandol has some of the oldest vineyards in France. It’s an easy bike ride down the coast from Sanary-sur-Mer. Other options include a land adventure to the nearby town of Castellet a typical hilltop village where you can explore and have a nice wine tasting. Golf at De La Fregate as well as water sports are also on option here.

Few travelers have discovered the small Catalan fishing town nestled between the Mediterranean and the Pyrenees. The town’s name comes from Venus (Portus Veneris) and was part of the kingdom of Majorca during the Middle Ages. The natural beauty of Port-Vendres comes alive in its sandy beaches, pebble coves, and many hiking trails, offering views of the Catalan coast and nearby vineyards. You can hike to Fort Saint-Elmo for panoramic views and to learn about the region's military history. Relax and watch fishing boats arrive at port with their daily catch, served up in the town’s many beachfront restaurants. Explore the town’s rich history by visiting the Obelisk, a 100-foot monument in the center of Royal Square—built in1783 to commemorate U.S. independence, supported by France and declared at the Treaty of Versailles that year. Explore the works of Scottish watercolorist Charles Rennie Mackintosh at his namesake museum, or stroll the gardens of the Dynamiterie de Paulilles, a former explosives factory and today a museum and nature preserve.

Roses (or Rosas in Spanish) is a coastal city and has the largest fishing fleet of the Costa Brava. Even with so many fishermen, this town in Girona thrives on tourism. The town is popular for its splendid beaches and loved for its unique location as it is the only beach resort facing west. This allows tourists and locals alike get to enjoy fantastic sunsets across the Gulf of Roses. SeaDream anchors just of the marina and may offer guests water sports activities.

Overlooking the Mediterranean city, Barcelona is a destination that welcomes exploration. Vibrant and metropolitan, this UNESCO-Awarded city is one of the best-preserved medieval cities in Europe. It is especially notable for its Art Nouveau architecture and the work of Catalan architect Antoni Gaudi, which can be seen throughout the city. His best-known work is the immense, unfinished church of the Sagrada Familia, which has been under construction since 1882 and is still financed by private donations. Completion is planned for 2026. SeaDream overnights in this bustling Mediterranean city and typically docks downtown at the World Trade Center, just steps away from the iconic tree-lined pedestrian La Rambla boulevard
