Valencia is the third largest city in Spain after Madrid and Barcelona. It has more than 2.5 million inhabitants in the metropolitan area. The city is recognized globally partly due to its Unesco Heritage Status as well as the City of Arts and Sciences. The Port of Valencia is a very busy commercial port. It is the 5th busiest container port in Europe and the largest in the Mediterranean. SeaDream docks as close to the city center as possible – just along the Grand Prix Raceway. SeaDream offers both day trips as well as a very popular evening adventure called “Valencia Buzzes at Night”.

Cartagena was founded in the 3rd century BC and has been a major naval station. It is located in the Region of Murcia, southeastern Spain. Thanks to its strategic position on the Mediterranean, Cartagena has been inhabited by many different cultures which have left their mark on its rich cultural heritage during a glorious and turbulent history. It’s a very pleasant and relaxing city to walk around. SeaDream makes it easy is the yacht docks in the center of town. Guests have an option of a walking discovery adventure as well as resort golf at La Manga. Some guests also enjoy independent usage of the mountain bikes.

Puerto Banus is a very upscale marina to the west of Marbella, Spain on the Costa del Sol. It was built in 1970 by Jose Banus, a local property developer, as a luxury marina and shopping complex for the jet-set. The focal point of Puerto Banus is the marina. It is also a scene for many exotic cars that are owned by international celebrities and wealthy owners that also own large mega yachts. Our local agent tells us that SeaDream is the only commercial yacht that has docked in Banus.

Gibraltar is a British Overseas Territory located at the entrance of the Mediterranean on the southern end of the Iberian Peninsula. Most visitors arriving by sea are impressed by the rock’s enormous visual impact. Only covering an area of 2.3 square miles (6.0 sq. km.) several sites are a must-see! Some of the “can’t miss” options include the Great Siege Tunnels, St. Michael’s Cave, The Moorish Castle, The Lighthouse at Europa Point and shopping – yes shopping. SeaDream docks at the passenger terminal and has the coaches for the land adventures just outside. It is an easy walk downtown to the duty-free area. Bikes are available should you want to bike up the rock.

Setubal sits pretty in the Lisbon and Tagus Valley region of Portugal on the edge of the Setubal peninsula, on the north bank of the Sado Estuary. This lovely historic town boasts notable landmarks such as the 16th-century Monastery of Jesus and the São Julião Church. A charming, strollable destination, Setubal is known for its vibrant food culture, including its local wines, fresh seafood, and local specialty, choco frito (fried cuttlefish). Stroll its waterfront, where traditional fishing boats bob gently against the backdrop of St. Philip fortress and the rugged Arrabida mountain range, or lounge one of its several beautiful beaches.

Portugal's bustling capital showcases a rich contrast of the historical and modern. Situated near the Tagus River and endlessly sunny, Lisbon embodies a unique beauty and an internationally acclaimed architectural singularity. Its charming hilly neighborhoods boast winding, cobblestone streets and pastel-painted homes and cafés, which happily serve up the city’s signature cuisine, including pastel de nata and custard tarts. From imposing Sao Jorge Castle, the view encompasses the city’s Old Town, Tagus Estuary, and suspension bridge; the National Azulejo Museum displays 5 centuries of decorative ceramic tiles.

voyages.title: Iberia & the Bay of Biscay
voyages.overview: Overview Ports Suites Land Adventures Testimonials Starting in Lisbon, tiles and golden light giving way to Porto, where the Dom Luis bridge leads to Vila Nova de Gaia's cool port-wine cellars and the Douro's tumbling terraces. Sail up the Garonne into Bordeaux, a UNESCO city of honey-stone facades, for lunch among Saint-Emilion's medieval lanes and a tasting at the futuristic Cite du Vin. La Rochelle's twin stone towers guard a bustling old port of oysters and Cognac, before Guernsey's granite cliffs and Victor Hugo's Hauteville House offer a secret the Channel keeps well. Anchor off Cowes, spiritual home of yachting since Queen Victoria's day, its racing fleets and Osborne House rounding out a quintessentially English day ashore. Your voyages ends docked in London, sailing up the Thames as Tower Bridge raises its bascules to welcome you into the Upper Pool beside HMS Belfast, one of the rarest arrivals in world cruising, the Tower's ramparts and Borough Market close at hand. This voyage offers guests the exclusive opportunity to extend their stay for SeaDream III's London Showcase on May 25, 2030, a rare chance to conclude with a celebration of the yacht in her first year of sailing.

days.note: Portugal's bustling capital showcases a rich contrast of the historical and modern. Situated near the Tagus River and endlessly sunny, Lisbon embodies a unique beauty and an internationally acclaimed architectural singularity. Its charming hilly neighborhoods boast winding, cobblestone streets and pastel-painted homes and cafés, which happily serve up the city’s signature cuisine, including pastel de nata and custard tarts. From imposing Sao Jorge Castle, the view encompasses the city’s Old Town, Tagus Estuary, and suspension bridge; the National Azulejo Museum displays 5 centuries of decorative ceramic tiles.

Straddling the mouth of the Douro River, the splendid city of Oporto holds such architectural importance that the entire historic center has been designated a UNESCO World Heritage site. A great place to begin your exploration is Praça da Liberdade, a lengthy public esplanade lined with graceful 19th-century buildings. You’ll find the city has no shortage of marvelous churches, from the imposingly fortified Porto Cathedral to the graciously appointed Clérigos Church, whose soaring bell tower offers panoramic vistas over the city’s picturesque red-tile roofs. In the 1906 Lello Bookstore, prepare to be swept away by elaborate art nouveau features including a sinuous double staircase and a luminous stained-glass skylight. But what’s a visit to Oporto without sampling its signature export, the fortified wine that shares the city’s name. Tour one of the illustrious cellars dotting the Douro’s southern bank, where port is crafted just as it has been for centuries, and savor exquisite samples of the sweet libation. When evening comes, take advantage of Oporto’s reputation as the best place to eat in Portugal, perhaps choosing among the delectable cod dishes for which the city is renowned.

France’s Atlantic shore between Pointe de Grave, at the mouth of the Gironde River, and Biarritz, at the foot of the Pyrenées, is known as Côte d’Argent. The river narrows near Bordeaux, center to one of the world’s most celebrated wine-producing regions. More than 10,000 vineyards dot the countryside, providing most of the Epicurean nation’s Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Cabernet Franc, Sémillon, Savignon Blanc, and Muscadelle grapes. Bordeaux reveals itself through taste and texture, historic stone façades, vine-covered hills, and the simple pleasure of lingering over a perfectly chosen glass. With hundreds of historical buildings and monuments, dozens of art galleries and museums, and distinctive French cuisine, Bordeaux is simply unmissable.

Twin medieval towers still guard the harbor entrance where a great chain once stretched to keep out raiders, a fittingly dramatic gateway to one of France's prettiest Atlantic ports. A short hop across the water, the Ile de Re rewards a bicycle and an afternoon among salt marshes, oyster beds and the little egrets that stalk them, while La Rochelle's own thalassotherapy tradition draws on the same Atlantic waters for a genuinely restorative spa afternoon. Around the old port, seafood brasseries serve the day's oyster and mussel catch with a chilled glass of the region's own Charentais wine. Maritime history, birdlife and a proper French table, all within a short walk of the quay.

Boasting an immensely picturesque coastline, the Channel Island of Guernsey has long attracted artists such as Auguste Renoir to its welcoming shores. In the capital of St. Peter Port, wander through commanding Castle Cornet, a 13th-century marvel of military engineering that sits on a rocky headland jutting out at sea. Admire some of the earliest heated glass houses at the Candie Gardens, whose elegantly landscaped grounds are laid out with Victorian thoughtfulness and contemplate Victor Hugo’s not entirely uncomfortable exile at Hauteville House, the splendid manor where he wrote Les Miserables. Hop on a bicycle to explore the picturesque hills and dales of the island, perhaps riding past a herd of the island’s famed namesake cows, and revitalize at an authentic tea house, where age-old traditions are carefully observed. For that perfect keepsake, shop along cobbled streets overflowing with charm, maybe pausing at a fresh-caught seafood restaurant for a taste of the island’s famed crab. No matter how you choose to spend your time, the leisurely pace of life in delightful Guernsey will replenish your spirit.

The spiritual home of British yacht racing, Cowes has watched sail regattas round its harbor mouth since before most yacht clubs existed, Cowes Week remains one of the sport's great fixtures. Queen Victoria's seaside retreat, Osborne House, sits a short drive away, gardens and beach included, while a handful of English vineyards on the island's sheltered south coast now produce sparkling wine serious enough to trouble Champagne. Red squirrels, found almost nowhere else in southern England, still thrive in the island's woods. A very British kind of maritime charm.

Synonymous with royalty, London is a living testament to the lofty achievements of the mighty kings and queens that have presided over this storied island nation. Witness the changing of the guard at gracious Buckingham Palace, a cherished custom that is both timeless and precisely on time, and tour the Houses of Parliament, the city’s other magnificently ornate center of power and a UNESCO World Heritage site. Cross the iconic Tower Bridge on your way to view the utterly dazzling Crown Jewels, which are kept in the once-forbidding Tower of London, another UNESCO site. After refreshing with a pint of beer at a classic English pub, sample the best of contemporary art at the essential Tate Modern, which is housed in a former brick power station. Next door, you’ll find the faithful reconstruction of Shakespeare’s Globe Theatre, where Romeo and Juliet can keep falling in love for eternity. Stroll through immaculately manicured Hyde Park, shop in tony Covent Garden and take in the entire city from the London Eye observation wheel, as the resonant chimes of Big Ben comfort both Londoners and visitors with time-honored tones known the world over.

voyages.title: London Ship Showcase
voyages.overview: Overview Ports Suites Land Adventures Testimonials Tower Bridge rises above the Thames as the SeaDream III London Showcase claims its place among the season's finest moments. This exclusive event closes SeaDream III's passage through the Iberian Peninsula and France's Atlantic coast and opens her journey into Northern Europe, introducing our newest yacht to one of the world's most storied rivers. Access to the London Showcase is available only to guests joining the voyage immediately before or after this event. Back-to-back savings are not applicable to Showcase experiences.

voyages.title: Celtic Shores & the Irish Sea
voyages.overview: Overview Ports Suites Land Adventures Testimonials Embark in London for a journey around Britain and Ireland's westward coasts, beginning at Portsmouth, where HMS Victory and the Mary Rose recall a thousand years of naval history beneath the soaring Spinnaker Tower. Continue to Fowey, a pastel river port steeped in du Maurier's Cornwall, then reach the remote Isles of Scilly, where turquoise shallows lap white sand coves and puffins wheel above Tresco's fabled Abbey Garden. Cross to Ireland at Cobh, Cork's poignant last port of call for the Titanic, before savoring Kinsale's yacht-filled harbour beneath Charles Fort and tracing famine history at New Ross. In UNESCO-listed Dublin, wander Georgian squares and browse the illuminated Book of Kells, then discover the Celtic and Viking layers of the Isle of Man at Douglas. Belfast's Titanic story and the basalt columns of the Giant's Causeway from Portrush give way to Islay's peated distilleries, Oban's fresh langoustine, and Arran's granite ridges. Your voyage comes to a close in Glasgow, on Ayrshire's sun-catching coast, within easy reach of golf's holiest links. This voyage offers guests the exclusive opportunity to arrive early for SeaDream III's London Showcase on May 25, 2030, a rare chance to open the journey with a celebration of the yacht in her first year of sailing.

Portsmouth lies on Portsea Island, a narrow peninsula that separates two inlets of the English Channel, Portsmouth Harbor to the west and Langstone Harbor to the east. Home to Britain’s Royal Navy, the city’s rich military history includes an historic dockyard that houses many notable ships, including HMS Warrior, the first iron-hulled warship, and HMS Victory, Admiral Horatio Nelson's flagship during 1805’s Battle of Trafalgar. Beyond military history, Portsmouth is marked by Spinnaker Tower, a 170-meter structure with sky-high observation decks providing views of the harbor. Browse the shops at Gunwharf Quays and explore Old Portsmouth for its pubs and restaurants, Portsmouth Cathedral, Royal Garrison Church, and Square and Round Tower, two historic defense towers dating to the fifteenth century. Relax and stroll the promenade at Southsea Beach, stretching from Old Portsmouth to the estuary, with King Henry VIII’s Southsea Castle jutting up to the water’s edge.

Dock in Fowey Harbor to explore the small town of Fowey, England, sitting pretty on the south coast of Cornwall, just a stone’s throw away from the Biomes House, the largest contained rainforest, and the award-winning garden restoration project, the Lost Gardens of Heligan. Established hundreds of years ago as a trading and navel town, Fowey boasts a heady mix of coastal walking paths, quaint streets, and luxe boutiques, backgrounded by a picturesque countryside and thirteenth-century Restormel Castle.

The Isles of Scilly, an archipelago off the Cornish coast of southwest England, is defined by its heathland and fringed by sandy beaches. On Tresco, one of the five inhabited islands in the archipelago, Tresco Abbey Garden is home to subtropical plants and the Valhalla Museum, displaying a diverse collection of artifacts. As a small, privately owned island, Scilly’s ambiance of exclusivity extends to its upscale cafés and art gallery. The tower of 17th-century Cromwell’s Castle stands north of Tresco and is one of a handful of stone fortifications that survive from England’s Interregnum (“between reigns”) period of 1649-1660.

Sitting pretty in southwest Ireland in Cork Harbor, one of the world’s largest natural harbors, Cork enjoys a rich maritime heritage. Founded in the sixth century as a monastic settlement, Cork was expanded by the Vikings and granted a charter in 1185 by Prince John. Also called "the Rebel City" for its support of the Yorkist cause during the Wars of the Roses, there is much to see and do both in and around the city. Cork is recognized for its St. Fin Barre’s Cathedral, a nineteenth-century Gothic-style cathedral with stained-glass windows, stone carvings, and tower that offers panoramic views of the city. The English Market, selling its wares since 1788, is one of the oldest and most historically rich covered markets in Europe, offering both local and international delicacies. Cork is your gateway abundant castles, most notably the Blarney Castle, home to the infamous Blarney Stone and the Rock of Cashel, also known as “High Kings of Tipperary” as it was the historical seat where the High Kings of that region were crowned and held court. The High Kings of Tipperary boasts thousand-year-old structures, including a round tower, Romanesque chapel, and Gothic cathedral. Whiskey lovers can also visit the Jameson Midelton Distillery and Museum in nearby Midleton, set on over 15 acres, to see the world’s largest pot still and experience premium whiskey tasting.

Sitting pretty in Kinsale Harbor at the mouth of the Bandon River, just south of Cork, Kinsale enjoys a rich history as a medieval fishing village and important naval port for over 500 years, known for its Battle of Kinsale. The colorful seaside village is strollable, providing easy access to historic sites, museums, and outdoor activities. Kinsale has a celebrated food culture, found in its restaurants, including the Michelin-starred Bastion, and annual gourmet food festivals. Notable buildings include Desmond Castle, built by the ninth Earl of Desmond circa 1500, which has taken on many roles over time, including functioning as a prison, ordnance store, workhouse, and, most recently, the International Museum of Wine. Charles Fort, a seventeenth-century star-shaped fort and Irish National Monument, offers panoramic views and self-guided walks. James Fort, on the river’s opposite bank, boasts grassy headlands and views of the harbor and Kinsale town. Beyond castles, golf lovers can tee off at the world-renowned Old Head Golf Links, sitting on a 220-acre headland jutting into the Atlantic, offering dramatic views and a challenging course.

A quiet market town on the River Barrow turns out to be the ancestral home of an American dynasty, the Kennedy Homestead at nearby Dunganstown still farmed by the family's Irish cousins, and well worth the short drive. The full-scale replica of the Dunbrody famine ship tells the harder side of that same story, of the millions who left this stretch of coast for America in the 1840s. Golf links wind along the Wexford coast nearby, while the Saltee Islands just offshore hold one of Ireland's great seabird colonies. A small, unassuming port with an outsized story to tell.

Dublin, the capital of the Republic of Ireland, sits on Ireland’s east coast at the mouth of the Liffey River. The Vikings settled in Dublin from the 841 AD onward, and existing remnants of Viking history infuse the city. During their reign Dublin became the most important town in Ireland as well as a center for western Viking expansion and trade. As the second city of the British Empire in the 18th century, Dublin entered its architectural golden age and is famous for the Georgian architecture of this period. Historic buildings include the thirteenth-century Dublin Castle and imposing St Patrick’s Cathedral, founded in 1191. City parks include landscaped St. Stephen’s Green and strollable Phoenix Park. The National Museum of Ireland explores Irish heritage and culture. You’ll find just as much allure in Dublin’s parks and expansive green spaces as you will in the city’s lively quarters—from cycling through the quiet glens of Phoenix Park to meandering amid orchids inside the glasshouses at the National Botanic Gardens.

The islands of Great Britain, Ireland, the Isle of Man, the Inner and Outer Hebrides, the Northern Isles of Orkney and Shetland—and thousands of smaller islands—collectively comprise the dreamy British Isles. Rugged cliffs, sandy beaches, and intimate yachting harbors and ports allow a view of island life you haven’t experienced unless you have approached these destinations by yacht. Yachting through the remote Isles of Scilly and castle-dotted, rural Isle of Man transport you to otherworldly locations.

Northern Ireland’s thriving capital of Belfast offers historic landmarks and museums, including the Ulster Museum, the aluminum-clad Titanic Belfast, and the Metropolitan Arts Center (The MAC), located in Belfast’s Cathedral Quarter. Among shipbuilding and the production of rope and tobacco, the city paved the way in the world’s linen industry, and many of its linen houses still remain in the city’s historic Linen Quarter. Stroll the Botanic Gardens, designed in the 19th century by Sir Charles Lanyon. Named for the five caves along the Belfast cliffs, Cave Hill Country Park offers walking trails with incredible views dotted with ancient history, including the nineteenth-century Belfast Castle and the old stone McArt’s Fort, sitting 1,200 feet above sea level. Take in the city’s lively food scene, including St. George’s Market boasting local delicacies. As your gateway to Northern Ireland, Belfast is perfectly positioned for exploration of Giant’s Causeway, Game of Thrones filming locations, and bicycling beyond Belfast.

The small seaside resort town of Portrush (“Port Rois” in Old Irish) sits quietly on the north coast of County Antrim, Northern Ireland. Set on a peninsula that juts into the Atlantic, Portrush boasts stunning beaches, including East Strand, West Strand, and White Rocks, each awarded “Blue Flag” status for their pristine waters. During medieval times, Portrush was a strategic landing place for the castle and settlement at Dunluce, and today its Old Town pays homage to its historic past. Portrush is the gateway to Giant’s Causeway, a geologic wonder of interlocking basalt columns jutting from the sea at the foot of dramatic cliffs.

days.port: Port Ellen, Isle of Islay, Scotland
days.note: In Port Ellen, you can spend the day touring world-renowned distilleries, wandering along a sheltered sweep of sand, or following coastal tracks toward the dramatic cliffs of Mull of Oa. The historic harbor and old maltings recall the village’s rich whisky past, while nearby waters often host seals and seabirds. With its mix of gentle scenery and iconic whisky culture, Port Ellen provides a warm introduction to Islay.

A resort town sitting on the west coast of Scotland in the Firth of Lorn, Oban (in Gaelic, meaning “Little Bay”), charms with its natural beauty. The horseshoe-shaped bay is protected by the island of Kerrera and, beyond that, the Isle of Mull, making it perfect for watersports such as kayaking, canoeing, and fishing. The town grew up around the distillery, founded in 1794, which whisky enthusiasts still visit today. Despite its small size, Oban is known as the “Seafood Capital” of Scotland, serving up fresh seafood in its pubs and restaurants. McGaig’s Tower, a circular tower built from Bonawe granite in 1897, stands on Battery Hill and overlooks the islands of Kerrera, Lismore, and Mull. Just outside the town, visitors find thirteenth-century Dunollie Castle, standing on a rocky ridge overlooking Oban Bay. North of Oban, the natural rock formation of Fingal’s Dogstone is closely tied to Celtic mythology as the location where the giant Fingal would leave his Dog Bran while hunting across the Hebridean Islands.

Often called Scotland in miniature for packing Highland scenery, castles and whisky onto one small island, Arran rises straight from the harbor at Brodick to the granite peak of Goat Fell. Brodick Castle and its gardens sit just above the pier, while the island's own distillery turns out a well-regarded single malt within an easy drive. Seven golf courses share this one small island, along with red deer, seals and a coastline made for walking. A whole Highland holiday, scaled down.

Sitting along the banks of the Clyde River, Glasgow is one of Northern Europe’s most endearing and culturally vibrant cities, boasting a variety of art and museums, galleries, luxe restaurants, and pubs. The city’s Gaelic name, Glaschu, fittingly translates as “dear green place.” Glasgow boasts an incredible architectural heritage, ranging from medieval times to the Victorian and Art Nouveau eras, set within a city full of abundant parks and green spaces, making it ripe for exploration. Glasgow is also home to Scotland’s national opera, ballet, and theater companies and is a UNESCO City of Music, presenting a lively music scene. Defined by a strong sense of community and welcoming ambiance, the dynamic city shines for diversity, from the city’s artsy West End to historic East End, home to the 12th-century Gothic Glasgow Cathedral.

voyages.title: The Hebrides, the Northern Isles & the North Sea
voyages.overview: Overview Ports Suites Land Adventures Testimonials Depart Glasgow for the Hebrides and the remote Northern Isles, calling first at Tobermory, Mull's rainbow row of harbour houses set above waters patrolled by white-tailed eagles. Continue to Portree, gateway to Skye's pinnacled Old Man of Storr and the surreal Quiraing, before reaching Kirkwall, where Orkney's Neolithic village of Skara Brae and the UNESCO-listed Ring of Brodgar predate the pyramids. Anchor off Fair Isle, Britain's remotest inhabited island, home to sixty islanders, a storied bird observatory and the knitwear pattern that bears its name, then berth at Lerwick, Shetland's northernmost port, where Iron Age brochs meet the endless daylight of the simmer dim. Invergordon opens onto Loch Ness and Urquhart Castle, while Dundee's striking V&A stands beside Captain Scott's Discovery. In Leith, climb Edinburgh's Royal Mile to its brooding castle, then sail on to Stavanger's timbered old town and quiet Lillesand before concluding in Oslo, where the Opera House gleams across the fjord and the unhurried calm of a Scandinavian summer lingers. This voyage offers guests the exclusive opportunity to extend their stay for SeaDream III's Oslo Showcase on Jun 22, 2030, a rare chance to conclude with a celebration of the yacht in her second year of sailing.

The city’s Gaelic name, Glaschu, fittingly translates as “dear green place.” Glasgow boasts an incredible architectural heritage, ranging from medieval times to the Victorian and Art Nouveau eras, set within a city full of abundant parks and green spaces, making it ripe for exploration. Glasgow is also home to Scotland’s national opera, ballet, and theater companies and is a UNESCO City of Music, presenting a lively music scene. Defined by a strong sense of community and welcoming ambiance, the dynamic city shines for diversity, from the city’s artsy West End to historic East End, home to the 12th-century Gothic Glasgow Cathedral.

A crescent of brightly painted harbor houses makes Tobermory one of the most photographed small ports in Scotland, its waterfront distillery turning out a well-loved single malt within sight of the pier. The Mull Eagle Watch tracks the white-tailed sea eagles reintroduced to these cliffs, Britain's largest bird of prey, while boat trips regularly turn up minke whales, otters and porpoises in the surrounding sound. A golf course clings to the hillside above town for those who'd rather play through the view. Small, colorful, and genuinely wild at the edges.

The northernmost island in the Inner Hebrides of Scotland, the Isle of Skye is defined by its rugged landscapes, medieval castles, picturesque fishing villages, and otherworldly natural landscapes—grassy moors, steep glens, tumbling waterfalls, rivers, sparkling mountainsides and pristine harbors, inviting exploration.

With seemingly unending miles of coastline and beautiful natural backdrops to explore, the Orkney Islands archipelago lies on the rugged northern tip of Scotland. Ideal for yachting, walking, hiking, and cycling, many of the islands along these shorelines are uninhabited. The capital of the Orkney Islands, Kirkwall, is full of character and Norse heritage. A Royal Burgh since 1486, Kirkwall’s name comes from the Norse word “Kirkjuvagr,” meaning “Church on the bay,” as exemplified by its St. Magnus Cathedral.

The Shetland Islands is a North Sea archipelago, of which only sixteen islands are inhabited, many only accessible via small sailing vessels. The archipelago is perfect for yachting, with a raw, rugged coastline and low rolling hills, providing opportunities for spying wildlife. Shaped by billions of years of shifting sand and sea, Shetland’s natural landscape is among the most dramatic in the world, teeming with wildlife. SeaDream calls on Fair Isle, a small remote island tucked away here, known for both its natural heritage and famous knitwear. Walk or bike its lovely surroundings, perhaps paying a visit to the internationally renowned Fair Isle Bird Observatory or the namesake Lighthouse, the tallest in Shetland.

The Shetland Islands is a North Sea archipelago, of which only sixteen islands are inhabited, many only accessible via small sailing vessels. The archipelago is perfect for yachting, with a raw, rugged coastline and low rolling hills, providing opportunities for spying wildlife. Shaped by billions of years of shifting sand and sea, Shetland’s natural landscape is among the most dramatic in the world, teeming with wildlife from puffins to native Shetland ponies. Lerwick is Shetland’s only town, founded as an unofficial marketplace to service seventeenth-century Dutch herring fleets, and the island’s capital since 1708.

Sitting pretty on an inlet in the North Sea, with stunning views of the western Beins and Black Isle, Invergordon was established by the Gordons of Invergordon Castle in the early 1800s. It became a Royal Navy base in 1913 and played a prominent role in World War I and World War II to which the Invergordon Naval Museum & Heritage Center pays tribute. Outside of its lovely harbor and maritime history, Invergordon is the gateway to the Scottish Highlands, a region defined by Loch Ness Lake the legend of the mythical Loch Ness creature. Scenic walking trails abound, including the Invergordon Mural Trail, decorated by murals painted by local artists, and the Saltburn Woodland Walk. Visit the impressive Dunrobin Castle, one of Britain’s oldest continuously inhabited houses and the largest in the Northern Highlands, and along the way explore local distilleries and sample different whiskies.

A vibrant city on the east coast of Scotland, Dundee boasts more hours of sunshine than any other Scottish city, shining on an abundance of green spaces. Nicknamed the “City of Discovery,” in 2014 Dundee was recognized by the United Nations as the United Kingdom’s first-ever UNESCO-awarded City of Design. Whether you are a history buff, a cultural enthusiast, or nature lover—or all three—Dundee offers a unique glimpse into Scotland. Wander the 400-acre Camperdown Country Park, dotted with neoclassical architecture and over 190 tree species. Engage in outdoor activities, including hiking and golfing, with easy access to St. Andrew’s Golf Course, where golf has been played for six hundred years. Dundee’s redesigned waterfront features the nautical museum Discovery Point, featuring the Royal Research Ship (RRS) Discovery, Captain Scott’s Antarctic expedition ship, and the nineteenth-century warship HM Frigate Unicorn. Galleries and art museums include the McManus Gallery, Verdant Works, and V&A Dundee, dedicated to Scottish design achievements and marked by an exterior that mimics of the cliffs of East Scotland. A walk around Dundee reveals quaint pubs and taverns, offering a selection of beer, whiskies, Scotch pies, and bangers and mash.

Scotland’s hilly capital of Edinburgh is renowned for its history, cultural richness, and architectural majesty. Walk in the footsteps of kings and queens at Edinburgh Castle, perched atop Castle Rock, home to Scotland’s crown jewels and the Stone of Destiny. The Old Town’s distinctive medieval layout, with its narrow streets and hidden courtyards, sets it apart from the planned elegance of Georgian New Town, together a UNESCO World Heritage site. Explore the Old Town’s historic Royal Mile and climb Arthur’s Seat, a hilltop in the 640-acre royal park that offers panoramic views of the city. Visit the National Museum of Scotland and Holyrood Palace, the official residence of the British monarch in Scotland.

Norway's oil capital keeps its wooden-house old town, Gamle Stavanger, immaculately preserved along the harborfront, one of the best-kept collections of 18th-century timber buildings in Northern Europe. It is also the launch point for the hike to Preikestolen, the sheer-sided Pulpit Rock that hangs six hundred meters above the Lysefjord below, one of Norway's iconic views for the reasonably fit. A serious new-Nordic dining scene has grown up around the old harbor to match the oil wealth. History and one of Norway's great hikes, in a single call.

Regularly named Norway's prettiest small town, Lillesand's white wooden houses climb from a sheltered harbor that has drawn sailors and holidaymakers for well over a century. A maze of skerries and islets just offshore makes for some of the country's best small-boat sailing and swimming, while the town's understated spa tradition takes advantage of the same clean southern coast air. Barely a few thousand people live here, and the pace shows it.

Norway is a land steeped in myth, where irascible gods armed with frost and lightning once inspired Viking clans to plunder foreign lands. These days, genteel customs imported from mainland Europe have softened the country’s hard edges, but traces of an unruly past still abound. The exceptional museums dotting the Bygdøy Peninsula hold some of the city’s foremost attractions, including a thousand-year-old longship that was preserved in mud and the 12th-century Gol Stave Church, an exemplar of Norway’s distinctive wood sanctuaries. No less fascinating is a visit to the 1892 Fram, a legendary ship revered for her vital role in early polar explorations. To witness the evolution of Oslo’s soul, contrast battle-hardened Akershus Fortress, a ruggedly elegant citadel wrapped in nearly impregnable ramparts, with the neoclassical Royal Palace, whose formal exterior encloses sumptuously appointed rooms. You might wish to view Edvard Munch’s iconic The Scream, which hangs in the outstanding Norwegian National Gallery amid priceless European and Scandinavian masterworks. In expansive Frogner Park, wander among Gustav Vigeland’s thought-provoking sculptures, and if you’ve worked up an appetite, choose among the many restaurants and cafés lining the charming waterfront district of Aker Brygge.

voyages.title: Oslo Ship Showcase
voyages.overview: Overview Ports Suites Land Adventures Testimonials The Oslofjord lies still beneath the city lights for the SeaDream III Oslo Showcase, a striking moment amid her first voyages. This exclusive event closes SeaDream III's passage through the British Isles and Norway's coast and opens her journey through the Baltic, introducing our newest yacht to the Nordic coast. Access to the Oslo Showcase is available only to guests joining the voyage immediately before or after this event. Back-to-back savings are not applicable to Showcase experiences.

voyages.title: The Baltic Capitals
voyages.overview: Overview Ports Suites Land Adventures Testimonials A roundtrip journey from Oslo that goes to Copenhagen next, where colourful Nyhavn quays and Tivoli's fairy-tale gardens set an effortlessly stylish tone for the world capital of new-Nordic dining. Continue along Poland's amber coast to Gdańsk, then reach Klaipeda, Lithuania's only seaport, pairing a half-timbered German old town with the UNESCO-listed dunes of the Curonian Spit. Riga follows, its medieval guild halls giving way to the world's finest concentration of Art Nouveau facades, before Tallinn's turreted, UNESCO-listed old town casts its fairy-tale spell along cobbled lanes that seem to belong to another age. In Helsinki, the white Lutheran Cathedral presides over Senate Square, while across town a church is carved straight into granite. The sail through Stockholm's pine-clad archipelago unfolds for hours before Gamla Stan's ochre lanes and the salvaged warship Vasa, and walled Visby, a UNESCO Hanseatic jewel on Gotland, tumbles with roses over limestone cottages. Return back to Oslo, where forest, water and Nordic design meet at the fjord's edge. This voyage offers guests the exclusive opportunity to arrive early for SeaDream III's Oslo Showcase on June 22, 2030, a rare chance to open the journey with a celebration of the yacht in her second year of sailing.

There’s much to treasure in glorious Copenhagen, one of Europe’s most beautiful capital cities. No visit is complete without indulging your inner child at the Tivoli Gardens, a fantastical amusement park and pleasure garden that melds the atmosphere of 19th-century Europe with recreations of Far East architecture, all amid wonderfully manicured grounds. After paying your respects to the city’s iconic statue of Hans Christian Andersen’s Little Mermaid, shop to your heart’s content on Strøget, an elegant lane flanked by sophisticated boutiques housed in graceful buildings. Although its exterior is handsomely austere, the interior rooms of the 18th-century Christiansborg Palace are sure to dazzle you with their extravagant stucco ceilings, brilliant chandeliers and gilded furniture. Fast forward to the 19th century at the spectacular Copenhagen Botanical Garden, where innumerable plant species are showcased in absolutely stunning historical glasshouses. Should you have the stomach for it, take in the entire city from the tower of the Church of our Saviour, which must be reached via vertiginous exterior spiral staircase. No matter how you’ve spent your day, a terrific place to wind down is the quayside Nyhavn district, where colorful historic buildings host an eclectic choice of cafés, bars and restaurants.

A Hanseatic port rebuilt stone by stone after the Second World War, Gdansk's Long Market glows with the pastel merchant houses and amber shops that made this the trading capital of Baltic amber for eight hundred years. The Solidarity movement that helped bring down the Iron Curtain was born at the shipyard gates here, told in full at the excellent European Solidarity Center nearby. Golf courses and wide sand beaches line the coast just outside the city, and the Vistula delta's wetlands shelter vast numbers of migratory birds each spring and autumn. A city with amber in its shopfronts and history in its shipyards.

The oldest city in Lithuania and one of the oldest on the Eastern coastline of the Baltic, Klaipeda boasts a perfect mix of charming Old Town architecture, maritime heritage, and rich culture. Formerly an important trading town of the Hanseatic League, Klaipeda is your gateway to the Curonian Spit, a UNESCO World Heritage site, renowned for its otherworldly sand dunes and quaint fishing villages, perfect for hiking or biking.

The Latvian capital holds the largest collection of Art Nouveau architecture anywhere in Europe, entire streets of swirling facades, gargoyles and sculpted faces best explored on foot through the Alberta iela quarter. The medieval Old Town sits a short walk away, UNESCO-listed and dense with Hanseatic history, while the vast Central Market, set inside a run of former Zeppelin hangars, is one of the continent's great food halls. Latvia's own spa and wellness tradition runs deep, not far away, the beach resort town of Jurmala has drawn health-seekers for over a century. A grand, underrated Baltic capital.

Tallinn, Estonia’s capital on the Baltic Sea, is the country’s cultural hub. Its legendary Old Town, a UNESCO World Heritage site and one of the best-preserved medieval cities in Europe, boasts cozy corner cafés, hidden courtyards, and Kiek in de Kök, a 15th-century defensive tower. Lose yourself in the twisting streets of the capital’s historic center, complete with museums and art galleries. The city's hallmark castle is described in countless fairytales. Your SeaDream yacht anchors steps from Tallin's Old Town, in the inner pond.

Helsinki showcases both the traditional with the modern, in every sense. The city’s architecture features stunning Art Nouveau buildings and sleek modern structures including the Sibelius Monument, while you explore the country’s rich heritage at the Suomenlinna Fortress or the Seurasaari open-air museum. Unwind in a traditional Finnish sauna, an integral part of Finnish culture, and take part in the city’s food culture, where beetroot salad and lohikeitto (salmon soup) are staples in its cozy cafés.

An enchanting municipality at the meeting point of Lake Mälaren and the Baltic Sea, the Swedish capital is one of the world’s great maritime cities. Stockholm’s maritime doorstep is a magnificent archipelago of more than 24,000 islands and islets–many just big enough to support a single cottage. As you yacht toward the 13th-century "city that floats on water,” landmarks such as Storkyrkan (Stockholm Cathedral) and Three Crowns Tower come into view. The medieval Gamla Stan district is the historic core of the original Stadsholmen Island settlement.

The Hanseatic walled trading town of Visby on the island of Gotland dates from the Viking Age, formed on a shore with a natural harbor, sheltered by steep cliff formations. This fairytale locale is a UNESCO World Heritage site, known for its well-preserved town wall and medieval fortification and towers. The town’s abundant churches include St. Mary’s Cathedral and the medieval ruins of St. Nicolai and St. Karin.

voyages.title: Coastal Norway & the Arctic Circle
voyages.overview: Overview Ports Suites Land Adventures Testimonials Sart your journey in Oslo and head to Skagen, where two seas meet at Grenen's shifting sandbar, then continue to Kristiansand's white timber Posebyen quarter and skerry-sheltered bathing coves. Bergen, cradled by seven mountains, reveals the Hanseatic wharf of Bryggen before the yacht noses deep into the UNESCO-listed Sognefjord to little Flåm, beneath waterfalls plunging a thousand metres. Olden sits under the blue ice of the Jostedal glacier, and the UNESCO showpiece of Geirangerfjord follows, the yacht's approach passing the Seven Sisters and Bridal Veil falls. Trondheim's Nidaros Cathedral rises over the Nidelva before the yacht crosses the Arctic Circle en route to the Lofoten Islands, anchoring first off Reine, a postcard of red rorbuer cabins beneath granite spires, then Svolvær, where kayaks trace turquoise bays beneath the long daylight of the Arctic summer. The yacht turns within the Trollfjord's narrow granite slot as sea eagles circle overhead, champagne poured on deck before the towering walls fall away. Your voyage concludes in Tromsø, the Arctic's most beguiling city, beneath the soaring Arctic Cathedral.

Skagen sits at the northernmost point of Denmark, tucked in a peninsula where the North Sea meets the Baltic Sea. This remote coastal town, settled in 1400s as a fishing village, provides stunning landscapes of white-sand beaches, unwavering grassland, and verdant forest. Notable is its Old Church, which since 1775 has been buried in sand, and the Skagen Museum, holding the impressionist works of the Skagen Painters, who drew inspiration from the area’s abundant natural light. To the south lies Råbjerg Mile, Northern Europe’s most prominent migrating sand dunes.

Southern Norway's largest town gathers around a sandy town beach that feels almost Mediterranean on a good summer's day, and a well-preserved old quarter of small white wooden houses, Posebyen, that survived the fires that leveled so much of the rest. A skerry-studded archipelago opens up just offshore for sailing and swimming, while several golf courses take advantage of some of the country's mildest weather. A relaxed, sun-catching counterpoint to the fjords further north.

Oslo is capital, but Bergen is the quintessential Norwegian city. A UNESCO World Heritage site, Bryggen (“the docks”) is filled with carefully preserved wooden buildings. Restored as shops, cafés, and museums, the attractive district looks as though it was lifted from another century. Stroll across Fisketorget, the open-air fish market and allow your senses to take it all in (and be sure to sample some fresh shrimp or smoked peppered mackerel). Ride the funicular to the top of Mount Fløien and admire the sweeping view before heading off to visit composer Edvard Grieg’s birth home.

One of Norway's most photographed fjord villages sits where the Aurlandsfjord meets a valley so steep the railway built to climb it remains one of the world's most dramatic, a switchback ascent past waterfalls to the Stegastein viewpoint high above. The Naeroyfjord beyond, the narrowest fjord in Europe and UNESCO-listed for it, closes in to barely two hundred and fifty meters wide in places. A handful of restaurants serve the valley's own smoked salmon and cured meats. Barely a few hundred people call it home, and the scenery does all the talking.

Located at the mouth of the Oldeelva River at the northern end of the Oldedalen Valley on the southern shore of the Nordfjorden, sits the charming village of Olden. Surrounded by steep mountains, blue glaciers, and bubbling waterfalls, Olden presents abundant kayaking, hiking, and biking opportunities. Olden is your gateway to the Jostedal Glacier, Europe’s largest mainland glacier, part of Jostedal Glacier National Park. Jostedal separates two of the longest fjords in the world, the Sognefjord and the Nordfjord.

The Geirangerfjord is the fjord of the postcards, sheer rock walls streaked by waterfalls with names like the Seven Sisters and the Bridal Veil, abandoned farms still clinging to impossible ledges above the water. A tiny village of a few hundred residents sits at its head, dwarfed by the scenery on every side, with a handful of restaurants serving reindeer and Arctic char to match the view. UNESCO listed the fjord for good reason, few landscapes anywhere compress this much drama into so short a sail.

Norway's medieval capital is anchored by the Nidaros Cathedral, the country's great Gothic pilgrimage church and coronation site for its kings for nearly a thousand years. Below it, the crooked, colorful wooden warehouses of Bakklandet line the Nidelva river, now filled with cafes and small restaurants rather than fish. Beaches and swimming spots dot the fjord just beyond town on a fine summer's day. A quieter, more historic counterpoint to Bergen and Oslo.

Norway’s celebrated archipelago of islands is heralded for its dramatic scenery, with peaks like the Svolvaergeita pinnacle jutting up into the sky. This is where majestic mountains meet brilliantly white sandy beaches, fishing villages dot the coastlines, and hiking trails crisscross their way through some of the most breathtaking landscapes in Norway. Reine, an authentic fishing village in Lofoten renowned for its scenic location by the majestic Lofoten peaks, is your gateway to the Lofoten Islands.

Norway’s celebrated archipelago of islands is heralded for its dramatic scenery, with peaks like the Svolværgeita pinnacle jutting up into the sky. This is where majestic mountains meet brilliantly white sandy beaches, fishing villages dot the coastlines, and hiking trails crisscross their way through some of the most breathtaking landscapes in Norway. Against the backdrop of the midnight sun and small villages, SeaDream overnights in Lofoten.

Nowhere are there fjords to match the grandeur of those in Norway, where the clear water reflects the mountains like a mirror. Sail between soaring granite cliffs and spy mountainside farms, charming villages, and an array of wildlife along this stunning coastline.

If you’re seeking a northern Eden, it doesn’t get much closer than Tromsø, an unhurried city cradled by spectacular fjords and titanic mountains. Among nature’s most magnificent displays, marvel at the nightless days of the midnight sun. Wind along the glasslike waters of the Balsfjorden, Kaldfjorden, Ullsfjorden and Malangen fjords, watching achingly beautiful panoramas unfold as you keep a sharp eye out for seals, eagles and reindeer. In Tromsø, delight in the angular forms of the Arctic Cathedral, which evokes a steep, snow-coated mountain or slabs of ice jutting into the sky. A short distance away, ride a cable car to nearly 1,400 feet above sea level for sweeping views of the town and the intense blues, greens and whites of the surrounding scenery. Examine a unique array of cold-climate plants at the Arctic-Alpine Botanical Garden, which showcases specimens from far-flung lands such as Tibet, and unwind with a cold one at celebrated Macks Ølbryggeri, a local institution that is proud to be “the world’s northernmost brewery.”

ports.name: Sailing through Nordre Isfjorden National Park

voyages.title: High Arctic Svalbard
voyages.overview: Overview Ports Suites Land Adventures Testimonials Embark from Tromsø for Hammerfest, one of the world's northernmost towns and home to the Royal and Ancient Polar Bear Society, then continue to Kirkenes on Norway's Russian frontier and Honningsvåg, gateway to Nordkapp's wind-scoured plateau at 71 degrees north. Sail past the seabird cliffs of Bear Island toward Svalbard, where Barentsburg's Lenin bust and northernmost brewery recall a Soviet outpost, and Pyramiden's abandoned streets stand silent beneath the Nordenskiöld glacier. Cruise the calving face of Adolfbukta and the protected wilds of Nordre Isfjorden and Forlandet, watching for walrus and Arctic fox, before Ny-Ålesund, the world's northernmost year-round settlement, where Amundsen's airship mast still stands. Kittiwakes swirl beneath the peaks of Kongsfjorden, and Magdalenefjord's glaciers calve beside centuries-old whalers' graves. Past the guillemot cliffs of Alkhornet, ending in Longyearbyen, the world's northernmost true town, where polar bears roam beyond the last street lamp under endless summer light.

One of the northernmost towns on earth wears that title with pride, burned to the ground by retreating German forces in 1944 and rebuilt from nothing since. The Royal and Ancient Polar Bear Society keeps the town's Arctic hunting history alive in a small, characterful museum, while the midnight sun keeps the harbor lit through the small hours of a summer night. A working town at the edge of the map, more than a tourist set-piece.

In Norway's far northeast, Kirkenes built its fortunes on iron ore and, more recently, on the king crab that now draws visitors out onto the Barents Sea on dedicated safaris. The town absorbed more Allied bombing than almost anywhere else in Norway during the Second World War and was liberated by Soviet troops in 1944, a history the local war museum tells unflinchingly. Husky kennels and a Snow Hotel built fresh each winter round out a town shaped as much by its remoteness as by its history. A genuine frontier post.

The gateway to the North Cape, the dramatic thousand-foot cliff plateau long billed as continental Europe's northernmost point, sits just a short drive from this small fishing town's harbor. Stand at the globe monument as the midnight sun refuses to set, or scan the surrounding cliffs for the kittiwakes and puffins that nest by the thousand along this stretch of coast. A short evening's sail from the town's own restaurants, where reindeer and king crab share the menu. As far north as most travelers will ever stand on solid ground.

The loneliest island in the Svalbard archipelago rises from the Barents Sea roughly halfway between mainland Norway and Spitsbergen, its cliffs holding one of the largest seabird colonies in the North Atlantic, several hundred thousand guillemots, kittiwakes and puffins nesting on ledges too sheer for almost anything else to reach. Wrecks litter the surrounding seabed, testament to weather that can turn in minutes this far into open water. A handful of Norwegian meteorologists are the island's only residents. About as remote a headland as this itinerary passes.

A working Russian coal town deep inside Norwegian territory, Barentsburg still houses a small community of Russian and Ukrainian miners beneath the world's northernmost bust of Lenin. The Pomor Museum traces centuries of Russian Arctic history, and the settlement's brewery, also the world's northernmost, pours a beer brewed on melted glacier water. A living piece of Soviet-era geopolitics, still functioning in the High Arctic.

A Soviet coal town abandoned wholesale in 1998, Pyramiden stands frozen at the moment its last residents left, a bust of Lenin gazing out over empty apartment blocks, a grand piano still in the culture hall, the world's northernmost swimming pool now drained and silent. Kittiwakes nest in their thousands in the cliffs behind the settlement, and a glacier calves into the fjord within full view of the crumbling waterfront. One of the strangest, most haunting stops in the entire Arctic.

A quiet bay deep inside Billefjorden delivers a full frontal view of Nordenskioldbreen, one of Svalbard's great tidewater glaciers, its blue-white face calving directly into the fjord in front of the ship. The surrounding shoreline holds the remains of early 20th-century coal-mining ventures, abandoned almost as soon as they began, a reminder of how unforgiving this coast has always been. A hushed, ice-fringed anchorage deep in the Arctic interior.

days.port: Sailing through Nordre Isfjorden National Park
days.note: Svalbard's largest system of protected fjords and glaciers unfolds along this stretch, tundra slopes grazed by reindeer running down to water regularly visited by beluga whales and bearded seals. Arctic terns and glaucous gulls wheel over cliffs that see barely any human presence beyond the odd research station. The park protects some of the most complete and undisturbed high-Arctic ecosystems left on the planet, glacier to shoreline to sea.

A narrow strip of national park protects Prins Karls Forland, a mountainous island running parallel to Spitsbergen's west coast, its beaches at Poolepynten home to one of Svalbard's most reliable walrus haul-outs, dozens of the tusked giants often visible hauled out together on the gravel. Glaciers spill from the island's interior peaks directly to the shore. A quiet, wildlife-rich sail along one of Svalbard's least-visited coastlines.

The northernmost permanent settlement on the planet is not a town so much as an international research station, its handful of year-round residents drawn from Norway, Germany, France, China, Japan, Korea, India and beyond. The mast Roald Amundsen used to launch the airship Norge on the first verified flight over the North Pole in 1926 still stands at the edge of the old mining settlement it replaced. Arctic terns dive-bomb visitors who stray too near their nests along the boardwalk. About as far from anywhere as a port call gets.

This broad, glacier-rimmed fjord shares its shores with Ny-Alesund, the world's northernmost permanent settlement, and its waters have made it one of the most studied stretches of coastline in the Arctic. Kongsbreen and Kronebreen, two of Svalbard's most active tidewater glaciers, calve into the fjord in full view of passing ships, while kittiwakes and Arctic terns work the cliffs above. A working laboratory for High Arctic science, and a genuinely spectacular one to sail through.

Dutch and English whalers first anchored in this sheltered bay in the early 1600s, rendering blubber at the shore station of Smeerenburg nearby in numbers that briefly made it one of the busiest, and most brutal, industrial operations anywhere in the Arctic. Wooden grave markers at Gravneset still hold the remains of whalers who never made it home. Glaciers now calve quietly into water that was once slicked with oil, one of Svalbard's most historically loaded, and most beautiful, anchorages.

A distinctive horned mountain marks the entrance to Isfjorden, its lower slopes improbably green for the Arctic thanks to a bird cliff above that fertilises the tundra below, drawing reindeer and Arctic fox to graze where almost nothing else grows this far north. Thousands of Brunnich's guillemots and kittiwakes nest on the ledges overhead. A single mountain that concentrates an entire Arctic food chain into one dramatic headland.

The world's northernmost town with a supermarket, a church and a pub still requires a rifle if you leave the settlement on foot, polar bears roam freely across Svalbard's tundra. Its permafrost is so complete that burial is not permitted, one of the more startling facts you'll pick up at the excellent Svalbard Museum, while the Global Seed Vault sits carved into a mountainside just outside town, a doomsday backup for the world's crops. Former mining infrastructure still threads the hillsides above a settlement now built as much around Arctic research as coal. As far north as ordinary life gets.

voyages.title: Fjords of Greenland, Fires of Iceland
voyages.overview: Overview Ports Suites Land Adventures Testimonials Depart Longyearbyen for Hornsund, Svalbard's grandest southern fjord, where polar bears pad the floe edge and beluga whales surface in milky pods. Continue to lonely Jan Mayen, brooding beneath Beerenberg, the world's northernmost active volcano, reached only by rare permit and favorable weather. The yacht threads Greenland's vast Scoresby Sund, drifting among icebergs beneath the Stauning Alps, before crossing to Iceland's Eastfjords at Seyðisfjörður, its rainbow-painted street leading to a small blue church. Siglufjörður recalls its herring boomtown days at the Herring Era Museum, while Akureyri, the graceful capital of the north, opens onto the thundering falls of Godafoss and the geothermal baths of Lake Mývatn. Ísafjörður, capital of the wild Westfjords, sits cradled by flat-topped mountains and mirror-still water, puffins crowding nearby Vigur island. A grand finale in Reykjavík, the world's northernmost capital, where the soaring Hallgrímskirkja and geothermal pools mark the gateway to Iceland's fire and ice.

days.note: The world's northernmost town with a supermarket, a church and a pub still requires a rifle if you leave the settlement on foot, polar bears roam freely across Svalbard's tundra. Its permafrost is so complete that burial is not permitted, one of the more startling facts you'll pick up at the excellent Svalbard Museum, while the Global Seed Vault sits carved into a mountainside just outside town, a doomsday backup for the world's crops. Former mining infrastructure still threads the hillsides above a settlement now built as much around Arctic research as coal. As far north as ordinary life gets.

Svalbard's southernmost great fjord cuts deep between some of the archipelago's sharpest peaks, jagged summits with names like Hornsundtind rising straight from tidewater glaciers that calve regularly into the sound. A Polish polar research station, staffed year-round, monitors the same glaciers from a small outpost on the shore. Bearded seals haul out on drifting ice, and the fjord's near-total exposure to the open Barents Sea makes a calm transit here a genuine privilege of timing.

One of the most isolated volcanic islands on earth, Jan Mayen is dominated by Beerenberg, the world's northernmost active volcano, its glacier-capped cone rising sheer from the Arctic Ocean. Barely two dozen Norwegian meteorological and military personnel rotate through the island's single station, the only permanent human presence, while its cliffs hold vast colonies of seabirds undisturbed by any real tourism. Landings depend entirely on weather and swell. Few yachts of any size will ever put this island on an itinerary.

The largest fjord system on earth swallows icebergs the size of small buildings, calved from the glaciers that feed it and drifting for weeks through a maze of channels larger than some European countries. East Greenland's dramatic, near-vertical peaks rise directly from water that few ships of any size ever navigate. Polar bears and muskox roam the surrounding tundra, and the sheer scale of the place is almost impossible to process from the deck of anything smaller than a ship, until you are on one.

A rainbow-painted street leads from the harbor straight to a sky-blue church in this East Iceland fjord town, its wooden houses shipped over prefabricated from Norway during the herring boom of the early 1900s. Waterfalls thread down the mountainsides that box the fjord in on both sides, and the town's small but fierce arts scene, born of its long isolation each winter, fills old herring warehouses with galleries and studios. One of Iceland's prettiest, and least crowded, ports.

Once the herring capital of the North Atlantic, its harbor thick with boats and its streets running with silver scales during the boom years, Siglufjordur tells that whole story at the Herring Era Museum, one of Iceland's best. The fjord town, boxed in by near-vertical peaks and only linked to the rest of Iceland by tunnel in recent years, has quietly reinvented itself as a ski and hiking base. A slice of Icelandic industrial history in a strikingly beautiful setting.

The unofficial capital of the north sits at the head of Iceland's longest fjord, ringed by mountains that keep it improbably mild for its latitude. The world's northernmost botanical garden flourishes here against all odds, and a round at the Arctic Open golf tournament is played through the small hours under a sun that never sets. Whale-watching boats head out from the harbor into Eyjafjordur's rich feeding grounds, while the town's geothermal pool and easy, walkable streets make for a gentler pace than Reykjavik's. The north's warm welcome, almost literally.

The capital of the wild, sparsely populated Westfjords sits beneath table-top mountains so steep that avalanche barriers line the slopes above town. Its cluster of eighteenth-century timber buildings are among the oldest in Iceland, and a plate of fish stew at the harborside Tjoruhusid restaurant is something of a rite of passage. Beyond town, the roadless Hornstrandir Nature Reserve shelters one of the world's few protected populations of Arctic fox. Iceland at its most remote and unfiltered.

The world's northernmost capital pairs Nordic design with a landscape that starts changing the moment you leave town. Climb the tower of Hallgrimskirkja for a view over rooftops the color of a paint chart, browse the harbor's design shops and the Harpa concert hall's glass facade, then head out on the Golden Circle to the rift valley at Thingvellir, the eruptive Geysir and the thundering Gullfoss falls. Back in town, a New Nordic tasting menu of Arctic char and skyr caps a day that can just as easily end in a geothermal soak. Small, cool and endlessly photogenic.

voyages.title: Greenland & the Gulf of St. Lawrence
voyages.overview: Overview Ports Suites Land Adventures Testimonials Reykjavik, Iceland's geothermal capital, opens the voyage beneath Hallgrimskirkja's spire and the glass-clad Harpa hall rising above a harbor built for Viking descendants, before a course north into the Arctic. In Tasiilaq, painted timber houses climb beneath Flower Valley as Sermilik Fjord calves icebergs offshore, then thread Prince Christian Sound, a corridor of granite walls and hanging glaciers where waterfalls tumble past the hamlet of Aappilattoq. Granite spired Nanortalik and green Narsaq, overlooked by Erik the Red's Brattahlid, lead to Qaqortoq, its ochre and blue houses tumbling toward the only fountain in Greenland and the rock cut Stone and Man sculptures, a UNESCO listed landscape. Continue to Nuuk, Greenland's capital, where the National Museum's Qilakitsoq mummies meet a fjord system among the world's grandest. Cross to Newfoundland's St. Anthony, gateway to the Norse landfall at L'Anse aux Meadows, then Corner Brook, its UNESCO listed Gros Morne tablelands rising from the Bay of Islands. Glide the dark waters of the Saguenay Fjord before Quebec City's UNESCO ramparts and Old Town welcome you ashore. Your voyage concludes in Montreal, where cobbled Vieux Montreal and the soaring Notre-Dame Basilica close this journey across two worlds joined by ice and stone.

East Greenland's largest settlement is also its wildest, a huddle of timber houses on Ammassalik Island facing a coastline of jagged peaks and pack ice that keeps this side of the country cut off from the world for much of the year. The Tunumiit people here kept a language and a culture distinct from West Greenland well into the twentieth century, still visible in the small museum's carved masks and drum-dance traditions. Icebergs run aground in the bay by the hundred, calved from one of the fastest-moving glaciers on earth. Remote even by Greenlandic standards.

A narrow, glacier-carved channel cuts through the southern tip of Greenland, granite walls rising sheer on both sides in a passage so tight in places that the ship's wake reaches both shores at once. Icebergs calved from glaciers further up the fjord drift through on the current, and the surrounding peaks hold some of South Greenland's most dramatic scenery. A spectacular shortcut around Greenland's southernmost cape.

Greenland's southernmost town takes its name, fittingly, from the Inuktitut for "place of polar bears". Turf-roofed buildings from the old colonial trading post now form an open-air museum on the harborfront, backed by the vertical granite spires of Ketil and Ulamertorsuaq that draw climbers from across the world. Icebergs calved from nearby glaciers drift past the anchorage in slow procession, and Norse ruins from the medieval Eastern Settlement lie scattered across the surrounding fjords. A raw, dramatic first taste of South Greenland.

The largest town in South Greenland gathers around Greenland's oldest fountain, its square ringed by a remarkable open-air gallery, more than forty sculptures carved directly into the surrounding rock faces by artists from across the Nordic world. A short boat ride away, the natural hot springs of Uunartoq Island let you soak in geothermal warmth with icebergs drifting past in the fjord beyond, while the ruined stone walls of Hvalsey Church, the best-preserved Norse building in Greenland and the site of the last written record of its medieval settlers, stand a few miles further on. History, art and a hot spring, in one small harbor.

Ringed by icebergs calved from the Eqalorutsit glacier, Narsaq sits at the gateway to Greenland's Norse country, the ruins of Erik the Red's own farmstead lie a short sail away across the fjord. Sheep farms carved from the same slopes the Vikings grazed still supply the country's wool and lamb, and the town's small brewery, among the world's most northerly, turns out a beer brewed with local glacial water. A geologist's paradise too, the surrounding hills hold some of the rarest mineral deposits on the planet. Understated, but rich in both history and ice.

A scatter of brightly painted wooden houses on a rocky headland, Paamiut is one of Greenland's smallest and least-visited towns, and precisely for that reason one of its most genuine. White-tailed eagles nest along the surrounding cliffs, among the best birdwatching on this coast, while the old colonial buildings and a working fishing harbor show a Greenland unshaped by tourism. Few ships of any size call here. That, more than anything, is the point.

Greenland's small, colorful capital packs Inuit culture and Arctic modernity into a single fjord-side afternoon. Browse the National Museum's mummies and kayaks, then cross to the Katuaq cultural center for contemporary Greenlandic art, before a plate of musk ox or snow crab at one of the country's few fine-dining tables. A round at Nuuk Golf Club, the world's northernmost, plays out beneath jagged peaks and the midnight sun, while a whale-watching run into Nuup Kangerlua fjord is as likely to turn up humpbacks as icebergs. The Arctic's most livable secret.

The unofficial capital of Iceberg Alley, where Arctic ice drifting down from Greenland runs aground each spring in scenes that draw photographers from around the world. Sir Wilfred Grenfell's pioneering medical mission, which brought healthcare to this remote coast in the early 1900s, is remembered at a museum and historic house in town, while L'Anse aux Meadows, the only confirmed Norse settlement in North America, lies a scenic drive up the coast. A hearty Newfoundland kitchen, heavy on cod and partridgeberry, rounds out one of the province's most remote and dramatic corners.

Newfoundland's second city sits on the Bay of Islands, a fjord-cut stretch of coast that Captain James Cook himself surveyed and mapped in the 1760s, well before his Pacific voyages made him famous. Marble Mountain rises straight from the water behind town, its slopes better known today for skiing than for the marble that gave it its name. Golf courses take advantage of some of the most dramatic scenery on the island's west coast. A rugged, unpolished introduction to Newfoundland.

A North Shore port town named for the seven islands that shelter its harbor, home to a scattered Innu community whose culture and history are shown at the town's small but excellent regional museum. The surrounding archipelago's cliffs and islets hold significant seabird colonies, guillemots and eiders among them, largely undisturbed by the iron-ore shipping that built the modern town. A working port with a genuinely wild edge.

Where the Saguenay Fjord, one of the longest in the world outside the Arctic, meets the St Lawrence, cold, nutrient-rich water wells up to create one of the richest whale feeding grounds in eastern Canada, belugas resident year-round, minke and even blue whales through the summer. The town's own dining scene draws on the region's wild blueberries and its distinctive tomme cheese, both genuine points of local pride. Fjord walls rise nearly a thousand feet on either side of the water, some of the most dramatic scenery east of the Rockies.

The only walled city north of Mexico still standing in its entirety, Quebec City's Chateau Frontenac towers over a UNESCO old town of cobbled lanes and 17th-century stone houses that could pass, at a glance, for provincial France. Ile d'Orleans, a short drive across the bridge, supplies much of the region's cider, maple and cool-climate wine, while the city's own Nordic-style spas, built around riverside steam and plunge pools, draw on a wellness tradition as old as New France itself. A beach along the St Lawrence and a genuinely serious dining scene round out North America's most European city.

North America's great bilingual city layers cobbled Old Montreal, its 17th-century stone buildings now home to some of the country's best restaurants, over a modern downtown built for a genuinely serious food and festival culture. The Lachine Canal's bike path and waterfront parks offer an easy afternoon on the water, while the Eastern Townships' vineyards, a short drive out, have quietly become a real source of Quebec ice wine and hybrid varietals. A round of golf on one of the island's historic courses and a stroll through a beach-lined riverfront park round out a city that rewards a slow wander as much as a fine meal.

voyages.title: Great Lakes Icons & New Discoveries
voyages.overview: Overview Ports Suites Land Adventures Testimonials Montreal's cobbled harbor gives way to the locks and lakes of Canada's heartland, the St. Lawrence Seaway threading toward Cornwall, where cycling trails meet the living culture of the Akwesasne Mohawk community. Handsome limestone Kingston, a UNESCO listed city once Canada's capital, opens onto the fabled Thousand Islands before Toronto's skyline rises around the soaring CN Tower and the bustling stalls of St. Lawrence Market. Locking through the Welland Canal, call at Port Colborne, gateway to Niagara's thundering falls and celebrated icewine country, then continue toward Lake Huron. At Sault Ste. Marie, watch towering freighters rise through the historic Soo Locks on the passage into Lake Superior, the largest freshwater lake on Earth. Sail on to Chicago, where SeaDream berths within reach of the Magnificent Mile and the Art Institute's galleries, then dune backed Muskegon, its golden beaches and craft breweries a relaxed change of pace on Lake Michigan's eastern shore. Milwaukee closes the journey through eight locks and five inland seas, German brewing heritage and a lakefront museum beneath Calatrava's soaring wings marking its final port.

days.port: Sailing through the St. Lawrence Seaway
days.note: The seaway's first stretch out of Montreal locks the ship up and over the Lachine Rapids, a natural barrier that stopped explorers for centuries before modern engineering solved it in the 1950s. Farmland and small river towns line the banks as the St Lawrence narrows, while ospreys and herons work the shallows on either side. A gentle, historic introduction to one of the great engineering achievements of the 20th century.

A St Lawrence River town shaped as much by the water as by the Akwesasne Mohawk territory that straddles the border just outside it. The Long Sault Parkway threads a chain of small islands and beaches created when the seaway was built in the 1950s, flooding the villages that once stood here, a history the local museum tells with real care. Ospreys and herons work the river's shallows, and a round of golf on the riverside links rounds out an easy, unhurried call. A quieter corner of the seaway, with a genuinely layered history.

days.port: Sailing through the St. Lawrence Seaway
