Where Lake Ontario empties into the St Lawrence, Kingston's limestone downtown and star-shaped Fort Henry recall its 19th-century role as a British garrison town and, briefly, the capital of the united Canadas. The Thousand Islands begin just beyond the harbor, a favorite among boaters and golfers alike for the scenery as much as the course itself. A strong university-town dining scene and sandy beaches along the lakefront round out a handsome, history-dense stop.

Canada's largest city stacks a genuinely global dining scene, drawn from one of the most diverse populations on the continent, beneath the CN Tower's needle-thin silhouette. The Toronto Islands, a short ferry from the financial district, offer sand beaches and quiet bike paths within full view of the skyline, while the eastern beaches and Rouge National Urban Park shelter a surprising range of migratory birds for a city this size. A round of golf at one of the city's storied courses rounds out a stop that rewards a proper wander through Kensington Market or the distillery district. Big-city energy, with the lake right at its edge.

Eight locks lift the ship more than a hundred meters in a single transit, the engineering solution that lets ships bypass Niagara Falls entirely on their way between Lake Ontario and Lake Erie. Viewing platforms along the canal draw local spectators who track ship movements the way others might follow sports scores, and passing through at deck level, lock by lock, is a genuinely rare vantage point on the whole operation. One of the great working canals of North America, experienced from the water rather than the road.

The southern terminus of the Welland Canal, the engineering marvel that lets ships bypass Niagara Falls entirely, Port Colborne is also the back door to one of North America's most decorated wine regions. The Niagara Peninsula's escarpment vineyards produce an ice wine now served at tables worldwide, alongside a serious and growing list of chardonnay and pinot noir. Herons and egrets work the canal's marshy edges, and a round of golf or a stretch of Lake Erie beach fill out an easy day before, or after, a wine tour proper. Falls-adjacent, without the crowds.

The Rock and Roll Hall of Fame anchors a lakefront that has quietly reinvented itself over the past two decades, its glass pyramid facing Lake Erie beaches busy with paddleboarders on a warm afternoon. The West Side Market, running since 1912, remains one of the best food halls in the Midwest, while migratory birds funnel through the lakefront parks each spring in serious numbers. An underrated stop that rewards anyone willing to look past its old reputation.

days.port: Sailing through Lake Erie & the Detroit River

days.note: The American twin of the two cities straddling the St Marys River, Sault Ste Marie sits beside the Soo Locks, still one of the busiest shipping chokepoints on the Great Lakes, freighters lift and lower here between Superior and Huron in full view of the public boardwalk. A round of golf on the region's forested courses takes advantage of a genuinely underrated stretch of Upper Peninsula scenery. A working border town with serious industrial history on full display.

days.port: Sailing through the Soo Locks & St. Marys River
days.note: The busiest lock system by tonnage in North America lifts and lowers ships between Lake Superior and Lake Huron, a chokepoint the entire Great Lakes iron-ore and grain trade has depended on for well over a century. Twin cities, one Canadian, one American, share the riverbank on either side of the locks. A working piece of industrial history, still very much in daily use.

days.port: Sailing through Lake Huron & Lake Michigan
days.note: Two of the five Great Lakes meet at the Straits of Mackinac, joined so completely that they are technically a single body of water, spanned by one of the longest suspension bridges in the world. Sand dunes rise along the Michigan shore in places, an unlikely desert landscape a stone's throw from some of the coldest water in North America. A long, open-water crossing between two genuinely inland seas.

The city that reinvented American architecture after the Great Fire of 1871 is still best seen from the water, a boat tour past the Wrigley Building and the Marina City towers explains the skyline better than any museum. Millennium Park's Bean and a lakefront that runs for miles of sand beach and bike path show a genuinely livable side to a city of this size, while Montrose Point's Magic Hedge is one of the best migratory birding spots in the entire Midwest. A round of golf on one of the city's lakefront courses and a proper deep-dish dinner round out the visit. Big shoulders, and a genuinely great lakefront.

Lake Michigan's dune coast reaches some of its most dramatic scale here, towering sand hills backing beaches that rival anywhere on the Great Lakes for a proper summer swim. Duck Lake State Park's wetlands shelter a genuinely rich variety of migratory birds, while a round of golf on one of the area's lakefront courses takes full advantage of the dune terrain. A classic, unpretentious West Michigan beach town.

ports.name: Sailing through Georgian Bay, the Lower Lakes & the Welland Canal

voyages.title: Thirty Thousand Islands
voyages.overview: Overview Ports Suites Land Adventures Testimonials Milwaukee's lakefront Art Museum, poised beneath Calatrava's soaring wings, opens onto the quiet inland seas of the Upper Great Lakes. At Escanaba, a coach ride carries you to the preserved nineteenth century ironworking town of Fayette, a harbor too small for any ship to enter directly, while sheltered Harbor Springs opens onto Little Traverse Bay's resort charm. Step ashore on Mackinac Island, where automobiles are banned and horse drawn carriages carry guests past the porches of the Grand Hotel and fudge shops along the harbor, a rare small ship passage into Georgian Bay's scattered thirty thousand islands. Quartzite ridges that once inspired the Group of Seven painters rise above Killarney, and Little Current, hub of the world's largest freshwater island, reveals Anishinaabe craft and culture along the North Channel. At Midland, cruise the island studded bay to Sainte-Marie among the Hurons, a reconstructed seventeenth century Jesuit mission. Your voyage concludes in Toronto, gliding beneath the CN Tower into a cosmopolitan harborfront alive with a hundred cultures.

days.note: No cars have been allowed on this Lake Huron island since 1898, horse-drawn carriages and bicycles fill in instead, a genuine step back into the 19th century the moment you step off the ferry. The Grand Hotel's porch, the longest in the world, has hosted five sitting US presidents, while Fort Mackinac's restored ramparts tell the island's earlier military history. Fudge shops line the main street in numbers that have become something of a local joke, and a round on one of the island's golf courses is played, necessarily, without a golf cart in sight.

A tiny fishing village wedged between Georgian Bay and the white quartzite peaks of the La Cloche range, painted repeatedly by Canada's Group of Seven for the improbable turquoise of its lakes. Killarney Provincial Park's granite ridges and clear water draw paddlers and hikers in equal number, while the village's own Herbert Fisheries, a takeout shack on the water, is something of a rite of passage for boaters passing through. A short but memorable stop between two of Ontario's great cruising grounds.

The gateway to Manitoulin, the largest freshwater island on earth, Little Current's swing bridge is the only road link across the North Channel and a genuine local spectacle when it opens for passing boats. Anishinaabe communities on the island, among them Wikwemikong, keep powwow traditions and craft markets very much alive, while a round of golf or a hike up the Cup and Saucer Trail's cliffs both reward the effort. A relaxed harbor town at the edge of a genuinely singular island.

Midland sits at the edge of Georgian Bay's Thirty Thousand Islands, but its real draw is inland, Sainte-Marie among the Hurons, a painstaking reconstruction of the Jesuit mission built here in 1639, tells one of the earliest and most consequential chapters of contact between European settlers and the Wendat people. Ospreys and herons nest along the bay's granite islets, while a round at one of the area's golf courses and a swim off one of its sand beaches round out the visit. A history lesson with genuinely beautiful water on either side of it.

days.port: Sailing through Georgian Bay, the Lower Lakes & the Welland Canal
days.note: Thirty thousand granite islands scatter across Georgian Bay's eastern shore, a landscape the Group of Seven made famous in Canadian painting, before the route narrows into the locks and canals that link the upper Great Lakes to Ontario and Erie below. Ospreys and loons work the bay's quieter channels, while the transition from wilderness to working canal happens within the space of a single day's sailing. A genuinely varied stretch of Canada's inland waters.

Sailing through Lake Superior & Lake Huron

voyages.title: The Greatest Lake
voyages.overview: Overview Ports Suites Land Adventures Testimonials Toronto's cosmopolitan harborfront falls away toward Lake Ontario's far shore, calling first at Kingston, its UNESCO listed limestone streets and star shaped Fort Henry set among the fabled Thousand Islands. Lock through the Welland Canal to Port Colborne, threshold to Niagara's wine country and thundering falls, then continue to Cleveland, where the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame anchors a revived Lake Erie waterfront. At Sault Ste. Marie, freighters rise and fall through the historic Soo Locks on the gateway to Lake Superior, the greatest of the Great Lakes, before the voyage reaches its wildest stretch. Rossport's sprinkle of islands and hidden waterfalls give way to Red Rock, its towering cliffs framing traditional Ojibwe lands, and Thunder Bay, where the Sleeping Giant watches over a reconstructed fur trading fort and thundering Kakabeka Falls inland. Retracing the lakes toward journey's end, arrive in Detroit along the storied river, its reborn riverfront, world class art museum and Motown's birthplace studios pulsing with the rhythm of an American comeback.

A working lake, still busy with the freighter traffic that built the cities along its shore.

The West Side Market, running since 1912, remains one of the best food halls in the Midwest, while migratory birds funnel through the lakefront parks each spring in serious numbers. An underrated stop that rewards anyone willing to look past its old reputation.

The second-largest of the Great Lakes by surface area holds more freshwater shoreline than almost anywhere else in North America, its eastern side scattered with the limestone islands of Manitoulin and the North Channel. Squalls can build with little warning on open water this large, and the lake has claimed its share of ships over the past two centuries. A genuinely vast, weather-shaped inland sea.

The American twin of the two cities straddling the St Marys River, Sault Ste Marie sits beside the Soo Locks, still one of the busiest shipping chokepoints on the Great Lakes, freighters lift and lower here between Superior and Huron in full view of the public boardwalk. A round of golf on the region's forested courses takes advantage of a genuinely underrated stretch of Upper Peninsula scenery. A working border town with serious industrial history on full display.

days.port: Sailing through the Soo Locks & the Lake Superior North Shore
days.note: The Soo Locks mark the gateway to the largest and coldest of the Great Lakes, and beyond them, Superior's north shore unfolds as rugged, sparsely populated cliffs and boreal forest running for hundreds of miles with barely a town in sight. Bald eagles are a common sight along this stretch, and the lake's sheer scale, deep enough and cold enough to behave like an ocean, has produced its own body of shipwreck lore. Industrial history giving way, quickly, to genuine wilderness.

A tiny fishing village on Lake Superior's rugged north shore, sheltered by the Nicol Islands archipelago just offshore and long favored by artists for the quality of its light. Boat tours wind through the islands' sea caves and cliffs, while the surrounding waters remain some of the cleanest and clearest on the entire lake. A handful of century-old cottages and a strong small-town fishing tradition round out one of Superior's most laid-back stops.

A small Lake Superior town named for the iron-stained cliffs that rise straight from the harbor, laced with shoreline trails that reward the climb with sweeping views over Nipigon Bay. The surrounding boreal forest and wetlands sit squarely within one of the richest birding corridors on the entire Great Lakes, warblers, loons and bald eagles all regular sightings. A rugged, little-visited stretch of Lake Superior's north shore.

Lake Superior's largest Canadian port sits beneath the Sleeping Giant, a peninsula whose silhouette really does resemble a reclining figure from the right angle, and beside the towering grain elevators that once made this one of the busiest ports on the continent. A monument to Terry Fox, whose cross-country run to fight cancer ended nearby in 1980, stands on the lookout above the harbor. Bald eagles and osprey are a common sight along the rugged shoreline. A working Lake Superior city with real natural drama at its edges.

days.port: Sailing through Lake Superior & Lake Huron
days.note: The largest freshwater lake in the world by surface area gives way, at the Straits of Mackinac, to Huron's more sheltered, island-studded waters, a transition between two very different Great Lakes personalities within a single day's sailing. Superior's cold water and open fetch can produce genuine ocean-scale swells, a fact more than one wrecked freighter has learned the hard way. A long crossing that rewards patience with real variety of scenery.

The birthplace of Motown tells its own story at the modest house on West Grand Boulevard where Berry Gordy built an empire, still a genuine pilgrimage for music fans. A riverfront long given over to industry has been steadily reclaimed as parkland over the past decade, while Belle Isle, a park designed by the same landscape architect behind New York's Central Park, shelters a real variety of birdlife within the city limits. A round of golf at one of the region's classic courses rounds out a city very much in the middle of its second act.

voyages.title: Niagara, Prince Edward County & the St. Lawrence
voyages.overview: Overview Ports Suites Land Adventures Testimonials Depart Detroit, its reborn riverfront giving way to Lake Erie, for Put-in-Bay on South Bass Island, where Perry's Victory memorial towers above limestone caves and a convivial harbor best explored by golf cart. Call at Port Colborne, gateway to Niagara's vineyards and icewine cellars, then lock through the Welland Canal before Kingston's UNESCO listed limestone streets open onto the Thousand Islands. Anchor off Picton in Prince Edward County, a peninsula of cool climate vineyards, cider houses and the dune backed sands of Sandbanks, then call at Brockville, the self styled City of the Thousand Islands, where a fairy tale castle rises from the river amid forested islets. Cornwall follows, its revitalised waterfront woven with the living culture of the Akwesasne Mohawk community. Your voyage concludes in Montreal, where the cobblestones of Vieux Montreal and the soaring towers of Notre-Dame Basilica close a week of vineyards, locks and limestone river towns.

This small Lake Erie island still marks the site of Commodore Perry's decisive 1813 naval victory over the British, commemorated by the towering Doric column of the Perry's Victory memorial, one of the tallest monuments in the country. A handful of historic wineries, some dating to the 1860s, make use of the island's mild lake-effect climate, while a round of golf and some of the best birding on Lake Erie round out a small island with an outsized place in American history.

The southern terminus of the Welland Canal, the engineering marvel that lets ships bypass Niagara Falls entirely, Port Colborne is also the back door to one of North America's most decorated wine regions. The Niagara Peninsula's escarpment vineyards produce an ice wine now served at tables worldwide, alongside a serious and growing list of chardonnay and pinot noir. Herons and egrets work the canal's marshy edges, and a round of golf or a stretch of Lake Erie beach fill out an easy day before, or after, a wine tour proper. Falls-adjacent, without the crowds.

Eight locks lift the ship more than a hundred meters in a single transit, the engineering solution that lets ships bypass Niagara Falls entirely on their way between Lake Ontario and Lake Erie. Viewing platforms along the canal draw local spectators who track ship movements the way others might follow sports scores, and passing through at deck level, lock by lock, is a genuinely rare vantage point on the whole operation. One of the great working canals of North America, experienced from the water rather than the road.

Where Lake Ontario empties into the St Lawrence, Kingston's limestone downtown and star-shaped Fort Henry recall its 19th-century role as a British garrison town and, briefly, the capital of the united Canadas. The Thousand Islands begin just beyond the harbor, a favorite among boaters and golfers alike for the scenery as much as the course itself. A strong university-town dining scene and sandy beaches along the lakefront round out a handsome, history-dense stop.

A strong university-town dining scene and sandy beaches along the lakefront round out a handsome, history-dense stop.

A limestone-soil peninsula jutting into Lake Ontario that has, in barely two decades, become one of Canada's most talked-about wine regions, more than forty wineries now share the County's back roads. Sandbanks Provincial Park's dunes, among the largest freshwater dune systems on earth, back onto beaches warm enough for a proper summer swim, while the surrounding wetlands are recognized as an internationally important bird area. A farm-to-table dining scene has grown up alongside the vines. Ontario's answer to Prince Edward Island, with rather more wine.

The self-styled City of the 1000 Islands sits where the St Lawrence widens into a maze of granite islets, many holding nothing more than a single boathouse and cottage. The Aquatarium tells the river's ecology and shipwreck history, several 19th-century wrecks lie preserved and diveable in the clear, cold water just offshore. Ospreys and herons nest along the shoreline, and a round at one of the area's riverside golf courses rounds out a quintessentially Canadian summer call. A thousand islands, and barely a crowd among them.

A St Lawrence River town shaped as much by the water as by the Akwesasne Mohawk territory that straddles the border just outside it. The Long Sault Parkway threads a chain of small islands and beaches created when the seaway was built in the 1950s, flooding the villages that once stood here, a history the local museum tells with real care. Ospreys and herons work the river's shallows, and a round of golf on the riverside links rounds out an easy, unhurried call. A quieter corner of the seaway, with a genuinely layered history.

The Long Sault Parkway threads a chain of small islands and beaches created when the seaway was built in the 1950s, flooding the villages that once stood here, a history the local museum tells with real care. Ospreys and herons work the river's shallows, and a round of golf on the riverside links rounds out an easy, unhurried call. A quieter corner of the seaway, with a genuinely layered history.

North America's great bilingual city layers cobbled Old Montreal, its 17th-century stone buildings now home to some of the country's best restaurants, over a modern downtown built for a genuinely serious food and festival culture. The Lachine Canal's bike path and waterfront parks offer an easy afternoon on the water, while the Eastern Townships' vineyards, a short drive out, have quietly become a real source of Quebec ice wine and hybrid varietals. A round of golf on one of the island's historic courses and a stroll through a beach-lined riverfront park round out a city that rewards a slow wander as much as a fine meal.

ports.name: Sailing through the Strait of Canso

voyages.title: The St. Lawrence, Maine & New England
voyages.overview: Overview Ports Suites Land Adventures Testimonials From Montreal, the St. Lawrence carries the yacht toward Quebec City, its UNESCO listed ramparts rising above the only walled city north of Mexico, then on to Tadoussac, where zodiacs venture into the glacier-carved Saguenay Fjord and cold upwellings at its mouth draw belugas and even blue whales close to shore. Round the Gaspe Peninsula to the pierced rock of Perce and the gannet colonies of Bonaventure Island, and call at Charlottetown, birthplace of Canada, its red sand beaches and Anne of Green Gables farmland unfolding beyond a red brick harborfront. A passage through the narrow Strait of Canso leads to Lunenburg, Nova Scotia's UNESCO World Heritage old town of ochre timber houses above a working fishing harbor. Down East Maine follows: tidal Eastport, granite ringed Bar Harbor beneath Acadia's Cadillac Mountain, workaday Rockland, and Portland, its brick Old Port stacked with acclaimed kitchens and craft breweries. Ending in Boston with the red brick Freedom Trail threading from Paul Revere's house to the Old North Church at the birthplace of a revolution. This voyage offers guests the exclusive opportunity to extend their stay for SeaDream III's Boston Showcase on October 3, 2030, a rare chance to conclude with a celebration of the yacht in her second year of sailing.

A round of golf on one of the island's historic courses and a stroll through a beach-lined riverfront park round out a city that rewards a slow wander as much as a fine meal.

The only walled city north of Mexico still standing in its entirety, Quebec City's Chateau Frontenac towers over a UNESCO old town of cobbled lanes and 17th-century stone houses that could pass, at a glance, for provincial France. Ile d'Orleans, a short drive across the bridge, supplies much of the region's cider, maple and cool-climate wine, while the city's own Nordic-style spas, built around riverside steam and plunge pools, draw on a wellness tradition as old as New France itself. A beach along the St Lawrence and a genuinely serious dining scene round out North America's most European city.

Widely considered the whale-watching capital of eastern Canada, Tadoussac sits exactly where the cold, deep Saguenay Fjord meets the St Lawrence, upwelling currents that draw belugas, minke, fin and the occasional blue whale within sight of the shore. The wooden Indian Chapel here, built in 1747, is the oldest wooden church still standing in North America, and the surrounding sand dunes and cliffs hold a genuinely rich variety of boreal birdlife. A round of golf on the town's small course rounds out one of Quebec's most naturally spectacular stops.

At the tip of the Gaspé Peninsula, where the St Lawrence finally gives way to open ocean, Gaspé is best known for what lies just offshore, the towering sea arch of Percé Rock and, beyond it, Bonaventure Island's colony of more than fifty thousand northern gannets, one of the largest and most accessible in the world. Forillon National Park's cliffs and forest trails ring the peninsula's tip, and the region's small fishing ports still turn out some of Quebec's best seafood. A dramatic, birdlife-rich edge of the province.

Canada's confederation was effectively born in this small Georgian capital, delegates met here in 1864 to first discuss uniting the colonies, a history the handsomely preserved Province House tells in full. Anne of Green Gables country lies a short drive across the island's red-soil farmland to Cavendish's dunes and beaches, while PEI's mussels and oysters, some of the best shellfish in Canada, anchor a genuinely excellent dining scene. Golf courses take full advantage of the island's rolling coastal terrain, and shorebirds crowd the red sandstone cliffs nearby. A small capital with an outsized role in Canadian history.

days.port: Sailing through the Strait of Canso
days.note: A narrow channel separates Cape Breton Island from mainland Nova Scotia here, spanned by a causeway that also, unusually, carries a lock to maintain water levels on either side. Fishing communities line both shores, their fortunes tied for generations to the strait's ice-free, deep-water access to the Atlantic. A short, characterful transit between two of Atlantic Canada's most storied coastlines.

A UNESCO World Heritage waterfront of saltbox houses painted in improbably bright colors, Lunenburg built and launched the Bluenose here in 1921, the racing schooner still pictured on the Canadian dime. Its shipbuilding heritage lives on in a working boatyard and a strong seafood scene built around the same scallop and haddock fleets that still work these waters. One of the best-preserved historic towns in Atlantic Canada, and one of the prettiest.

The easternmost city in the continental United States is the first place the country sees the sunrise each morning, a genuine point of local pride in a town built almost entirely around fishing and aquaculture. The Old Sow, the largest tidal whirlpool in the Western Hemisphere, churns in the bay just offshore, drawing porpoises and seabirds to the nutrient-rich water it stirs up. A small, salt-worn fishing town at the very edge of the map.

The gateway to Acadia National Park, where Cadillac Mountain's granite summit is, for part of the year, the first place in the United States to see the sunrise. Rockbound coastline and spruce forest ring a town built originally as a Gilded Age summer retreat, its grand "cottages" still visible along Frenchman Bay. A lobster dinner on the water, a round of golf at one of the region's classic courses, and some of the best birding on the Maine coast round out New England at its most dramatic.

The gateway to Acadia National Park, where Cadillac Mountain's granite summit is, for part of the year, the first place in the United States to see the sunrise. A lobster dinner on the water, a round of golf at one of the region's classic courses, and some of the best birding on the Maine coast round out New England at its most dramatic.

Maine's self-proclaimed lobster capital also holds the country's densest concentration of lighthouses, several visible from the harbor on a clear day. The Farnsworth Art Museum's collection of three generations of the Wyeth family, painters who made this coast their life's subject, is a genuine draw for art lovers well beyond Maine. A dining scene built almost entirely around the day's catch rounds out a small, working harbor town.

New England's unofficial food capital packs a genuinely serious dining and craft-brewing scene into a compact, cobblestoned Old Port, lobster rolls and oyster happy hours included. Portland Head Light, the oldest lighthouse in Maine, stands sentinel over a rocky shoreline that has changed remarkably little since it was built in 1791. A round of golf on the coastal links and some of the best birding on the Maine coast round out a small city that consistently punches above its weight.

America's most walkable big-city history lesson, the Freedom Trail's red brick line connects the sites of the Revolution in a couple of unhurried hours, from the Old North Church to the USS Constitution still afloat in the harbor. Boston Harbor's islands, a short ferry from downtown, hold surprisingly rich colonies of nesting seabirds for a major East Coast city. A round of golf at one of the region's historic clubs and a plate of the city's famous chowder round out a stop as dense with things to do as it is with history.

voyages.title: Boston Ship Showcase
voyages.overview: Overview Ports Suites Land Adventures Testimonials History and harbor meet in Boston, where the SeaDream III Boston Showcase lands amid centuries of maritime history. This exclusive event closes SeaDream III's passage through Eastern Canada and New England and opens her journey along the Mid-Atlantic and Southern coasts, introducing our newest yacht to one of America's oldest port cities. Access to the Boston Showcase is available only to guests joining the voyage immediately before or after this event. Back-to-back savings are not applicable to Showcase experiences.

voyages.title: The American East Coast
voyages.overview: Overview Ports Suites Land Adventures Testimonials From Boston's Freedom Trail, the course turns for Martha's Vineyard's Oak Bluffs, its gingerbread cottages and antique carousel setting a leisurely island tone, then continue to Newport, where Gilded Age mansions line the Cliff Walk above crashing Atlantic breakers. Sail into New York past the Statue of Liberty as Manhattan's skyline rises to meet the yacht, before Philadelphia's Independence Hall and Annapolis's colonial State House trace America's founding story along the mid-Atlantic. At Norfolk, the battleship USS Wisconsin stands watch over the largest natural harbor on the East Coast, and from Beaufort, North Carolina, tenders carry guests to Shackleford Banks, where wild Banker horses have run free for four centuries. Charleston's church spires and Spanish moss give way to Savannah's leafy, fountain cooled squares, then Florida's St. Johns River city and the Space Coast lead south. Nassau brings the voyage to its close, pastel colonial buildings and the Straw Market's color greeting you at the edge of the Bahamian sea. This voyage offers guests the exclusive opportunity to begin with SeaDream III's Boston Showcase on October 3, 2030 or conclude with the Nassau & Palm Beach Showcases on October 26, 2030, a rare chance to mark either end of the journey with a celebration of the yacht in her second year of sailing.

A round of golf at one of the region's historic clubs and a plate of the city's famous chowder round out a stop as dense with things to do as it is with history.

A whimsical cluster of gingerbread cottages, painted in every color imaginable, rings the campground where 19th-century Methodist revivals once drew thousands each summer, now one of the most photographed streets in New England. The Flying Horses Carousel nearby, running since 1876, is the oldest continuously operating carousel in the country. Beaches, a round of golf and some of the island's best seafood shacks round out a stop that feels, deliberately, like summer frozen in time.

America's Gilded Age built its grandest stage sets here, the Cliff Walk threads between the Atlantic and a run of Vanderbilt and Astor mansions so ostentatious they were called cottages by the families who built them. Newport's sailing pedigree runs just as deep, home to the America's Cup for more than half a century, while a handful of Rhode Island vineyards have quietly built a following well beyond the state. Beaches, birdlife along Ocean Drive and a seriously good raw bar round out one of New England's most storied small cities.

The city needs no real introduction, but a harbor arrival still delivers one of the great skyline views anywhere on earth, the Statue of Liberty and the downtown towers rising together as the ship comes in. Central Park's Ramble is, improbably, one of the best urban birding spots in North America during spring migration, while the city's wellness scene, from rooftop spas to serious longevity clinics, has become as talked-about as its restaurants. A round of golf at one of the metro area's historic courses and a dinner at virtually any table you can name round out a city that still, somehow, exceeds the hype.

The birthplace of American independence keeps the Liberty Bell and Independence Hall exactly where the founders left them, a short walk from a food scene that has quietly become one of the country's most exciting. The Philadelphia Museum of Art's steps are, inevitably, a Rocky pilgrimage for almost everyone who climbs them, while Pennsylvania's small but serious wine country lies a scenic drive beyond the city. Egrets and herons work the wetlands along the Delaware, and a genuinely great cheesesteak rounds out a city with far more to it than its most famous export.

days.port: Sailing through the Chesapeake & Delaware Canal
days.note: A canal first proposed in the 1760s and finally completed in 1829 still shortens the run between the Chesapeake and Delaware bays by hundreds of miles, sparing ships the long and often rough passage around the Delmarva Peninsula. Marshland and quiet waterside towns line much of the route, largely unchanged since the canal's earliest days. A short, historic shortcut linking two of the Mid-Atlantic's great estuaries.

The sailing capital of America gathers around the US Naval Academy's waterfront campus and a handsome colonial State House, the oldest state capitol still in legislative use in the country. Chesapeake Bay blue crab, picked from the shell at a checkered-paper table, is close to a civic religion here, while ospreys and herons work the bay's marshy tributaries in serious numbers. A handful of Maryland's emerging wineries lie a short drive inland. A small, historic town built entirely around the water.

Home to the largest naval base in the world, Norfolk's harbor still moves to the rhythm of the US Atlantic Fleet, a history and a present the excellent Nauticus museum explains in full. The Chrysler Museum of Art holds a genuinely world-class glass collection, a surprise for a navy town, while the Great Dismal Swamp nearby shelters black bears and some of the richest birdlife in coastal Virginia. Beaches and golf courses along the water round out a city defined, quite literally, by its harbor.

North Carolina's third-oldest town keeps a genuinely well-preserved colonial waterfront, and just offshore, wild horses still roam the dunes of Shackleford Banks, descendants, local lore holds, of shipwrecked Spanish mustangs. Blackbeard met his end in these waters in 1718, a history the town's maritime museum tells with real relish, while shorebirds crowd the barrier island beaches nearby. A quieter, history-rich alternative to the Outer Banks further north.

The Lowcountry's grand old lady keeps her cobbled streets and pastel Rainbow Row houses immaculately preserved, a horse-drawn carriage tour past wrought-iron gates and walled gardens is still the classic introduction. Nearby plantations tell a fuller, harder history alongside their architecture and gardens, while championship golf at Kiawah Island and a shrimp-and-grits dining scene now ranked among the country's best round out the visit. Egrets and herons work the surrounding marsh in serious numbers. Genteel on the surface, and increasingly honest about what lies beneath it.

Georgia's oldest city lays itself out around more than twenty live-oak squares, Spanish moss draped overhead, a design that has barely changed since James Oglethorpe founded it in 1733. Bonaventure Cemetery's marble angels and moss-hung avenues, made famous by Midnight in the Garden of Good and Evil, remain one of the South's most atmospheric walks, while Tybee Island's beaches lie a short drive from downtown. A round of golf, a properly slow-cooked Lowcountry dinner and some of the best birding on the Georgia coast round out one of the South's most beautiful cities.

Florida's largest city by area follows the St Johns River for miles of Riverwalk, restaurants and parks, a genuinely underrated stretch of urban waterfront. The Timucuan Preserve protects one of the largest remaining stands of undisturbed coastal marsh in the state, rich with wading birds, while Kathryn Abbey Hanna Park's beach is one of the best and least crowded stretches of sand on the First Coast. A city that rewards visitors willing to look past the interstate exits.

The gateway to Kennedy Space Center, where the launch pads that sent astronauts to the moon still stand a short drive from the pier, ready for a genuinely goosebump-inducing tour. Manatees gather in the warm water canals nearby through the cooler months, while Cocoa Beach's famously consistent surf lies just south. A round of golf on the Space Coast's flat, sunny courses rounds out a stop built as much around the future as the beach.

The Bahamian capital buzzes with colour, pastel colonial buildings, the bustling Straw Market and forts that once guarded against pirates. SeaDream berths in the heart of Nassau yet keeps you clear of the mega-ship throng, so you can slip away to a quiet cove, dive a coral garden with the marina's gear, or sip a rum punch on a powder-soft beach. Climb the Queen's Staircase, sample fresh conch at Arawak Cay, then return aboard as the harbour lights shimmer.

Enter the heart of Africa by visiting the Panther Ridge Conservation Center or get up close and personal with manatees at the Manatee Lagoon. If you’re more into urban sightseeing, visit CityPlace for the top-rated dining, entertainment, and shopping experiences.

voyages.title: Cartagena Gold & the Turquoise Reef I
voyages.overview: Overview Ports Suites Land Adventures Testimonials A roundtrip from Palm Beach, where Henry Flagler's marble-columned Whitehall recalls Gilded Age Florida, sets out for Key West's shuttered Hemingway villa and its six-toed cats, then turns south for Cayman Brac, a speck of some two thousand souls where a forty-metre limestone bluff hides caves once used as hurricane shelter, a call few other ships make. San Andrés answers with the Seaflower UNESCO Biosphere Reserve's sea of seven colours, Johnny Cay's coco loco beneath the palms, and the lilt of Raizal creole English four hundred miles from the Colombian mainland. Cartagena de Indias opens its UNESCO-listed walled city, Getsemaní's street art and ramparts leading to dinner in a colonial courtyard. The Holandés Cays of San Blas follow, more than 350 palm-dotted islets where the Guna alone hold sway, dugout canoes pulling alongside with hand-stitched molas, reached only by a ship this size. Rise through the Gatun locks and glide across rainforest-fringed Gatun Lake transiting the Panama Canal, then wander Panama City's UNESCO-listed Panama Viejo ruins and feast on ceviche at the Mercado de Mariscos. Kayak to Red Frog Beach and snorkel the Zapatilla Cays off Bocas del Toro, wander Carambola's gardens at Roatán's Coxen Hole, home to a UNESCO-recognized Garifuna community, and walk the stilt-built, car-free lanes of Guanaja above the Mesoamerican reef, the world's second largest. Placencia's UNESCO-listed Belize Barrier Reef unfolds through Silk Cayes and Laughing Bird Caye, before Puerto Morelos, its reef just off the beach and a leaning lighthouse in the square, returns you to Palm Beach. This voyage offers guests the exclusive opportunity to arrive early for SeaDream III's Nassau & Palm Beach Showcases on October 16, 2030, a rare chance to open the journey with a celebration of the yacht in her second year of sailing.

America's last island unwinds at yacht pace. Wander Hemingway's shuttered villa and its six-toed cats, sip a cold conch chowder on Duval Street, then join the nightly ritual at Mallory Square as fire-eaters and buskers salute the sinking sun. Because SeaDream III can linger overnight, guests catch that green-flash sunset ashore and still make Fort Zachary Taylor's reef by morning. Key lime pie, of course, is compulsory.

The quietest of the three Caymans, home to more iguanas than people and not a single traffic light. Bloody Bay Wall drops from eighteen feet to well over a thousand within a few fin kicks, one of the Caribbean's most celebrated dives, while the Booby Pond Nature Reserve shelters the region's largest colony of red-footed boobies alongside magnificent frigatebirds. A handful of beach bars and bone-white sand round out an island that has stayed, deliberately, almost exactly as it was.

Colombia's Caribbean outpost dazzles in that famous sea of seven colours. Snorkel the calm pool of La Piscinita among sergeant majors, feel the spray of the Hoyo Soplador blowhole, and boat to Johnny Cay for grilled fish and coco loco beneath the palms. voyages.title: The Bahamas, the Out Islands & Hispaniola
voyages.overview: Overview Ports Suites Land Adventures Testimonials Depart West Palm Beach for Grand Bahama's Taino Beach, then continue to Nassau's pastel waterfront before the ship anchors for a full day at her own fold-out marina, awash in flat turquoise water for swimming, paddleboards, and lunch on deck. In the Exumas, Staniel Cay delivers the sunlit Thunderball Grotto and the swimming pigs of Big Major Spot, while Long Island's Gordon's Beach unrolls three empty miles of sand near the world's deepest blue hole. San Salvador, Columbus's first landfall in the New World, offers wall diving and a quiet out-island calm before Christmas Eve settles over Salt Cay, a UNESCO-listed hamlet of sixty souls, its Georgian salt pans and wandering donkeys unchanged in two centuries. Christmas Day arrives beneath Monte Cristi's soaring El Morro mesa, its Victorian gingerbread town giving way to the bare reef sandbar of Cayo Arena. In Samaná, humpback whales return each winter to calve within sight of Cayo Levantado. Your voyage closes in the UNESCO-listed streets of San Juan, where blue cobblestones and centuries-old forts guard a harbor made for lingering.

If you’re more into urban sightseeing, visit CityPlace for the top-rated dining, entertainment, and shopping experiences.

The Bahamian capital buzzes with colour, pastel colonial buildings, the bustling Straw Market and forts that once guarded against pirates. SeaDream berths in the heart of Nassau yet keeps you clear of the mega-ship throng, so you can slip away to a quiet cove, dive a coral garden with the marina's gear, or sip a rum punch on a powder-soft beach. Climb the Queen's Staircase, sample fresh conch at Arawak Cay, then return aboard as the harbour lights shimmer.

As part of the Exuma Cays, Staniel Cay is a magical corner of the Bahamas. Located south of Nassau, this island is an unsung paradise. Visit the infamous swimming pigs at Pig Beach, where numerous pigs race over to get your attention right above crystal-clear waters. Dive or snorkel in the sun-kissed beaches of Exumas and enjoy local dining options for an exclusive look at the Bahamas’ culture and cuisine.

Colorful coral reefs and serene beaches make Long Island a haven for snorkeling, diving, and bone fishing. Relax under the shade of pine trees at Gordon’s Beach, the southernmost white-sand beach on the island. Explore Long Island from the perspective two of its most impressive natural wonders, the Hamilton Caves, dripping with stalactites, and Dean’s Blue Hole, the world’s second-deepest saltwater blue hole, surrounded by limestone bluffs. The island is also home to St. Mary the Virgin Anglican Church, a now-abandoned stone church constructed by the Spanish in the 1600s and reputed to be the oldest in the Bahamas.

One of the smallest inhabited islands in the Bahamas, San Salvador boasts sparkling inland lakes, reef-filled sea waters, miles of secluded white-sand beaches, and dive sites teeming with sea life. A stone cross on the shores of Long Bay mark Columbus’s landfall on the island; offshore, an underwater monument designates where La Pinta dropped anchor. Pace yourself to the rhythm of the island with a leisurely swim or bike ride around the bay.

Nestled in the southeast Turks and Caicos sits the 2-mile-long island of Salt Cay. With its stretch of white sands fringed by coconut palm trees and a lush rain forest, Blue Lagoon Island—or Salt Cay—offers an idyllic escape. With very few permanent residents and no paved roads, Salt Cay is the quintessential island that has been lost to time. Donkeys, the ancestors of which used to pull carts during the nineteenth century when the island was a main sea-salt producer, now roam freely all over the island. Bygones of the salt salinas, windmills, and old colonial architecture remains around Balfour Town and Dean’s Dock, including Harriott White House. With its rich history packed into a such a small space, the island has been nominated as a UNESCO World Heritage site.

A dusty, little-visited corner of the northwest coast where Dominican history was actually written, Marti and Maximo Gomez signed the manifesto launching Cuba's war of independence here in 1895, and the house still stands. El Morro, the flat-topped headland outside town, is a national park thick with frigatebirds, herons and shorebirds above centuries-old salt flats still worked by hand. The mango harvest and a plate of goat stewed in bitter-orange sauce round out a call that trades resort polish for the real, unvarnished country.

Lying on the northern coast of Samana Bay, Samana is one of the Dominican Republic’s lesser traveled exotic gems. Its natural wonders take the shape of coconut palms contouring the sea, tropical rainforests, brilliant, white-sand beaches hugging the coastline, and charming villages. Discover local markets, dine in seaview restaurants, and perhaps spot some humpback whales. Adventurers can explore the island via ATV tour or by ziplining in Samana Bay.

San Juan, founded in the 1520’s by Spanish settlers, is both the largest city and the capital city of Puerto Rico. A territory of the Unites States, Puerto Rico is comprised of the large main island as well as five smaller islands, including the popular islands of Vieques and Culebra (both ports of call on select SeaDream voyages). SeaDream docks in Old San Juan, the oldest part of the city. Parts of this historic port city are still surrounded by stone walls dating back to the 1500’s. Narrow cobblestone streets, small shops, and points of interest like Cathedral of San Juan Bautista make this charming city a great place to stroll. Guests sailing into or departing from San Juan will enjoy views of Castillo de San Felipe del Morro, a mid- 1700’s Spanish fortress. San Juan Luiz Munoz Marin Airport is approximately a 30-minute drive to the port in Old San Juan. Currency in Puerto Rico is USD.

voyages.title: New Year in St. Barths & the Leeward Islands
voyages.overview: Overview Ports Suites Land Adventures Testimonials Ring in the New Year in St. Barths on this voyage from San Juan's UNESCO-listed old town through the British Virgin Islands, where Norman Island, the very Treasure Island Stevenson imagined, offers a beach party of champagne and caviar on the sand after snorkeling its sea caves. Continue to Spanish Town, gateway to The Baths, where house-sized granite boulders shelter turquoise grottoes, then anchor in North Sound to swim and kayak from the yacht's own marina beneath Virgin Gorda's dramatic peaks. St. Barths follows in full holiday splendor, red-roofed Gustavia wrapped in French style and Riviera glamour, its harbor filling with the world's finest yachts as New Year's Eve gives way to a new year among them. Sail on to San Salvador, Columbus's UNESCO-listed first landfall in the Bahamas, and Nassau's pastel waterfront, pirate forts rising above a bustling Straw Market. Palm Beach closes the voyage, Flagler's marble-columned Whitehall and the couture windows of Worth Avenue the last taste of Gilded Age glamour.

Norman Island is located at the southern tip of the British Virgin Islands. It could very well be the very same island reputed to be the inspiration for Robert Louis Stevenson's pirate novel Treasure Island. It is said that the island was named after a pirate who purchased it at some point during the early 18th century. The island is uninhabited and privately owned by Dr Henry Jarecki. Its area is about 600 acres (2.4 km²), and it is about 2.5 miles (4 km) long. A large harbor is known as "The Bight" offers one of the most protected anchorages in the area. Guests will enjoy some great hiking opportunities as well as snorkeling and scuba diving. Another attractive option may be to check out the Willie T that is generally anchored in the harbor or simply have a beverage at the Pirates Bight Bar.

Nearly every publication written about Virgin Gorda will emphasize the need to visit “The Baths” – don’t miss it! SeaDream generally arrives early and anchors off Spanish Town to give guests an early start to view The Baths before all of the tourists arrive from the neighboring Islands. You may also consider excellent scuba diving options or an opportunity to swim with the dolphins. SeaDream navigates scenically up the coast and arrives in North Sound to anchor just off the Bitter End Yacht Club. Here we offer watersports, land adventures, hiking options with the crew and tenders to the Bitter End! Depending on the voyage, you may also visit Prickly Pear Island for another signature Champagne & Caviar Splash® option with an incredible setting.

Perhaps our most treasured destination in the Caribbean! This small island belonging to the French West Indies has so much to offer our SeaDream guests. Incredible shopping only steps away from the pier. Incredible beaches, resorts, restaurants and activities both day and night. SeaDream has created various land adventures for you to discover the island from sea or land. Ask one of the officers to take you on a hike or bike ride around the island. Another great activity here is to simply relax and watch all of the incredible yachts arriving and departing just off your SeaDream yacht.

The Bahamian capital buzzes with colour, pastel colonial buildings, the bustling Straw Market and forts that once guarded against pirates. SeaDream berths in the heart of Nassau yet keeps you clear of the mega-ship throng, so you can slip away to a quiet cove, dive a coral garden with the marina's gear, or sip a rum punch on a powder-soft beach. Climb the Queen's Staircase, sample fresh conch at Arawak Cay, then return aboard as the harbour lights shimmer.

The combination of urban centers and cultural treasures make Palm Beach the perfect getaway. Enter the heart of Africa by visiting the Panther Ridge Conservation Center or get up close and personal with manatees at the Manatee Lagoon. If you’re more into urban sightseeing, visit CityPlace for the top-rated dining, entertainment, and shopping experiences.

voyages.title: The World Cruise
voyages.overview: Overview Ports Suites Land Adventures Testimonials Six months, three oceans, and more than forty countries. Depart Palm Beach on a once-in-a-lifetime circumnavigation of the entire world aboard SeaDream III, crossing both the Panama and Suez Canals on a route spanning every inhabited continent but Antarctica. Among its many once-in-a-lifetime calls, the moai of Easter Island rise in silent rows across a volcanic landscape few travelers ever reach, and remote Pitcairn, home to the descendants of the Bounty mutineers, ranks among the most isolated inhabited islands on Earth. An inland reach from Callao leads to Machu Picchu, the lost citadel of the Inca high in the Andes, while further along the route lies Komodo, where the last dragons on the planet still roam. The circumnavigation also reaches Petra, its rose-red facades carved into the cliffs of the Jordanian desert. Six months after setting out, the voyage ends beneath a raised Tower Bridge in London, the rarest kind of journey, and rarely offered.

days.note: The combination of urban centers and cultural treasures make Palm Beach the perfect getaway. Enter the heart of Africa by visiting the Panther Ridge Conservation Center or get up close and personal with manatees at the Manatee Lagoon. If you’re more into urban sightseeing, visit CityPlace for the top-rated dining, entertainment, and shopping experiences.

America's last island unwinds at yacht pace. Wander Hemingway's shuttered villa and its six-toed cats, sip a cold conch chowder on Duval Street, then join the nightly ritual at Mallory Square as fire-eaters and buskers salute the sinking sun. Because SeaDream III can linger overnight, guests catch that green-flash sunset ashore and still make Fort Zachary Taylor's reef by morning. Key lime pie, of course, is compulsory.

The quietest of the three Caymans, home to more iguanas than people and not a single traffic light. Bloody Bay Wall drops from eighteen feet to well over a thousand within a few fin kicks, one of the Caribbean's most celebrated dives, while the Booby Pond Nature Reserve shelters the region's largest colony of red-footed boobies alongside magnificent frigatebirds. A handful of beach bars and bone-white sand round out an island that has stayed, deliberately, almost exactly as it was.

Reached only by small craft, this Raizal island floats in a sea the locals count in seven colours. Hike El Pico for a horizon of turquoise reef, kayak the mangroves of McBean Lagoon to Crab Cay, and snorkel the third-largest barrier reef on Earth. Lunch is black crab with breadfruit and coconut rice at a Manzanillo beach shack, reggae drifting on the trade winds. An anchorage the mega-ships will never reach.

Colombia's Caribbean outpost dazzles in that famous sea of seven colours. Snorkel the calm pool of La Piscinita among sergeant majors, feel the spray of the Hoyo Soplador blowhole, and boat to Johnny Cay for grilled fish and coco loco beneath the palms. SeaDream III's shallow draught anchors close to the powder-soft shore, and the Creole-speaking Raizal culture lends every rundown supper a genuine island soul.

An archipelago of jade lagoons and Afro-Caribbean rhythm. From the marina, kayak to Red Frog Beach, snorkel the coral gardens off the Zapatilla Cays, and drift into Dolphin Bay where bottlenose pods surface at the bow. Wade among the cushion sea stars of Starfish Beach, then eat rondon stew in stilt- house Bocas Town. SeaDream III threads between the islands and stays for sunset, something the large ships anchored offshore can only envy.

Perhaps the voyage's most magical call: 350-odd palm-dot cays governed by the indigenous Guna themselves. Anchor off a single-palm islet, wade waist- deep to a sandbar with nothing but sea in every direction, and snorkel warm shallows over starfish. Buy intricate hand-stitched molas direct from Guna women and share fresh-caught lobster grilled on the beach. No jetty, no crowds, no big ship can enter, only a yacht like SeaDream III.

One of travel's great set-pieces, savoured from your own sun deck. Watch SeaDream III rise in the mighty Gatun locks, glide across the rainforest-fringed Gatun Lake past freighters queuing for their turn, then thread the sheer rock of the Culebra Cut. A canal historian narrates as howler monkeys call from the banks and the Bridge of the Americas marks the Pacific. An engineering wonder, experienced intimately rather than from a distant rail.

Cosmopolitan Panama City rewards a lingering stay. Stroll the restored plazas of Casco Viejo for rooftop cocktails against a skyline of glass towers, trace the colonial ruins of Panama Viejo, and take in Frank Gehry's kaleidoscopic Biomuseo on the Amador Causeway. Feast on just-landed ceviche and cold Balboa beer at the Mercado de Mariscos. Berthed at Fuerte Amador, SeaDream III sits minutes from the old town, not an hour's coach away.

An uninhabited Pearl Island of talcum sand and warm turquoise, where television's Survivor once pitched camp. Drop the watersports marina and kayak, paddleboard or snorkel over coral straight from the swim platform, then laze on a beach with only your fellow guests for company. These waters made Panama's colonial fortunes in pearls; from July to October humpback whales breach offshore. A castaway idyll no large ship can access.

Often called the Galapagos in miniature, this island off Machalilla delivers the wildlife without the airfare. Trek the clifftop trails past comical blue- footed boobies nesting at your feet, watch frigatebirds inflate scarlet throats, and spot Nazca boobies on the wing. Back aboard the tender, snorkel clear water alive with sea turtles and tropical fish. SeaDream III anchors right in the bay, delivering guests ashore before the day boats arrive.

Ecuador's vibrant river-port capital of commerce. Amble the palm-lined Malecon 2000 boardwalk, climb the 444 painted steps of Santa Ana hill through the bohemian Las Penas quarter, and share Parque Seminario with its resident troop of land iguanas. This is the cradle of the world's finest cacao, so a tasting of single-origin Ecuadorian chocolate is a must. A lively, characterful counterpoint to the coastline's wild anchorages.

Peru's north coast is a pageant of vanished civilisations. Walk Chan Chan, the largest adobe city ever built and capital of the Chimu, then marvel at the polychrome friezes of the Moche Huacas of the Sun and Moon. At Huanchaco, fishermen still ride the same curved reed caballitos de totora their ancestors paddled 3,000 years ago. In Trujillo's colonial plaza, a marinera dance and fresh ceviche complete the day.

Gateway to Lima, the undisputed gastronomic capital of the Americas. Book a table at a World's-50-Best temple such as Central or Maido, then walk off the tasting menu along Miraflores' cliff-top Malecon and through bohemian, mural-splashed Barranco. The Larco Museum's pre-Columbian gold and erotic ceramics astonish, while the perfect pisco sour is a civic duty. SeaDream III's overnight berth lets guests dine late and linger.

The desert meets a sea teeming with life. Cruise by launch to the Ballestas Islands, where Humboldt penguins, sea lions and thousands of seabirds throng guano-white rocks past the giant Candelabra geoglyph. Explore the ochre cliffs and flamingo lagoons of the Paracas National Reserve, taste pisco at a colonial-era bodega, or fly out over the enigmatic Nazca Lines. Vivid, cinematic and utterly unlike anywhere else on the coast.

Chile's northern frontier, where the Atacama, the driest desert on Earth, tumbles to the Pacific. Climb El Morro headland for sweeping ocean views and its stirring war history, admire the prefabricated San Marcos Cathedral engineered by Gustave Eiffel, and meet the Chinchorro mummies, older than Egypt's pharaohs. Drive the Azapa Valley for plump olives and geoglyph-etched hillsides. The doorstep to the great desert beyond.

A duty-free beach city framed by a colossal wall of desert dune. Wander the timber mansions and boardwalks of Baquedano Street, relics of the nitrate boom, then step into the eerie saltpetre ghost town of Humberstone, silent since the works closed. Adrenaline-seekers paraglide from Cerro Dragon straight down onto Cavancha beach. Sun-lounging, history and thrills, all within easy reach of SeaDream III's berth.

The capital of Chile's mineral north opens onto the surreal Atacama. Photograph La Portada, the great sea-carved stone arch rising from the surf just up the coast, then venture inland toward salt flats, flamingo lagoons and the clearest day skies on the planet, home to the ALMA observatory. It is also the natural launch point for San Pedro de Atacama's lunar valleys. A frontier of extraordinary light and space.

Twin city to genteel La Serena and the gateway to the fabled Elqui Valley. Wind inland past vineyards to Pisco Elqui, tasting the grape brandy at its source, then stay after dark for stargazing at Mamalluca, beneath some of the darkest, clearest skies on Earth. By day, stroll La Serena's neo-colonial streets and long Pacific beaches, or the Cross of the Third Millennium. SeaDream III's late stay makes those legendary starlit days possible.

Chile's bohemian port tumbles down forty-odd hills in a mosaic of tin-clad houses, groaning funiculars and Latin America's boldest street art. Ride the century-old Ascensor Reina Victoria up to Cerro Alegre, lunch among the ghosts of poets at Pablo Neruda's La Sebastiana, then slip inland to the Casablanca Valley for Sauvignon Blanc drawn straight from the barrel. As your world voyage begins, the intimacy of just 230 guests turns a UNESCO labyrinth into your own unhurried discovery.

Here reality out-storied fiction: castaway Alexander Selkirk survived four years alone on this Juan Fernandez isle, seeding Defoe's legend. Trek to Selkirk's Lookout, the very saddle from which he scanned an empty horizon for rescue, dive for the prized spiny lobster, and seek the ruby-throated Juan Fernandez firecrown, a hummingbird found nowhere else on earth. With the marina folded open, kayaks and Zodiacs reach coves no large ship could ever consider.

Among the planet's remotest specks of land, Alejandro Selkirk lies a further 180km out to sea, its basalt cliffs rising sheer from the swell where fur seals haul out and petrels wheel overhead. Fewer travellers have set foot here in a decade than crowd a single big-ship gangway on any morning. Anchoring offshore, SeaDream III lowers her watersports marina so you can Zodiac beneath cascading waterfalls and snorkel water so clear it seems lit from below.

Nowhere on earth feels quite so far beyond as Rapa Nui. Stand before the fifteen restored moai of Ahu Tongariki at dawn, their monolithic backs to a molten Pacific; wander the Rano Raraku quarry where half-carved giants still sleep in the volcanic tuff; and climb to Orongo's birdman village perched on the rim of a crater lake. An overnight at anchor lets you savour a Polynesian umu feast ashore long after the day-trippers' flights have lifted away.

A near-perfect ring of coral at the very edge of the Pitcairn group, uninhabited Ducie is one of the least-visited atolls on the planet. Its glassy turquoise lagoon and rubble islets shelter tens of thousands of seabirds, including the world's largest colony of Murphy's petrel, while species found nowhere else patrol the reef. Only a small yacht carrying her own tenders can pause here at all, gifting you a raw wilderness that few living souls will ever witness.

Home to just a few dozen souls, every one descended from the Bounty mutineers and their Tahitian companions, Pitcairn is Britain's remotest inhabited outpost. Dive on the Bounty's anchor and cannon in Bounty Bay, share a table with families whose surnames trace straight back to 1790, and hike to Christian's Cave, where Fletcher himself once brooded over the horizon. Landing depends on the swell and a longboat, an arrival earned rather than merely booked.

The Gambier's serene lagoon, ringed by jagged emerald peaks, is the cradle of Tahiti's legendary black pearl. Marvel at the coral-and-shell Cathedral of St Michael, raised by Pere Laval's converts to seat more worshippers than the whole archipelago's population, then visit a family pearl farm to watch the nacre lifted dripping from the water. Overnighting here, you trade the crowds of Tahiti for a lagoon that feels entirely, unhurriedly your own.

One of the largest atolls in the Tuamotu chain, Hao is entered through the dramatic Kaki pass, where the tide sluices like a river and the drift-snorkeling is exhilarating. Once a remote French support base for Pacific testing, it has settled back into a sleepy world of coconut groves, pearl farms and stalking reef herons. From the swim platform, kayak the shallow flats and cast for bonefish before an evening ashore among genuinely welcoming villagers. Swimming and non-motorized craft only here; motorized watersports need the local authority's permission. Discover with SeaDream.

A UNESCO Biosphere Reserve, Fakarava is diving legend made real. At the southern Tumakohua pass, hundreds of grey reef sharks hang motionless in the current, the famous wall of sharks that draws divers from across the globe. Snorkel powder-pink motu, watch manta rays glide the shallows, and toast the day with oysters straight from the pearl farm. SeaDream's shallow draught and marina put this fragile paradise within reach, well away from the fleets of liveaboards.

Polynesia's beating heart, Papeete rewards the curious. Lose an hour in the Marche de Papeete amid tiare garlands, vanilla pods and iridescent black pearls; trace Gauguin's palette and Bougainville's landfall at Pointe Venus, with its black-sand beach and white lighthouse; then dine dockside at the beloved roulottes as ukuleles drift on the warm day air. Berthed in the very center, your yacht becomes a serene retreat from the island's lively pulse.

Moorea is the postcard Polynesia dreams of: two cathedral bays, Cook's and Opunohu, gouged deep between spires of green. Climb by 4x4 to the Belvedere lookout above the pineapple plantations, snorkel with blacktip sharks and stingrays in warm waist-deep shallows, and watch the last light soften the ridgeline of Mount Rotui. From the marina you can paddleboard straight off the yacht across a lagoon the color of melted turquoise.

The most famous lagoon on earth still stuns in the flesh, Mount Otemanu's basalt fang rising sheer above water banded jade, teal and sapphire. Snorkel the coral gardens, glide alongside manta rays and blacktips, and circle the island by tender to grasp it's impossible palette. As evening falls the day-boats melt away, and at anchor with the marina open, SeaDream III lets you swim in that legendary water beneath a sky set ablaze with stars.

Many seasoned travelers call Aitutaki's lagoon the loveliest in the South Pacific, a vast triangle of impossibly pale water freckled with fifteen motu. Wade ashore at One Foot Island for a passport stamp on a bare sandbar, snorkel among giant clams with lips of electric blue, and picnic where the only footprints are your own. Small enough to slip inside where big ships must anchor far offshore, your yacht makes this Eden feel wholly private.

One of the world's smallest nations and a single upthrust slab of coral rock, Niue has almost no beaches, and needs none. Its magic lies below: clamber through the Talava sea arches, swim the sunlit Limu Pools, and squeeze into chasms where shafts of light pierce water of near-unreal clarity, visibility often beyond seventy meters. In season, humpback whales calve so close to shore that you may catch their song while snorkeling straight from the swim platform. Swimming and non-motorized craft only here; motorized watersports need the local authority's permission.

days.port: International Date Line - Lose a Day

days.note: Vava'u is one of a mere handful of places on earth where you may lawfully swim alongside humpback whales, hovering beside a mother and her calf in warm blue water, an encounter that leaves grown travelers in tears. Between swims, thread the maze of forty-odd islands, snorkel into Swallows' Cave and dive the hidden air pocket of Mariner's Cave. Carrying her own tenders, SeaDream III slips through channels the big ships simply cannot enter.

Fiji's lively capital wears its history in colonial verandahs, Indo-Fijian curry houses and the superb Fiji Museum, keeper of the Bounty's rudder and relics of the cannibal era. Take part in a welcoming sevusevu kava ceremony, browse the teeming municipal market heaped with chilies and yaqona root, then escape to the rainforest pools and birdsong of Colo-i-Suva. This is the human, cultural heart of your Pacific crossing, warmly and vividly alive.

Set on a horseshoe harbor, Port Vila blends Melanesian custom with French savoir-faire. Swim the aquamarine Blue Lagoon, stand beneath the triple- tiered Mele Cascades, and sit cross-legged in a kastom village for a string-band welcome and a shell of famously potent kava. Snorkel straight from the marina over technicolor reef and wreck-strewn shallows before a French-Pacific dinner ashore, a fitting and flavor-rich finale to your voyage.

Cairns is your threshold to the Great Barrier Reef, a short run out to the outer-reef pontoons and the best snorkeling in Australia. Snorkel the coral gardens of the outer Agincourt Ribbons, drift past clownfish and reef sharks, then trade the sea for the world's oldest rainforest at Daintree, where cassowaries stalk the Kuranda canopy. Toast the day with a chilled Margaret River white as the tender returns. Big ships queue at the pier; you simply dive in.

Lizard Island is the Reef's most exclusive outpost, twenty-four powder-white beaches ringing a granite isle few vessels can reach. Dive the legendary Cod Hole to meet potato cod the size of a Labrador, or snorkel the giant clams at Watsons Bay straight from the swim platform. Hike to Cook's Look for the panorama that showed Captain Cook his escape through the reef. With just 230 aboard, the anchorage feels like your own private atoll. Swimming and non-motorized craft only here; motorized watersports need the local authority's permission.

Where the Coral Sea meets the Arafura, tiny TI is the beating heart of the Torres Strait. Climb to Green Hill Fort for its old guns and a 360-degree island panorama, trace the boom-and-bust saga of the pearling luggers, and feel the distinct Melanesian pulse of Islander song and dance. A crossroads of empires and oceans that only a nimble, shallow-draught small ship can comfortably reach and truly savor.

Merauke is Indonesia's wild south-eastern frontier, a place almost no cruise ship ever calls. Venture into Wasur National Park, the Serengeti of Papua, where agile wallabies bound across savannah studded with cathedral-like termite mounds and flocks of magpie geese darken the sky. Meet the Marind people, whose bird-of-paradise dances predate any map. This is the raw edge of the archipelago, reached only because a small yacht can go where the big itineraries dare not.

Dili wears its history openly: Portuguese pastel facades, the soaring Cristo Rei statue watching over the bay, and museums that tell Timor-Leste's hard- won independence. But the real prize lies offshore at Atauro Island, whose reefs were crowned the most biodiverse waters on Earth, richer in reef-fish species than anywhere yet surveyed. Drop the marina and snorkel walls ablaze with color, then sip single-origin Timorese coffee ashore. A frontier nation, met on its own terms.

The waters around Labuan Bajo hold some of the richest reef life in Indonesia, with Komodo dragons roaming the islands deeper in the national park. Trek across Komodo Island's dry hills to find them in the wild, then cool off with a swim over coral gardens thick with manta rays and turtles. Padar's summit trail is worth the early start for the view alone, three bays of different colored sand spread out below. A day here moves from dragons to reef to a hilltop panorama, all within the same park.

Pulau Kenawa is barely more than a green hill rising from coral shallows off Sumbawa: uninhabited, roadless and impossibly serene. This is a marina day made in heaven, all kayaking along mangrove fringes, paddleboarding glassy turquoise flats and snorkelling a house reef flickering with parrotfish. Climb the lone grassy summit at golden hour for a 360-degree sweep of the Flores Sea, then watch the sun melt away from the aft deck. An island too small for any ship but yours.

Benoa opens the whole of Bali to you. Watch the sun drop behind the sea-cliff temple of Uluwatu as barefoot dancers stamp out the hypnotic Kecak fire ritual, or rise early for the mirror-calm Tegallalang rice terraces above Ubud. Wander incense-scented temple gates, browse the silver workshops of Celuk, and feast on crackling babi guling. Back aboard by evening, you sidestep the resort crowds who never see Bali empty. The Island of the Gods, on your schedule.

Semarang is your gateway to Borobudur, the largest Buddhist monument on Earth: a mountain of grey volcanic stone crowned with bell-shaped stupas, best met at sunrise as mist lifts off the Kedu plain and 500 serene Buddhas emerge from the haze. Pair it with the soaring Hindu spires of Prambanan, then stroll Semarang's Dutch colonial Old Town and its candy-pink Blenduk church. It's a long, rewarding day inland, and you return to your own suite rather than a hotel.

Just off frenetic Jakarta lies its antidote: the Thousand Islands, a scatter of palm-topped coral cays within a national marine park. Anchor over clear shallows to snorkel bright reef gardens and visit the turtle hatchery on Pramuka, or step ashore at Onrust to explore the ruins of a 17th-century Dutch East India fortress. Drop the marina for a lazy afternoon of paddleboards and swimming in bathwater-warm seas. A castaway idyll a world away from the megacity's roar.

Kuching is Borneo at its most beguiling, a graceful riverfront city of white rajah forts and golden domes. Journey to Semenggoh to watch semi-wild orangutans swing in for the morning feeding, or trek Bako National Park's mangrove boardwalks in search of the pot-bellied, big-nosed proboscis monkey found nowhere else on Earth. Visit an Iban longhouse, then feast on tangy Sarawak laksa at the day market. The rainforest island of legend, explored and back aboard by nightfall.

Brunei is the last of the old sultanates: fabulously wealthy, serene and green. Glide by boat through Kampong Ayer, the world's largest water village, a labyrinth of stilted houses on the Brunei River, then marvel at the gold-domed Omar Ali Saifuddien Mosque mirrored in its own lagoon. Take a small- boat safari up the mangrove creeks to spot proboscis monkeys and saltwater crocodiles at dusk. A gilded, unhurried realm that few travellers ever reach.

Kota Kinabalu sits between jungle-clad Mount Kinabalu, Borneo's granite giant, and a necklace of coral islands just offshore. Drop the marina and tender to the Tunku Abdul Rahman park to snorkel over clownfish and drift past reef sharks, or venture inland to canopy walkways and roaring waterfalls beneath the sacred peak. Time it for KK's famously fiery sunset over the South China Sea, cocktail in hand on the aft deck. Borneo's wild beauty, in effortless comfort.

Puerto Princesa sits between two very different worlds, inland limestone mountains hiding the Underground River, a navigable cave system running eight kilometers beneath the rock and ranked among the New7Wonders of Nature, explored by boat past stalactites and monitor lizards watching from the forest above the entrance. Sabang, the river's gateway, offers its own detours, from a calm mangrove paddle to a more physical climb and rappel through the limestone caves at Ugong Rock. Closer to the city, Honda Bay scatters small islands good for a half day of swimming and snorkeling, while Puerto Princesa itself, often called the cleanest and greenest city in the Philippines, adds a baywalk, a strong local food scene, and nearby pearl farms producing Palawan's signature golden south sea pearls. Few ports offer this much range in one call, ancient geology, open water, and everyday city life, all within reach of the ship.

El Nido is desktop wallpaper made real: towering black limestone karsts erupting from jade lagoons across Palawan's Bacuit Bay. This is the marina's finest hour. Kayak into the Big Lagoon's cathedral of cliffs, snorkel Secret Lagoon through a crack in the rock, and paddle to talcum-soft strands reachable only by tender. Sea turtles graze the seagrass while sea eagles wheel overhead. A big ship can only gaze from afar; you drop anchor and slip right in.

Boracay's White Beach is regularly voted the finest strand in Asia: four kilometers of flour-soft, blindingly white sand lapped by luminous turquoise. Anchor offshore and let the marina come alive, diving Crocodile Island's coral walls, kitesurfing the breezy eastern shore, or snorkeling the quieter reefs off Puka Beach. As evening falls, sail a traditional paraw outrigger into a tangerine sunset, then retreat to your suite while the beach bars fill. Paradise, minus the queues.

Glide into Victoria Harbour as the skyline ignites, SeaDream III overnights here, so the Symphony of Lights becomes your private nightcap from the deck. Ride the century-old Star Ferry at dusk, hunt Michelin-starred dim sum in Central, then take the funicular up Victoria Peak for the whole city laid out at your feet. A dawn sampan through Aberdeen's floating village and a fitting with a bespoke tailor round out a port that rewards those who stay long past sundown.

Hainan is China's tropical secret, palm-fringed Yalong Bay, jade-green shallows and a warmth that feels a world away from the mainland. Head out to Yalong Bay to swim or kayak from the beach concession. Ashore, stand beneath the towering Guanyin statue at Nanshan, soak in mineral hot springs, then sip fresh coconut on sands most Western travellers never reach. It is the resort coast the guidebooks forget.

Few ships can linger where SeaDream III can, anchored among Ha Long Bay's thousands of emerald limestone pinnacles, far from the day-tripper flotillas. Kayak into hidden grottoes and floating fishing hamlets, then watch mist curl around the karsts at first light with a coffee in hand. Overnight at anchor and this UNESCO seascape belongs, for a few golden hours, almost entirely to you.

Come ashore at Da Nang for two of Vietnam's great treasures. By day, explore the cave-temples of the Marble Mountains and the jungle-clad Cham ruins of My Son; by dusk, wander Hoi An's lantern-lit lanes, where silk tailors stitch to measure and street kitchens perfume the day air. Order a bespoke suit at breakfast and collect it before you sail. China Beach's golden sands await in between.

Saigon assaults the senses in the best possible way, a million motorbikes, French-colonial grandeur and rooftop bars above the fray. Trace the country's history at the Cu Chi tunnels and the War Remnants Museum, then barter through Ben Thanh Market for silk and spice. Cross into the Mekong Delta by sampan for floating markets and fruit orchards. Return to SeaDream's calm at day, the day's intensity happily left ashore.

From the port, plunge into the glorious chaos of the City of Angels. Watch dawn gild the spires of the Grand Palace and the reclining Buddha at Wat Pho, then trade tuk-tuks for a long-tail boat threading the khlongs to the flower and fruit markets. As day falls, a rooftop bar and a private table of som tam, massaman and mango sticky rice await. With overnights aboard, you savor Bangkok's cool evenings without ever repacking a bag.

Thailand's original royal retreat trades big-city buzz for genteel seaside charm. Stroll the palm-lined beach and the atmospheric old fishing-jetty cafes, browse the artful Cicada day market, or tour Monsoon Valley's improbable tropical vineyards with a chilled glass in hand. It is refined, unhurried Thailand, a graceful match for an intimate yacht that favors the roads less travelled. Discover with SeaDream.

Forty-two emerald islands rise sheer from the Gulf of Thailand, and there is no pier here, only anchorages that SeaDream III was built for. Kayak from the swim platform to the hidden Emerald Lagoon, climb to the panoramic viewpoint that inspired the novel The Beach, then snorkel turquoise shallows and picnic on a sandbar all your own. A day of raw natural drama, reachable only by those who arrive by sea. Swimming and non-motorized craft only here; motorized watersports need the local authority's permission. Discover with SeaDream.

Samui greets you with swaying coconut palms and the serene golden gaze of the Big Buddha above the bay. Laze on Chaweng's fine sand, browse Fisherman's Village at Bophut where old teak shophouses become a Friday walking street, or retreat to a hilltop spa for a traditional Thai massage. Chase jungle waterfalls inland, then let SeaDream's marina turn the warm Gulf into your private playground.
